News.title: Indonesia hit by 6.2 magnitude earthquake on volcano-filled island Java
News.content:
Indonesia hit by 6.2 magnitude earthquake on volcano-filled island Java

The latest tremor came a day after another magnitude 6.2 earthquake struck the Banda Sea near Indonesia’s Maluku Island on Friday, September 11

View 2 Images Borobudur in Java, Indonesia (Image: Getty Images)

Indonesia has been struck by a magnitude 6.2 earthquake at a depth of 376km, it has been announced.

‌



The earthquake was confirmed in Java by ⁠the German Research Center for Geosciences (GFZ) on Saturday, September 12.

‌



The latest tremor came a day after another magnitude 6.2 earthquake struck the Banda Sea near Indonesia’s Maluku Island on Friday. That quake occurred at a depth of 143 km (89 miles) and had no tsunami potential, according to Indonesia's geophysics agency.

‌



Java is an island which lies between Bali and Sumatra and is dotted with volcanoes. It is described as a the geographic and economic centre of Indonesia and is home to more than half of its population.

View 2 Images Mount Merapi spews lava onto its slopes during an eruption as seen from Srumbung village in Magelang, Central Java, on November 4, 2024. (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

The quake was recorded about 115km (71 miles) north-east of Teluknaga, on the island of Java, the USGS said.

There were no immediate reports of damage or casualties.

This is a breaking news story - more to come.

News.title: Mum-of-two's body found in park as her sister issues heartbreaking message to killer
News.content:
Mum-of-two's body found in park as her sister issues heartbreaking message to killer

Mum-of-two Natasha Connors Kernan, 29, was found dead in Ravensdale Park, Dublin, on August 25, with gardaí treating her death as murder

View 3 Images Natasha Connors Kernan (left) and her sister Kym Kernan

The sister of a 29-year-old woman whose body was found in a park has called on the person responsible to "own up to what you did" in a heartbreaking plea.

Mum-of-two Natasha Connors Kernan was found dead in Ravensdale Park, Dublin, on August 25. Gardaí (Irish police) are now treating her death as murder.

Speaking to the Irish Mirror on Friday, Natasha's sister Kym Kernan, 28, appealed directly to the person responsible, saying: "Own up to what you did. You took a daughter, mother, you took a sister, you took a loved one. We need to know what happened to her, and if anyone saw anything, just please say it.

"Don’t keep it in because it’s not like we can get her back. We need to know what happened to her because we need to grieve in the way we need to."

View 3 Images The body of Natasha Connors Kernan was found in Ravensdale Park in Kimmage, Dublin, on August 25 (Image: Collins Photo Agency)

Kym described her sister as a devoted mother with a "bubbly" personality. "We are all destroyed over what happened. She was my best friend. I grew up with her my whole life," she said. "My sister was bubbly. No matter what room she went in, she would light it up."

Natasha was a mother to two young children, a girl and a boy, who have been left devastated by her death, Kym said. "My niece is destroyed. She was a mammy's girl, and she's destroyed," she said.

Kym said she struggled to explain Natasha's death to her niece, telling her that her mother had been in the park and fallen and hit her head. "I didn't know what way to tell the story. It's not an easy thing to do," she added.

View 3 Images Natasha Kernan Connors was 'so lovable'

Kym said she received a phone call from her father's girlfriend telling her that her sister had died. "It didn’t feel real and it still doesn’t. I don’t think it’s going to feel real until I find out who did this to her and why," she said.

The grieving sister said the fact Natasha was found in a park near Crumlin "made no sense", pointing out that her sister had been staying at her father's girlfriend's home and "was not homeless".

Kym added that she could not think of anyone who would want to harm her sister. "Everyone loved my sister. She was so lovable," she said.

Following Natasha's death, a video circulated on social media in which her mother, Yvonne, was seen standing between individuals who falsely claimed that her daughter's death was caused by a migrant.

Yvonne has since denounced the claims as false, and Natasha's sister has revealed that the family were told from day one that an Irish man was responsible for her death.

Kym said: "With my mam's situation, my mam is vulnerable enough without all this, and she was pushed into that. We were told way before that it wasn't a migrant.

"We were told from the get-go that it was nothing to do with migrants. I was disgusted. Two of my brothers are Muslim, and I'm sick of the fact that migrants are blamed for everything."

News.title: Giant 'very offensive' shark on Brighton crazy golf course sparks furious planning row
News.content:
Giant 'very offensive' shark on Brighton crazy golf course sparks furious planning row

The 9.5m-tall fake shark hangs from a gallows-like structure over one of Jungle Rumble Adventure Golf's pirate-themed holes on Brighton seafront – but an objector has called the depiction "very offensive"

View 5 Images The giant fake shark has been branded 'very offensive'

A towering 9.5-metre fibreglass shark on a crazy golf course has sparked a planning dispute - after complaints it unfairly portrayed the species as "criminals".

‌



Jungle Rumble Adventure Golf installed the eye-catching feature at its Brighton seafront venue back in August last year, where it looms over one of the pirate-themed course's holes, suspended from a gallows-like structure.

‌



The company filed for retrospective planning permission last month, but has since faced a formal objection branding the display "ugly" and "very offensive".

‌



5 View 5 Images The sculpture was installed in August 2025 5 View 5 Images It has sparked a series of complaints

Steve Irwin's heartbreaking last two words revealed by friend who watched him die READ MORE :

Mum attacked by shark said its face was 'horrific' and she only survived by thinking of her daughter READ MORE :

The complaint, submitted on August 29, read: "I would like to submit an objection to the Large Shark being held up on a gallows.

"It is ugly but also its very offensive to have a marine animal being depicted as a criminal having been slaughtered for no reason. Sharks are a vital form of marine life and should be protected if we are to regain healthy seas which can help mend our planet.

‌



"There is the most amazing story of our sea rewilding and returning huge amounts of different species and it therefore feel compleatly inappropiate to have a symbol of slaughter and destruction in a children's play area such as mini golf.

"We need to educated our kids to protect and fight to preserve our wildernesses and seas. Not to hunt and destroy such a vital species in our ecosystem."

View 5 Images The eye-catching sculpture towers over the golf course

‌



A heritage assessment, which is available to view online, confirms the shark remains "clearly visible" from the beach, Madeira Drive and Madeira Terrace. However, it determined that given Brighton seafront's long-standing history of recreational pursuits such as mini golf, the new features complement the area well.

The report stated: "The works are therefore considered to represent contemporary additions associated with the established recreational use of this part of Brighton's lower seafront without detracting from the significance of the East Cliff Conservation Area or the setting and significance of nearby designated heritage assets."

View 5 Images The sculpture looms over one of the pirate-themed course's holes, suspended from a gallows-like structure

Article continues below

The proposals also satisfied biodiversity requirements as they're situated within an existing location and therefore pose no significant environmental impact.

Brighton & Hove City Council will make a decision on the application at a later date.

Jungle Rumble Adventure Golf declined to comment.

News.title: Hundreds of tributes after 'heartbreaking' death of Stockport nursery manager with 'kindest soul'
News.content:
Hundreds of tributes after 'heartbreaking' death of Stockport nursery manager with 'kindest soul'

Tiny Stars Day Nursery in Stockport has announced the death of its manager, Sarah Hughes, with tributes pouring in for the 'truly beautiful, caring and compassionate woman'

View 2 Images Tributes have been paid to Sarah Hughes, the manager of Tiny Stars Day Nursery in Edgeley, Stockport (Image: Tiny Stars Day Nursery Edgeley Ltd/Facebook)

Tributes have poured in following the death of the "much-loved manager" of a nursery in Stockport.

‌



Tiny Stars Day Nursery in Edgeley, which cares for babies and children up to the age of five, announced on Facebook that its manager, Sarah Hughes, had sadly died.

‌



The nursery wrote on Thursday: "It is with profound sadness that we share the heartbreaking news that our much-loved Nursery Manager, Sarah, has sadly passed away.

‌



"Sarah was an incredibly important part of the Tiny Stars family and dedicated so much of her life to caring for the children, supporting families and leading our wonderful team. She will be deeply missed by us all.

"We know that many of our families and children will have known Sarah well, and we understand that this news will come as a great shock and cause a great deal of sadness. At this incredibly difficult time, our thoughts and love are with Sarah’s family and loved ones."

View 2 Images Sarah Hughes was 'an incredibly important part of the Tiny Stars family', the nursery said (Image: Tiny Stars Day Nursery Edgeley Ltd/Facebook)

‌



The nursery said staff and families would "continue to support one another" and "continue to provide the love, care and stability that the children need", adding that this was what Sarah, who was a mum herself, would have wanted.

More than 200 people have since paid tribute to Ms Hughes in comments on the post, which had received more than 3,800 reactions at the time of reporting, the Manchester Evening News reports.

"I'm so devastated to read this," one mother wrote. "Sarah was much more than the manager at my son's nursery. She has supported me through my own personal issues over the years even though she had so much to face herself. What a truly beautiful, caring and compassionate woman. Sending my heartfelt condolences to her family, friends and colleagues."

Article continues below

Another parent commented: "Absolutely heartbreaking to hear this. Sarah was always so lovely, the kindest soul and will be missed! She’s been a massive part of my family’s journey with Tiny Stars, thinking of you all."

The nursery said it would open as normal on Friday, but acknowledged that it would be an "incredibly difficult and emotional time" for the whole team.

It added: "If any families are able to keep their children at home tomorrow, we would be incredibly grateful. This would help us to support our staff and one another as we come to terms with this devastating loss. We completely understand that this will not be possible for every family, and we will of course continue to be there for those children who need to attend."

News.title: At least 44 injured after train derails and carriage overturns in northern France
News.content:
At least 44 injured after train derails and carriage overturns in northern France

A train carrying 180 passengers derailed between the cities of Rouen and Caen in northern France, leaving at least 44 people injured

View Image A TER train carrying 180 passengers derailed in northern France (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

At least 44 people have been injured after a train carrying 180 passengers derailed in northern France, with one carriage overturning.

‌



The TER train, travelling between the Normandy cities of Rouen and Caen, derailed at around 7.45pm local time (6.45pm BST) on Friday, local authorities said. The crash happened near the commune of Cléon, just south of Rouen.

‌



An 18-year-old woman is in a critical condition, while 43 others sustained "non-life-threatening" injuries, authorities said.

‌



One carriage overturned and four carriages derailed, French broadcaster BFMTV reported.

A police source told the broadcaster that the train struck an unidentified object.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



"All of a sudden, we felt strong vibrations. The train lifted off the tracks," Ilario Imbert, 15, told French newspaper Ouest-France. "Windows broke. The carriage in front of us derailed and rolled over. We passed it. We were still on the tracks."

A mass-casualty emergency plan was activated, with 140 firefighters deployed to the scene.

SNCF Réseau, which manages France's rail network, told the AFP news agency that services on the line had been suspended and power to the tracks had been cut to allow emergency services to work.

Article continues below

"The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Réseau said.

The ⁠local authority, the prefecture of Seine-Maritime, advised the public to avoid the area.

The public prosecutor's office has reportedly launched an investigation into the cause of the incident.

News.title: Children injured on Rotherham fairground ride as emergency services swarm
News.content:
Children injured on Rotherham fairground ride as emergency services swarm

Three young people - including two children - were injured on a ride at Maltby Crags Fair in Rotherham on Friday evening

View Image A large emergency services presence was reported at Maltby Crags Fair (file image) (Image: Getty Images)

Three young people have been injured on a fairground ride in Rotherham, sparking a major emergency services response.

‌



Police and paramedics were called to Maltby Crags Fair on Friday evening following reports of an incident on a ride. South Yorkshire Police said two children, aged 11 and 13, and a 21-year-old woman were injured and taken to hospital for treatment. The incident is understood to have happened at around 7.30pm.

‌



At least six police vehicles attended the scene, according to local outlet The Star.

‌



A force spokesperson said: "Emergency services are currently in attendance at an incident at Maltby Crags Fair in Rotherham after two young people, aged 11 and 13, and a 21-year-old woman [were] injured while on a ride.

"They have been taken to hospital for treatment and the fairground has now closed for the evening (11 September).

Article continues below

"Blyth Lane was closed between Muglet Lane and Victoria Road to allow people to safely exit the fairground but has since been reopened."

Former Rother Valley MP Alexander Stafford said in a Facebook post: "News from the fair in Maltby, where a ride has reportedly injured a child. I believe only one child is involved, but please check on your children if they are currently there."

News.title: Two women brutally attack man, 70, out walking his dog around Middlesbrough park
News.content:
Two women brutally attack man, 70, out walking his dog around Middlesbrough park

Leanne Yates, 41, and Chloe Thompson, 27, have been jailed for brutally attacking a 70-year-old man 'who was doing no more than walking one of his dogs' in a Middlesbrough park

View 3 Images Leanne Yates, 41, and Chloe Thompson, 27, subjected a 70-year-old dog walker to a 'terrifying' attack (Image: Cleveland Police)

Two women have been jailed after brutally attacking a pensioner "who was doing no more than walking one of his dogs".

‌



Leanne Yates, 41, and Chloe Thompson, 27, subjected the 70-year-old man to a "terrifying" attack in a Middlesbrough park, which involved Yates repeatedly kicking and stamping on him. Yates was sentenced to three years and nine months in prison, while Thompson was jailed for three years.

‌



Teesside Crown Court heard the pair, who were part of a group, approached the pensioner and asked him if he had money in Ayresome Gardens on the evening of March 9. He told them he had none before returning home with one of his dogs and later going back to the park to walk his second dog.

‌



The victim saw the group, which included another woman and a man, on the pathway and tried to move out of the way to let them pass, Teesside Live reports.

View 3 Images Leanne Yates was jailed for three years and nine months (Image: Cleveland Police)

Prosecutor Cainan Lonsdale said CCTV showed the man in the group striking the pensioner in his face. The victim punched back, but the same man then "made another blow to his face", knocking him to the ground.

‌



Mr Lonsdale said CCTV showed Thompson "dragging and pulling [the victim] from the grass area onto the pavement", while Yates was seen "stamping and kicking him".

The group searched the pensioner's pockets and took his satchel, but discarded it after finding it contained only a dog lead, dog bags, a hat and gloves. Mr Lonsdale said Yates then "stamped on [the victim] again".

The pensioner returned home, and his partner helped him get to hospital. Photographs showed his right eye closed, bruising under his left eye and a large cut on his cheek. He said his "vision was affected" by the attack.

‌



Both women were arrested and found to be carrying drugs.

View 3 Images Chloe Thompson was jailed for three years (Image: Cleveland Police)

Yates, of no fixed address in Middlesbrough, pleaded guilty to attempted robbery, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and possession of a Class A drug.

‌



Thompson, of New Street, Thornaby, admitted attempted robbery, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, two counts of possession of a Class C drug and failing to surrender.

The court heard both women had experienced difficult backgrounds and struggled with substance misuse.

Mitigating for Yates, Charlie Thompson said his client "has had a miserable life" and had suffered "dreadful abuse as a child and a teenager", which led her to substance misuse and sex work.

Article continues below

Judge Richard Wright said the offence was so serious that both women had to go to prison, but that the length of their sentences had been significantly reduced to reflect the mitigation in each case.

The judge said: "Each of you have had difficult lives and backgrounds, not of your making. Yates, you took the lead in kicking and stamping on him. Thompson, you dragged him about. This was a terrifying ordeal for him."

He added: "When you attack a 70-year-old man in the dark, who was doing no more than walking his dog, when you put him to the ground and kick and stamp on him - you go to prison."

News.title: Israel carries out targeted ‘earthquake-like’ explosion rocking 'underground Hezbollah base'
News.content:
Israel carries out targeted ‘earthquake-like’ explosion rocking 'underground Hezbollah base'

Images released by the Israel Defense Forces claimed to show a fireball lighting up the sky with the damage done by the blast more than a mile deep, as troops remain on site

View 3 Images Israel's forces have destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah (Image: AP Photo/Hussein Malla)

Israel's military claimed it rocked an underground Hezbollah base so powerfully that the explosion was the equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake.

‌



Officials claimed the complex operated by the Iran-backed Shiite militia in southern Lebanon had been destroyed, and said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to obliterate two tunnels more than a mile beneath the Ali Taher Ridge.

‌



The US Geological Survey said in a statement that the blast was so strong it triggered seismic activity, as images were released by the Israel Defense Forces. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz said this afternoon that troops remained in place to stop the organisation from restoring its capabilities.

‌



The base contained Hezbollah's command centres, with missile and drones storage rooms and living areas for soldiers. Tremors and the sound of the explosion were felt across Nabatieh and its surrounding areas.

View 3 Images Benjamin Netanyahu and his Defense Minister Israel Katz released a joint statement (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Iran and US in nailbiting race against time over new Middle East shipping threat READ MORE :

"This was strategic terror infrastructure built over two decades, with Iranian funding and planning," Netanyahu and Katz confirmed, adding forces had established "operational control" over the ridge.

‌



"The IDF will remain in the security zone and will continue destroying terror infrastructure and thwarting any attempt by the Hezbollah terrorist organisation to re-establish itself and restore its capabilities," they said.

"The State of Israel will continue to defend the northern communities from within Lebanon - and any attempt to harm our citizens and our forces will be met with force."

‌



This week, the UK Government accused its Israeli counterparts of turning a blind eye to "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" in the West Bank, as Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced an import ban on goods from illegal settlements.

View 3 Images People from Mansouri record the smoke billowing from an Israeli-controlled detonation (Image: AP Photo/Hussein Malla)

In the strongest condemnation yet from the UK, imports of produce like dates, mangoes, avocados, grapes and herbs, as well as olive oil and kosher wine would be banned with the on-going occupation of the West Bank described as "unlawful", with Britain's move “the least the people who face such suffering deserve".

Article continues below

Mr Burnham said at PMQs that: “Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice" - and announced those who help build or finance settlements will also face sanctions. He said: “Where people are being bullied out of their homes and intimidated, we will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them.

"That is leadership on the world stage: Britain being true to what it’s always been about. That is what the British people expect of us and that is what this government will do.”

The action triggered an immediate backlash from the US and Israel.

News.title: Reform receives record £36m donation from crypto billionaire
News.content:
Reform UK has received a Â£36m donation from a British cryptocurrency billionaire - a record for a UK political party.

Writing in the Daily Telegraph, external, Ben Delo said he was making the move because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field".

The sum is the biggest single donation ever given to a political party in the UK.

Party leader Nigel Farage said he was "honoured and humbled" by the gift.

Delo said he was donating Â£1m a month between now and the latest date Labour could call a general election in 2029 - but that he would give all the money up front in case the government tried to limit mega-donations in future.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

But Labour previously introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas.

Sheffield-born Delo, who has already donated Â£4m to Reform, has previously said he will move back to the UK from Hong Kong in order to continue his backing for the party.

Last year, Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a Bank Secrecy Act violation.

In the Telegraph, Delo wrote: "Unlike the people who express mock concern for the health of 'our democracy' while doing everything they can to keep it as a cartel, I want a fair fight and a level playing field.

"My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."

News.title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
News.content:
MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270, majority 16, against the proposed legislation.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short term.

The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.

Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years had it been approved.

MPs were given a free vote, meaning they did not vote on party lines.

Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.

News.title: Masked men, lorries and road blocks: How anti-migrant activists are changing tactics
News.content:
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.

The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.

In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.

In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.

Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.

It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).

"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.

The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."

The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".

On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.

His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normany in France.

On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.

It organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.

News.title: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
News.content:
"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."

Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" â Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.

"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."

Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.

Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).

"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."

"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.

News.title: 'Never, ever forget' - America marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
News.content:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, US presidents past and present have commemorated the lives lost when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

President Donald Trump led a Pentagon ceremony, while US Vice-President JD Vance attended a memorial at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, along with all four living former US presidents and first ladies.

Moments of silence were held to mark the timings of the attacks and the names of nearly 3,000 people who died were read out.

Two beams of light illuminated the Manhattan sky for a Tribute in Light on Friday evening, as other landmarks in the state lit up in blue in commemoration.

News.title: Zverev through to third Grand Slam final in a row
News.content:
Alexander Zverev beat Karen Khachanov at the US Open to reach a third Grand Slam final in a row and continue his bid for a second major of the year.

The top seed put in a commanding performance to beat the Russian 6-3 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (8-6).

Germany's Zverev is the favourite in New York after ending his long wait for a Grand Slam title with his French Open triumph in June.

He reached the Wimbledon final in July, losing in four sets to world number one Jannik Sinner.

The 29-year-old will play either eighth seed Ben Shelton or 11th seed Frances Tiafoe in Sunday's showpiece, with the two Americans set to meet in Friday's night session.

"I think it [Sunday] will be incredibly special especially, these two guys are crowd favourites and everyone loves them," said Zverev.

"Tonight will be an epic semi-final and I am looking forward to watching it. Hopefully I can not make their American dream come true."

With Sinner and defending US Open champion Carlos Alcaraz suffering with injuries this year, Zverev has found a consistency that has allowed him to reach all four Grand Slam semi-finals.

He started off the tournament in New York slowly, being taken to five sets in his opening two matches, but has not dropped a set since.

Zverev faced brief moments of pressure against world number 50 Khachanov, saving two set points in the third set, but otherwise remained in control.

"After the second round, at about 3am I was sitting with my team in the locker room and we were laughing at how bad I was playing," Zverev said.

"That sense of humour helped me. I obviously have improved a bit otherwise I would not be in the US Open final."

Zverev won 13 of 15 points behind his first serve and all nine points at the net in the first set as he broke Khachanov to go 5-3 up before serving out the opener.

Khachanov fought back after going a break down early in the second set and forced a tie-break, saving set point with a magnificent backhand to polish off a 22-shot rally.

In a pivotal point of the match, it was Zverev who took the initiative to earn another set point, converting it as he outlasted Khachanov in a draining rally with some magnificent defence from the baseline.

In the third set, both players remained on serve without conceding a single break point to reach another tie-break.

It was Khachanov who settled quickest into the tie-break, opening up a lead and creating two set points - both of which were saved by Zverev.

From there the top seed never looked back, ultimately clinching victory as Khachanov put a forehand long.

After reaching his sixth major final, Zverev stood arms wide in celebration facing his coaching team, before going to the net to shake hands with Khachanov.

Victory means Zverev is into his second US Open final after suffering a heartbreaking five-set loss to Dominic Thiem in 2020.

News.title: Is a September heatwave forecast for the UK?
News.content:
Temperatures are set to climb across the UK this weekend, reaching summerlike levels in some places.

It will feel warm and muggy - especially where there are sunny spells - although heavy rain also features in the forecast.

The warmth will persist into Monday in many areas but nowhere is expected to reach heatwave criteria and cooler conditions are due to return by midweek.

Computer weather models paint a very mixed picture for the second half of September but, while there are likely to be some warm spells, there are currently no definitive signs of a heatwave.

News.title: Children and woman injured on fairground ride
News.content:
Two children and a woman have been injured while on a fairground ride in South Yorkshire, police said.

Emergency services were called to Maltby Crags Fair in Rotherham on Friday evening, which closed early after the incident.

South Yorkshire Police said three people, aged 11, 13 and 21, had been taken to hospital for treatment. The extent of their injuries is not yet clear.

Blyth Lane was closed between Muglet Lane and Victoria Road to allow people to safely exit the fairground, the force added, with the road since reopening.

Yorkshire Ambulance Service confirmed the two injured children were taken to Sheffield Children's Hospital after it attended the fair at about 18:50 BST.

Two ambulances and three rapid response vehicles were sent to the scene, the service said.

News.title: Battle to save the tiny, gooey snail only found in one lake in the UK
News.content:
A tiny snail found in only one lake in the UK has been dubbed as precious as an Egyptian artefact as conservationists bid to save it.

Several British zoos are setting up so-called ark populations of the glutinous snail, one of Europe's rarest species, using creatures bred in a back garden in Ceredigion.

"Beguiled by their cuteness," conservationist Ian Hughes has made it his "life-defining" mission to protect the threatened mollusc, which was once widespread in UK waters.

"There was a point where we'd got more snails in our garden than have ever been seen in the wild," he said.

News.title: UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI
News.content:
The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.

The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.

But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".

"Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.

The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible.

"Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said.

"You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."

Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.

The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."

In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.

Speaking on 1 September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers.

"If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned.

The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.

The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.

In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.

News.title: Families of British victims mark 25th anniversary of 9/11
News.content:
Families of British victims of 9/11 were among those who gathered in London's Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks in the US.

The event, hosted by UK charity Since 9/11, was held near a memorial sculpture made from steel recovered from the ruins of the World Trade Center.

In a video address played to attendees, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "On this anniversary, we must remember that hatred and fear did not have the last word on 9/11."

There were 67 British citizens among the 2,977 people murdered on 9/11.

The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester, with the US ambassador to the UK, have separately attended a special Changing of the Guard ceremony while a number of vigils are taking place in the US.

A memorial has been held at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, with relatives of the victims reading out their names.

At a ceremony at the Pentagon, in Virginia, President Donald Trump said the US would "never, ever forget", adding "on days like 9/11, we learn what a country is truly made of".

News.title: Police to crack down on face coverings at protests
News.content:
The police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

Rowlinson said: "We have been consistently clear that violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest and we will investigate incidents like this thoroughly and take robust action against those responsible.

"Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."

He also pointed out the force will not tolerate abuse aimed at police or partner agencies online.

This comes after RNLI volunteers were targeted on social media.

"We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made," Rowlinson said.

"This arrest also sends a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events. If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution."

The disorder in Portsmouth followed a separate anti-migrant protest at the Port of Dover the day before.

News.title: Running costs of vaccine damage scheme more than double amount paid to victims
News.content:
The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose.

"It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.

Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme.

Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered.

The government is due to respond to her recommendations.

The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments.

The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed".

"When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell.

He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help."

The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly".

"In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said.

NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS".

News.title: Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she helped fund with climb
News.content:
The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical.

"I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said.

"But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important.

"It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.

Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour.

"When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."

He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".

The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through.

"There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.

News.title: Man admits murder of woman missing for 28 years
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a woman who went missing 28 years ago, after telling police he disposed of her decomposed body months after he killed her.

Patricia Lashley, who was 33 at the time, was last seen near her home on Hall Street, Dudley, in September 1998.

Trevor Dunkley, 66, pleaded guilty to her murder and a separate count of preventing her lawful burial at a hearing at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Friday.

Dunkley's barrister Balbir Singh told Judge Michael Chambers KC that Lashley's body had never been found, and had decomposed after initially being put in the cellar.

"When he was moving about nine months to a year later, the skeleton was disposed of into the bins," Singh added.

Dunkley, of Himley Road, Dudley, showed no emotion in the dock as his barrister told the court that the charges had been brought based on a police interview.

He was remanded in custody and is due to be sentenced at the same court on 6 November.

News.title: Girls given legal right to wear trousers in schools in Northern Ireland
News.content:
Murray estimates that "about 50%" of girls who attend Craigavon Integrated College currently choose to wear trousers to school on a regular basis.

"It's really helpful for our girls in the colder winter months because a lot of our children will walk to school, so having that flexibility I think is really important.

"It's also in line with the period dignity recommendations, so a lot of our girls feel much more confident having that flexibility to wear trousers when they want," she added.

There are already laws on school uniform in Northern Ireland, and Givan had previously said they give girls the legal authority to challenge their schools.

Education committee members, however, had called on the minister to go further.

Some assembly members have now accused the minister of making a "U-turn", with "substantial sums of public money" spent on drafting legislation "to fix his error of judgement".

It comes after assembly members passed a new law last year, aimed at addressing the cost of school uniforms in Northern Ireland - with these updated guidelines on wearing trousers now legally binding under the School Uniforms Act.

Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's The Nolan Show, Givan said the change would come into immediate effect ahead of the next academic year.

"I don't need to go through the assembly to give effect to this," he said.

"Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me, and as of the next academic year... schools will be required that this has to be available if it is requested upon."

The minister explained that this change will not apply during the 2026/27 academic year, in order to allow schools to change their uniform policies.

Givan added that the change will also apply to physical education.

GoFundMe has been accused of deceptively adding “tips” to donations that go to the company and not helping others.

The fundraising site has skyrocketed in popularity since it launched in 2010, helping strangers connect with grieving families struggling to pay for funeral costs or those who can’t afford to pay for medical bills after a tragic accident. Donors can send money to those in need through GoFundMe with a click of a button.

But when people go to donate to a charitable cause of their choice on the site, they are also hit with an automatic tip to the company that they can opt out of, a practice that a recently filed lawsuit claims is tricking donors into paying more.

“Once automatically added, GoFundMe makes the ‘tips’ difficult to remove, forcing consumers to hunt around for a way to remove them,” according to a lawsuit filed in a federal court in Illinois last month by Sandra Donovan of Illinois and Ebony Baker of Georgia, who have both made donations on GoFundMe.

The Independent, which obtained the lawsuit from ClassAction.org, has reached out to GoFundMe for comment.

open image in gallery GoFundMe has been accused of deceptively adding 'tips' to donations that go to the company and not helping others ( GoFundMe )

The lawsuit also challenges how GoFundMe explains the tipping option on its site.

When donors go to pay on the site, the company has a blurb that reads, “GoFundMe has a 0% platform fee for organizers and relies primarily on the generosity of donors like you to operate our service.”

But the lawsuit argues that this description is “false,” adding, “In reality, completely unbeknownst to those who donate through its website, GoFundMe funds its services by charging charitable organizations hefty transaction fees on each donation they receive.”

GoFundMe says on its site that while it's free to create a fundraiser, the company charges “one small transaction fee per donation.”

open image in gallery Donors expect 'that their money will go where they intend—toward helping others, not toward undisclosed or preselected middleman fees like the ‘tips’ charged by GoFundMe,' the lawsuit said ( GoFundMe )

The fee varies slightly depending on who creates the fundraiser. Individuals and businesses are charged 2.9 percent of the donation plus $0.30, while certified nonprofits are charged 2.2 percent of the donation plus $0.30.

“Donors act quickly, often emotionally, and with the reasonable expectation that their money will go where they intend—toward helping others, not toward undisclosed or preselected middleman fees like the ‘tips’ charged by GoFundMe,” the lawsuit claims.

Donovan and Baker “paid money they did not knowingly authorize, conferring an improper financial benefit on GoFundMe” because of the company’s business practices, the lawsuit argues.

Donovan and Baker's lawyers are asking the court to certify the case as a class action and are demanding a jury trial to stop GoFundMe's “deceptive conduct and return its ill-gotten gains,” according to the lawsuit.

A judge who ruled 13 years ago that Hispanics were racially profiled in then-Arizona Sheriff Joe Arpaio’s immigration crackdowns has rejected a bid to end the court’s supervision of the sheriff’s office.

Maricopa County failed to show that the objectives of the court’s orders — such as correcting the practices that led to the profiling — had been achieved, U.S. District Judge Murray Snow said in a ruling Thursday. He also found “a durable remedy” hadn’t been established to ensure the violations wouldn’t occur again if court supervision ended.

County officials, frustrated with the steep costs of court supervision, had argued Arpaio’s immigration policies are no longer in place, that racial bias no longer infects its operations and its past two studies of traffic stops show the sheriff’s office has changed. The U.S. Department of Justice, which in the past had frequently sided with plaintiffs, supported ending court supervision.

The case centered on 20 large-scale traffic patrols launched by Arpaio that targeted immigrants from January 2008 through October 2011. The patrols involved large numbers of sheriff’s deputies flooding an area of metro Phoenix — including some Latino neighborhoods — over several days to stop traffic violators and arrest other offenders. The plaintiffs were Latinos who had been stopped, detained, questioned or searched by Arpaio’s officers while in a vehicle in Maricopa County.

The judge's ruling from 13 years ago required expensive court-ordered overhauls of the agency’s traffic patrol operations and, later, its internal affairs unit.

In his latest ruling, Snow called into question the studies cited by the county.

In analyzing the duration of stops, the sheriff’s office excluded the longest stops, such as those involving suspected drunk drivers, language barriers and other factors. The excluded encounters accounted for at least half of the agency’s stops in 2024 and 2025, the judge said.

Snow then cited analysis from a plaintiffs’ expert who evaluated all traffic stop data in 2023 and 2024.

The expert found a 4.7-minute difference in stop duration between Hispanic and white drivers. Snow wrote “these figures differ drastically from the relatively minute, statistically insignificant differences” found in the agency’s reports that excluded the longer stops.

Snow said the county offered limited evidence to explain the disparities.

While the county was seeking to end all supervision of the sheriff’s office, the judge directed lawyers on all sides to determine whether there might be certain requirements they would agree could be done away with from the court orders.

In a statement, two leaders on Maricopa County’s governing board expressed disappointment in the ruling and signaled the county would appeal.

“Continued federal oversight of MCSO would serve only to further deplete public funds and divert taxpayer dollars from the sheriff’s primary responsibility: fighting crime and protecting public safety,” said board chair Kate Brophy McGee and vice chair Debbie Lesko.

In a statement, Sheriff Jerry Sheridan's office said it believed it “has implemented durable remedies for violations that occurred 19 years and three administrations ago.” The agency said it looks forward to working with the opposing side to see if portions of the order can be eliminated.

Arpaio, who was voted out of office in 2016, was found in both civil and criminal contempt for disobeying a 2011 order to stop his traffic patrols that targeted immigrants. He was spared a possible jail sentence when his misdemeanor conviction was pardoned by President Donald Trump in 2017.

U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, the Republican challenger to Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs, has criticized the official who was hired by the court to monitor the sheriff’s office and has proposed legislation that would impose term limits and compensation caps on such monitors.

News.title: Homicide detectives arrest man over death of Black woman found hanging from tree in Mississippi
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Police in Jackson, Mississippi, arrested a man on Friday in connection with the killing of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned home in the area last month.

Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney identified the arrested man as Jacque Ratliff. She said officers apprehended him on the street after failing to encounter him at the address on their warrants.

“That arrest today is an important development in this investigation but it is not the conclusion,” Brackney said at a press conference on Friday. “This case remains active and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads.”

Police secured warrants for Ratliff’s arrest after the Hinds County coroner determined on Thursday that Fortune’s death was a homicide.

Jackson, Mississippi, police arrested a man on Friday in connection with the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned home ( GoFundMe / Etta Avolio )

Brackney said she was aware of the local and national attention to the case given Mississippi’s history, but she insisted she could not yet comment on the nature of the death beyond the medical examiner’s findings. She also declined to comment on what caused Fortune’s death and how long she had been at the location where her remains were found.

“We owe it to Ms. Fortune, to her family and the integrity of this investigation to let the evidence guide us,” Brackney said.

Raliff will be charged with homicide, according to police.

The suspect had an “association” with Fortune before the killing, but Brackney declined to further describe the relationship.

Mississippi is estimated to have had the most lynchings in the nation between 1882 and 1968, with at least 581 recorded incidents in the state, according to the NAACP.

Fortune’s family have said they don’t believe she died by suicide.

"Tasia always let us know if something happened to her, that she was going to fight," her mother, Christy Spivey, told WAPT. "Tasia loved life. Tasia loved living life, like, there's no way, no way that she took her own life."

As of Friday evening, Ratliff had not appeared in local jail logs and it was unclear if he had legal representation.

More arrests are expected in the case, Brackney said.

A 15-year-old boy has been rescued after his fishing boat capsized in the frigid Bering Sea off Alaska’s coast. His older brother and cousin, who were on the trip, did not survive.

Derek Parker Aghnaanga, set sail with his 35-year-old brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, last Friday to catch halibut, their mother, Vina Kulowiyi, told The New York Times. Their cousin had also joined them on the trip.

The group — from Savoonga on the northern coast of St. Lawrence Island — was supposed to return early Sunday, according to the Coast Guard, but never made it home. Derek's brother and cousin died sometime after the small boat flipped, according to the rescuers.

Derek’s mom called him a “survivor,” writing on Facebook that “he was never afraid the whole time.”

“He lived on prayer with no food and water,” the mom said.

open image in gallery A 15-year-old boy has been rescued after his fishing boat capsized off Alaska’s coast. His older brother and cousin, who were on the trip, did not survive ( Carlos Alexis Escartin via AP )

Derek clung to the top of the capsized skiff for days, Adam White, the captain of another fishing boat who helped rescue the teen, told local news outlet KTUU-TV.

“I mean, that’s one tough kid,” White said.

Coast Guard planes and helicopters began searching for the skiff Monday after family members reported the three missing the night before.

After Derek was found, the Coast Guard coordinated the rescue with White’s boat, the “Northwest Explorer.”

Video of the rescue shows the boy in a bright yellow jacket kneeling atop the overturned skiff. The boat's crew tosses the boy a line, tugging the skiff closer until they can pull him into a rescue basket.

open image in gallery Derek Parker Aghnaanga spent days on top of his capsized fishing boat in the Bering Sea, pictured, with no food or water after he set sail with his older brother and cousin last Friday ( Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty Images )

The boy was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he got onto the boat, the Coast Guard said. The fishing boat crew warmed him with blankets and hot packs, its captain said.

“Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff and then he said that in the previous night before our rescue that his cousin had slipped away off the top of the skiff,” White said.

The bodies of Derek’s brother and cousin were found after the teen was hoisted to safety near St. Lawrence Island — a remote Alaskan island that’s closer to Russia than it is to the United States.

Alaska State Troopers identified the two who died as Kulowiyi and 34-year-old Barton Rookok.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

The California labor leader behind a proposal to tax billionaires has been accused of harassing and intimidating several women who work for an affiliated union.

The allegations against Dave Regan, president of the SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, are detailed in an investigative report commissioned by SEIU California and obtained Friday by The Associated Press. It includes interviews with several current and former SEIU members and others who say Regan tried to intimidate union leaders into supporting the billionaires' tax, which goes before voters in November.

The Los Angeles Times was the first to report on the allegations.

The report also includes allegations that Regan physically assaulted an SEIU leader more than 15 years ago amid a political dispute and that more recently he engaged in harassing behavior against other women who work for the organization.

Regan acknowledged using curse words with union leaders but denied the physical assault allegation.

“I will own up to and take responsibility for anything that I’ve said and anything that I’ve done,” Regan said at a news conference. “But I absolutely am not going to stand by and ... be expected to accept flat out lies.”

The ballot measure, Proposition 40, would impose a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires living in the state to help backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare for low-income people. The proposal has caused a rift within the Democratic Party and among labor unions that are typically aligned. While Regan's union supports it, the larger SEIU California has not taken a position.

The SEIU-UHW alleged that opponents of the measure worked to make public the report, which was labeled as being completed in June, in order to hurt the initiative's chances of passing.

“The billionaires are trying to play us all, but we’re not falling for it,” the union said in a statement. “We want our healthcare and our money back. Tax the billionaires.”

“Unrelated verbal interactions spanning nearly two decades are being stitched together and stripped of context to manufacture a false narrative about the union’s leadership,” it added.

SEIU California said it took action in response to the allegations to uphold values of respect, fairness and equity in the workplace.

“We ask members every day to stand up to power and speak out against abuses. We are inspired by their courage, and our leaders, too, are saying, ‘Enough!’” the group said in a statement.

According to the report, SEIU California executive director Tia Orr told investigators that Regan told her in December that the union needed to support the tax measure by Jan. 1 or “I'm coming for you.” Orr later told members that she felt unsafe, and she learned about other allegations of Regan threatening or berating female union leaders and staffers.

SEIU California has filed charges against Regan with the SEIU International Union alleging a pattern of bullying, extortion and threats.

The report also alleges Regan acted aggressively toward Courtni Pugh, the union's former executive director, amid a political dispute sometime before she resigned in 2009. Pugh told investigators he yelled at her, kicked in her office door and backed her up against a bookcase. That followed Regan yelling expletives and telling her she was not tough enough for the job, the report said.

SEIU-UHW called Pugh’s allegations a “trumped-up claim from 17 years ago” and noted that the political firm she works for has worked for groups opposing Proposition 40. Pugh did not immediately respond to a request for comment about her involvement with the ballot measure.

But in a statement, she called Regan's response “offensive to the women and people who have had to endure his threatening behavior.” She said she told colleagues about the incident at the time and it was well known around SEIU.

“I chose to participate in the investigation because I saw that his behavior had continued and in hopes that no one else would have to endure this kind of treatment from him,” Pugh added.

Mississippi police have arrested a man in the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month.

Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said at a news conference Friday that police had secured search and arrest warrants for the man and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street.

The state medical examiner’s office determined Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney said, allowing them to execute the warrants they already had on hand.

“This case remains active and additional arrests will be pending,” Brackney said.

Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said Friday after police told her of the arrest that, "I just started crying and told them ‘thank you, thank you, thank you.’”

Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but was asking her daughter's friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock.”

“We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said.

Police discovered Fortune’s body hanging in the backyard of an abandoned home in Jackson on Aug. 3.

Fortune died less than a year after the hanging deaths of 21-year-old Trey Reed, a Black student at Delta State University in Cleveland, and Cory Zukatis, an unhoused white man in his 30s, in Vicksburg.

Police in Cleveland concluded Reed’s death was a suicide. Autopsy results were consistent with a preliminary examination of the body by the Bolivar County coroner, which found no evidence of foul play.

Reed’s family and their attorneys called for an independent autopsy and for authorities to share security camera recordings.

The Mississippi State Medical Examiner determined Zukatis died by suicide.

News.title: Well-preserved tooth from Pacific mastodon found in a creek in San Francisco Bay Area
News.content:

Brigid Lynch was working along a wooded creek in a mountainous part of the San Francisco Bay Area when something that didn't look like the rocks she'd been studying caught her eye. It turned out to be the fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon.

“I keep joking it wasn’t hard to find,” Lynch, a geomorphologist at Balance Hydrologics, said Friday. “It was just sitting there in the middle of the creek, halfway in, half out of the water.”

Lynch made the discovery earlier this year while working on a habitat restoration project for the threatened California red-legged frog in a Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District preserve in San Mateo County. The public land management agency that preserves over 70,000 acres of land in the Santa Cruz Mountains region announced the find this week. The fossil has been donated to Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability.

“It’s in great condition,” said Chrissy Garcia, curator and manager of Doerr School of Sustainability’s specimen collections. “So we’ve got both the crown and the root of the fossil. You can even see root canal.”

“It’s exciting to have a specimen of this quality, and having it be a local find,” she said.

Garcia said the tooth from the Pacific mastodon, an extinct elephantlike species, is about 9 inches (23 centimeters) long.

Ron Tykoski, vice president of science and curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Perot Museum of Nature and Science in Dallas, said mastodon fossils “pop up with some degree of frequency, depending on where you live.”

He said there are multiple species of mastodon that roamed for a few million years in North America, up till 10,000 to 12,000 years ago.

“The way this was found is actually the way a lot of specimens are found, just somebody who happened to be in the right place,” Tykoski said.

Garcia said that they’ll likely try to determine the exact age of the fossil, and will make a 3D copy to give to the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District. The district says it will use the copy for public outreach and education.

Ryan McCauley, a spokesperson for the district, said the discovery on land they are preserving helps show the value of protecting open spaces and habitats.

“That this tooth, that this molar, was found in the context of trying to protect the habitat and save another species from potentially going extinct I think really just drives home the point of why it's so important to care for these open spaces and these natural lands,” he said.

News.title: Razaullah’s incredible hitting scrambles England’s minds
News.content:
England will look to complete the series whitewash as they hold a commanding position coming into day three of the third and final Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston in what could be the final day of the English Test summer.

England finished up their first innings on 453 on day two, with a mammoth 320-run lead over Pakistan. Five England batsmen passed the fifty mark; Emilio Gay, Harry Brook, Dan Lawrence, Jamie Smith and Ollie Robinson, but none went on to convert those half centuries into hundreds. It means that Ben Duckett’s century against New Zealand at Trent Bridge back in June will be the only England Test hundred of the summer, the first time that has happened in a six-Test summer. England managed 21 half centuries over the course of the summer, so it works out as 4.76% conversion rate.

Having seen England pile on the runs, Pakistan then lost a wicket with the first ball of their second innings, with Saim Ayub making a pair to sum up a miserable return to their Test side for the opener having been jettisoned in as part of wholesale changes for the visitors. Abdullah Shafique followed three balls later, with Robinson taking both wickets as his fine summer continued. Robinson now has 28 wickets across four Tests this summer at a staggering average of 7.75. Joe Root made history yesterday, taking his 220th catch, the most by an outfielder in Test history. Rain though prevented England the opportunity of potentially wrapping up a two-day finish in a Test in this country for the first time since 2000.

Pakistan will resume on 52/2, still 268 runs behind England, with Azan Awais resuming on 29 not out and will be joined by Shan Masood, who is on 21. Pakistan are yet to reach 200 or bat more than 51 overs in this series so the series whitewash may not be a million miles away. Will we see any rare Pakistan resistance in this series or will England’s seamers dominate again? Play on day three from Edgbaston is set to get under at 11am and it could be the final day of not just the series but the English Test summer.

News.title: Interest rates predicted to rise four times by July
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Britain’s economy grew unexpectedly in July, handing Chancellor John Healey some breathing space ahead of the Budget.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc during the month, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Analysts had expected the UK economy to flatline.

Officials said pubs and clubs, advertisers and alcohol makers reported an increase in turnover linked to the World Cup, while many firms also said the second hottest July on record had a positive impact.

The data showed Britain’s economy may be benefitting from the massive investments in AI, with activity in telecoms expanding by 1.1pc in July, computer programming up 3.5pc and information services up 1.1pc.

The data will lend support to the “optimistic story” that John Healey tried to tell about the economy in a major speech this week.

Growth also accelerated from 0.3pc in June after Andy Burnham took over as Prime Minister in July.

It slightly eases pressure on the Chancellor after the cost of government borrowing costs rose to levels not seen in decades after a jump in the price of oil reignited a bond market sell-off.

The Treasury’s 10-year interest rate rose above 5.3pc on Thursday, a level not seen since 2007. It threatens to wipe around £10bn from Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom before his first Budget next month, according to economists at the Item Club. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Badenoch must scrap triple lock, says senior Tory MP | Politician urges Conservatives to ‘slaughter some sacred cows’ to stabilise the public finances

2) | Michael O’Leary demands sacking of ‘incompetent’ air traffic control chief | Ryanair boss urges Transport Secretary to dismiss Martin Rolfe after IT meltdown grounds passengers

3) | Guardian staff threaten walkout over pay as paper hails record revenues | Journalists’ union will ballot members over strike in protest against company’s offer

4) | Hotel bosses criticise Burnham’s fresh assault on hospitality | Prime Minister gives mayors power for unlimited levy on stays in blow for pubs and families

5) | Iceland to become first British supermarket to open in Falklands | New shop will begin trading before Christmas despite rising tensions with Argentina over islands

What happened overnight

Oil prices remained at their highest level since May as tensions flared in the Middle East.

Brent crude was above $105 a barrel after after Iran-backed Houthis seized control of Yemen’s keyport of Mocha, threatening Saudi oil exports in the Red Sea.

Asian shares declined, tracking Wall Street losses. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8pc to 63,442.30, while South Korea’s Kospi lost 2.3pc to 6,872.39.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dipped 0.8pc to 24,753.54. The Shanghai Composite index was down 1.8pc to 3,862.73.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 1.2pc to 8,712.20.

Taiwan’s Taiex lost 1.7pc, while India’s Sensex declined 1pc.

On Thursday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 dropped 0.6pc in its fourth straight loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 0.6pc, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite fell 0.7pc.

News.title: Mainoo looks primed for battle with Man City’s new-look midfield
News.content:
This was Manchester United’s first foray back into the Champions League for 1,003 days, but even with hazy memories of the competition, they know full well they are unlikely to have it this easy again in Europe this season.

After an unconvincing beginning to their Premier League campaign and with Manchester City the visitors to Old Trafford on Sunday, Michael Carrick will have been grateful for a gentle start to life back among Europe’s elite.

Little-known Sabah of Azerbaijan have quite the story to tell, but the closest they got to making this an awkward evening for United came in the first half when, already trailing 1-0, Joy-Lance Mickels miscued an inviting header from close range. Otherwise, it was one-way traffic.

United’s biggest threat on the night was complacency, but there was none of that. This was a professional, unfussy display with a few nice flourishes. Kobbie Mainoo impressed again in central midfield and Carrick was able to substitute a number of his best players early with the derby in mind, as well as resting Luke Shaw entirely.

Goals from Matheus Cunha, Bruno Fernandes and Benjamin Sesko in the first half killed the game as a contest before Lisandro Martínez scored a fourth with just over 20 minutes remaining.

News.title: ‘All I see are dead bodies’: The survivors of Syria’s chemical massacres
News.content:
“Unfortunately, I am still alive,” says Mohammed Suliaiman Abo Alkair, his green eyes heavy and distant.

The 38-year-old steps from his living room onto the roof and gestures towards a cluster of trees – a lone patch of green in a sea of grey rubble. It was there, at two in the morning 13 years ago that the whistle of a rocket ended not in an explosion but a thud.

For a moment, there was relief; the feeling of being spared. But then came a cloud of the nerve agent sarin.

Almost everyone around Mohammed died. His family and one small boy in a neighbouring house were the only ones to survive.

That August night, as Damascus slept, forces loyal to the Syrian President Bashar al-Assad launched eight sarin-filled rockets at the opposition-held districts of Zamalka, Ein Tarma and Jobar. The US government estimated that 1,429 people were killed, including 426 children. Other estimates put the number at 1729.

For more than a decade, nobody was held to account. Mr Assad denied the attack, shielded those responsible and later used sarin again – at Khan Sheikhoun in 2017, and in at least ten further attacks documented by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons.

Only after Mr Assad fled Syria in December 2024 did the prospect of justice emerge. Investigators for Syria’s new government have since uncovered previously undeclared chemical-munitions caches, and the authorities have detained 18 suspects. None has yet been tried or punished.

But as attention turns at last to justice, the survivors remain invisible, absent from the reckoning. For now at least they remain largely invisible.

News.title: What an AI Armageddon might actually look like
News.content:
Jacob Coxon has left AI developer Anthropic with a public reckoning. For three years, the 27-year-old Brit trained models at OpenAI and Anthropic.

Both AI startups acted irresponsibly, Coxon wrote on X on Wednesday. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Jacob Coxon warned.

The response from his manager arrived just hours later. Evan Hubinger, Head of Alignment Research at Anthropic, also confirmed the warning: “We are, in fact, earnestly convinced that AI could kill all humans! I think the probability of that happening within the next decade is greater than ten percent.”

Anthropic, he added, does not yet have a solution to this problem.

When the head of safety at a multibillion-dollar technology company casually predicts humanity’s downfall at the hands of his own product, the debate leaves the realm of academic thought experiments.

The warning comes from the engineers writing the code. Both developers point to an industry dynamic in which competitive pressures outweigh safety concerns.

But what exactly are AI developers afraid of? What is the hypothetical scenario in which artificial intelligence brings about Armageddon?

News.title: Stephen Fleming learning nothing from rout of Pakistan
News.content:
Stephen Fleming arrives next week to start his job as England Test coach and his first task will be to apply his famously meticulous mind to assess a whitewash of Pakistan.

England are not quite there yet. Rain denied them a two-day win at Edgbaston, Pakistan finishing 52 for two, another 268 behind after England’s 453 all out.

But when the game does finish, and England complete a rout that started with Ollie Robinson taking a wicket with the first ball of the series, it will be time to look ahead to a proper challenge: a three-match series against Test champions South Africa over Christmas.

That series will give Fleming a much better guide to where his team stand in the lead-up to the Ashes summer. This one is less clearcut. Fleming has been in daily contact with Joe Root and will lean heavily on him and Marcus North. the national selector, for insight, but drawing definitive conclusions is impossible because of the lack of competitive cricket.

A quartet of quicks has emerged, led by Robinson, whose 21 wickets in the series at 6.6 look like a misprint. A double-wicket maiden to start Pakistan’s second innings would normally be headline-grabbing stuff. This time it felt almost predictable, even disappointing for those wanting to see some sort of contest.
