The poll comes amid bilateral tension over remarks by Argentine political and military officials on the Strait of Magellan, and over Milei's speech at the Madrid Forum, a gathering of right-wing leaders held in Santiago on September 3.

Asked about the Falklands, 68% of respondents said the islands are British, 17% said they are Argentine and 15% did not answer. The result runs contrary to Chile's official position: in the joint declaration signed by both presidents at La Moneda, Chile reiterated its long-standing backing for Argentina's sovereignty claim. Sixty-two percent disagreed with Kast reaffirming “Chile's support for Argentina's legitimate sovereignty rights over the Malvinas Islands,” while 22% agreed and 16% did not answer.

Argentina maintains its claim to the islands, whose residents voted by 99.8% to remain a British Overseas Territory in a 2013 referendum.

In his speech opening the forum, Milei used a derogatory term to describe leftists and praised what he called four decades of stability and growth following the 1973 overthrow of Salvador Allende. Chilean opposition parties condemned the remarks as a vindication of the coup. According to the poll, 57% considered Milei's words a serious lack of respect toward Chilean political actors, 21% a lack of respect but not a serious one, and 18% said they were not disrespectful.

The dispute over the Strait of Magellan was triggered by comments from the Chief of the General Staff of the Argentine Air Force, Gustavo Valverde, who included the strait among areas of Argentine sovereignty, and by Argentine Decree 457/2021, which describes it as a space shared by both countries. In light of these statements, 69% of respondents believe Argentina has territorial ambitions over Chile, while 24% think it respects Chilean sovereignty in line with existing treaties. In the previous edition of the survey, in the first week of September, the figure stood at 71%.

On the 2021 decree, 54% said Kast should demand that Milei repeal it, while 37% considered the joint declaration sufficient. In it, both presidents reaffirmed the 1881 Boundary Treaty and the 1984 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, which establish Chilean sovereignty over the strait.

Sixty percent of Chileans consider Argentina an unreliable partner. By contrast, Japan (83%), Canada (80%) and England (78%) topped the list of the most trusted partners.

Respondents said Chile should prioritize trade relations with China (60%), the European Union (49%), Canada, Australia and New Zealand (46%), India and Southeast Asia (37%), Latin America (37%) and the United States (32%).

The survey also put Kast's approval rating at 35%, with 61% disapproving of his government.

World.title: Peru joins the Americas Shield during Rubio's visit to Lima
World.content:
Peru joins the Americas Shield during Rubio's visit to Lima

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 21:45 UTC Full article

Fujimori said the move relaunches joint work between the two countries and rejected the idea that it compromises Peruvian sovereignty

Peru will join the Americas Shield, the US-backed security coalition against transnational organized crime, President Keiko Fujimori announced on Thursday after meeting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Government Palace.

The announcement closed a Rubio tour of Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, Washington's largest diplomatic push in South America since Donald Trump's return to the White House. In Bogotá he had raised with President Abelardo de la Espriella the prospect of a “golden age” in bilateral relations, and in Quito he described Ecuador as the most determined partner in toughening the response to drug trafficking.

The coalition was set up on March 7, 2026, in Doral, Florida, with thirteen founding members: the United States, Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay and Trinidad and Tobago. Colombia joined during this tour and Peru does so now. In a column published this week in the Peruvian daily El Comercio, Rubio also noted that Peru becomes a major non-NATO ally, a bilateral US designation.

Fujimori said the move relaunches joint work between the two countries and rejected the idea that it compromises Peruvian sovereignty. “Peru's sovereignty is intact,” she said, recalling that the entry of foreign troops requires express authorization from Congress, a requirement she said would remain. Rubio also dismissed those objections, saying people were anticipating problems that do not exist. He added that the United States has the capacity to act unilaterally but prefers to work with partners, and that it cannot enter sovereign nations. Among the results of cooperation he cited the capture in Bolivia, with FBI support, of the leader of the Peruvian gang Los Pulpos.

Former Peruvian foreign minister Hugo de Zela has warned that the country does not benefit from being caught in the confrontation between the United States and China and should act according to its own interests.

The visit came amid friction with Beijing. China's embassy in Lima published messages saying it has never demanded that other countries take sides and that the Western Hemisphere is no one's “backyard,” and noted that Peru is the second largest destination for Chinese investment in Latin America, with a stock of US$30 billion. The messages responded to Rubio's column, in which he accused China of predatory practices, opaque contracts and unsustainable debt in the region.

The most visible point of that competition is the Chancay megaport, inaugurated in 2024 and 60% controlled by Chinese company COSCO Shipping Ports. Washington has questioned whether infrastructure on that scale could serve as logistical support for Chinese naval forces.

World.title: Gibraltar reaffirms British sovereignty on National Day, first since UK-EU treaty
World.content:
Gibraltar reaffirms British sovereignty on National Day, first since UK-EU treaty

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 21:19 UTC Full article

Crowds gather in Casemates Square for Gibraltar's National Day rally, marking 59 years since the 1967 sovereignty referendum. Photo: Jim Watt

Once again, it is the 10th of September, when Gibraltar celebrates its National Day on the anniversary of the 1967 referendum on whether to remain British or join Franco’s Spain. The result was decisive, and despite the demise of the fascist dictatorship, Gibraltar remains resolutely British.

A large crowd gathered in Casemates Square for the political rally, though it was not quite as packed as in previous years. Many people took advantage of the public holiday for a long weekend away, with some businesses closing on Friday to facilitate this.



As usual, a cross-party delegation attended from both Houses of the UK Parliament, including Amanda Martin (Labour), Martin Vickers (Conservative), Dr Al Pinkerton (Liberal Democrats), and long-time Gibraltar supporter Andrew Rosindell (Reform). Members of the House of Lords and a contingent of former MPs who hold the Freedom of the City were also present.

The UK Minister for Europe, Lord Stewart Wood, arrived late due to air traffic delays, making his first visit to the Rock for National Day.

Fabian Picardo, the Chief Minister, gave a lively speech reminding the crowd that—whatever others may think—the territory belongs to the people of Gibraltar, and nothing can change that. He indicated that this would be his final time taking to the platform as Chief Minister.

He read aloud a letter from King Charles and another from the UK Prime Minister, who reaffirmed that the UK Government remains “unwavering in its commitment to Gibraltar, to British sovereignty, and to the principle of self-determination”.

In a statement, Deputy Chief Minister Dr Joseph Garcia noted that this National Day marks the first since the UK-EU treaty was signed. He added that the agreement proves preserving British sovereignty and maintaining close ties with Europe are not mutually exclusive.

He went on to say that self-determination means Gibraltar's future can only be freely and democratically decided by its people. That principle, he stressed, is neither weakened by the treaty, diluted by closer cooperation with European neighbours, nor diminished by ongoing work with the European Union to improve citizens' lives.

Organisers announced that the evening would conclude with a fireworks and drone formation display.

By Jim Watt - Gibraltar

World.title: Falklands Legislative Assembly sends greetings to Gibraltar on its National Day
World.content:
Falklands Legislative Assembly sends greetings to Gibraltar on its National Day

10th Thursday, September 2026 - 12:23 UTC Full article

The text says the future of a people belongs to that people alone

The Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly, the archipelago's elected body, sent a message of greeting on Thursday to the government and people of Gibraltar to mark their National Day, and arranged for the flags of both territories to fly alongside one another throughout the day at Victory Green in Stanley.

In its public statement, the assembly described the two territories as kindred communities, separated by an ocean but bound by a British identity held by their own free choice and by a determination to decide their own future. The text says the future of a people belongs to that people alone.

Gibraltar's National Day commemorates the referendum of September 10, 1967, in which 12,138 voters chose to retain the link with the United Kingdom against 44 who preferred transfer to Spanish sovereignty. It is the 59th anniversary of that vote.

This year's celebration is the first since the entry into force of the treaty governing Gibraltar's relationship with the European Union, signed on July 14 in Brussels by British and EU representatives, with Gibraltar's Chief Minister Fabian Picardo and Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares present. The agreement, provisionally applied since July 15, removed routine checks at the land border with Spain, crossed daily by some 15,000 workers, and states expressly that it does not alter British sovereignty or the territory's constitutional status.

Both territories appear on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories and their sovereignty is subject to competing claims. Spain claims sovereignty over Gibraltar and Argentina claims the Falklands, and neither state recognizes the results of the votes held in those territories as settling the question. In the 2013 referendum in the South Atlantic islands, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

The message was issued during a week of rising tension over the South American archipelago, with criminal complaints and administrative proceedings opened by Argentina against oil companies and an intervention by the British prime minister in the House of Commons. The assembly did not link its statement to those events.

World.title: Mexico’s 2027 election cycle has begun: What to know
World.content:
Listen to this article

The 2026-2027 election cycle began on Thursday, and though the stakes are high for the control of Congress, the majority of governorships and all 16 Mexico City borough leaders, the process has already been marred by accusations about the autonomy and transparency of the agency in charge.

A record 102 million Mexicans are eligible to participate in the June 6, 2027, vote. The National Electoral Institute (INE) said it will set up 176,141 polling places, some 6,000 more than during the 2024 federal elections.

Controversy flared up during the agency’s opening electoral session, however, when INE Councilor Arturo Castillo challenged the institution’s credibility.

“The INE seems to have abdicated its role of overseeing and arbitrating elections,” he said, describing a scenario of premature campaigning and irregularities that he said could compromise confidence in the outcome.

Castillo also criticized INE President Guadalupe Taddei for appointing 12 new executive directors over the past year without the consensus of the General Council, some of whom did not meet legal requirements for their appointment.

Two other INE councilors raised questions about new procedures and past oversights, while representatives of opposition political parties complained about what they see as the failure to enforce electoral regulations.

These denunciations contrasted with Taddei’s assertion that the INE was ready to organize the election, while insisting the playing field is level.

What’s at stake in next June’s election

Beyond the selection of more than 20,000 public officials, the vote will serve as a national referendum on the governing project of Morena and the performance of President Claudia Sheinbaum. It will also determine the relative strength of opposition forces ahead of the 2030 presidential election.

While Morena seeks to consolidate its territorial dominance and protect its legislative majority in the Chamber of Deputies (all 500 seats are on the line), some parties will be battling for political survival. The election will also see 17 states choose new governors.

The once-dominant PRI is fighting to remain one of the top five parties in Congress, while the conservative PAN is desperate to preserve its hold on three governor’s mansions.

These two parties also hope to remain relevant in Mexico City, where PRI-PAN alliances control five of the capital’s 16 borough halls, while the PAN aims to maintain its status as the No. 2 party in the Mexico City Congress.

Two new political parties will make their debut in the upcoming elections: PAZ (a party linked to the evangelical church) and Somos México (a center-left party that emerged from opposition to reforms of the INE championed by Morena).

Although the election cycle has officially begun, the formal candidate selection process is not due to begin until Jan. 4, with parties permitted to hold primaries through Feb. 12. After that, the formal campaign season will take place from April 4 through June 2.

Complaints about alleged irregularities

Criticism of the INE is primarily related to alleged violations of the campaign schedule regulations.

Ahead of the 2018 elections, Morena designated so-called state coordinators who were tasked with guiding the party in the run-up to gubernatorial elections. Since they were then inevitably nominated as candidates, critics say their actions as state coordinators should be regarded as campaign violations.

At the same time, office-holders seeking re-election or aiming for a new post have been known to stage public events and rallies before the official campaign season, proceedings that could be seen as violating election law.

With reports from El País, Animal Político, El Universal, Texas Public Policy Foundation and Lider Empresarial

World.title: Mexico’s Supreme Court allows home cannabis edibles, but with a limited practical effect
World.content:
Mexico’s Supreme Court has ruled that people with personal recreational cannabis authorizations can now make marijuana-infused edibles for their own personal use — but people still cannot legally buy or sell them.

The ruling — which applies to gummies, brownies and other homemade edibles laced with cannabis — expands what the Federal Commission for Protection against Sanitary Risks (Cofepris) must allow under an authorization for adult recreational self-consumption.

The Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation (SCJN) said incorporating marijuana or THC into prepared or semi-prepared food for personal consumption is ordinary cooking, not the manufacture of a product subject to specialized health controls.

The ruling, approved by a 7-2 vote and issued on Thursday, ordered Cofepris to issue new authorizations allowing such food preparation for the permit holder’s exclusive personal consumption.

The practical effect is narrow: A person with a Cofepris authorization for recreational self-consumption may prepare a THC-infused brownie, cookie or gummy for personal use. But the authorization does not allow sales, public retail, distribution or supply to third parties, including giving the food to friends.

The decision arose after Cofepris granted an applicant a recreational self-consumption authorization but expressly barred the preparation of cannabis in prepared or semi-prepared foods.

The Supreme Court found that restriction to be improper if the food was intended exclusively for the applicant’s personal use, and ordered Cofepris to issue an updated, corrected authorization.

The decision does not cover cannabis used in medicines, herbal remedies, cosmetics, vaping products, dietary supplements or other goods subject to specialized health controls.

The ruling is the latest development in Mexico’s piecemeal approach to adult marijuana use.

In 2021, the Supreme Court invalidated portions of the General Health Law that imposed an absolute administrative prohibition on recreational self-consumption of cannabis and THC. The Court held that the ban disproportionately restricted the right to the free development of personality.

The declaration allowed for the legal planting, cultivating, harvesting, preparing, possessing and transporting of cannabis and THC for personal recreational use.

But it did not establish broad legalization or a regulated commercial market.

It also required protections for third parties: Cannabis cannot be used in front of minors or in public places where nonconsenting people are present, and users may not drive or operate dangerous machinery while under the influence.

Cofepris reiterated in July that the court’s decisions do not recognize a right to commercialize, supply, sell, distribute or import cannabis. The permits apply only to authorized recreational self-consumption.

In an opinion column in the newspaper El Universal, Jorge Larrea Espinosa called Mexico “an intermediate legal zone” — a place where adults have limited, permit-based self-consumption rights, while a fully regulated recreational market remains stalled in Congress.

With reports from Infobae, Expansión, Zeta Tijuana and EFE

World.title: 5 new US routes are coming next month to Guadalajara’s airport, with a direct Paris flight to follow
World.content:
Describing the Guadalajara International Airport (GDL) as “the best in Latin America,” Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus this week announced that the budget airline Volaris will add five direct routes to key cities in the United States next month.

Additionally, a new Guadalajara-Paris route is scheduled to begin operations on April 13, 2027, expanding the airport’s long-haul connectivity with the French capital, which will become the second European destination with direct service from GDL (Aeroméxico has been operating flights to Madrid since December 2021).

Lemus said his administration is “working hard to make GDL the best connected” airport in Latin America, and Volaris’ executive vice president Holger Blankenstein seemed to second the motion as he confirmed that his airline will launch new flights between the Jalisco state capital and Atlanta, Washington Dulles, Boston, Raleigh-Durham and Nashville, Tennessee.

The Atlanta and Washington connections will begin operations on Oct. 2, while the latter three are scheduled to get underway on Oct. 15, increasing the number of destinations from GDL to 71 and boosting total operations to more than 100 flights per day.

The flights to Washington Dulles, Nashville and Raleigh-Durham will have three weekly frequencies; routes to Atlanta and Boston will have four weekly frequencies.

While Blankenstein highlighted the expanded travel options for Volaris customers and new opportunities to connect with key U.S. cities through direct flights and affordable fares, Guadalajara officials emphasized strengthened ties with the U.S. and new possibilities for commercial, cultural and tourism exchange.

Jalisco Tourism Minister Michelle Fridman Hirsch described the new routes as “an important step forward [for Jalisco], because it brings our destinations closer to key points and expands the options for direct connection to one of our main international markets.”

As for the Paris flight, the new connection will have three weekly frequencies, offering up to 800 seats per week in each direction on Boeing 787 Dreamliner planes.

“The long-awaited direct connection with Paris confirms our region’s potential to sustain long-haul flights and reflects Aeroméxico’s confidence in an airport that continues to expand its infrastructure and operational capacity to meet growing demand,” GDL administrator Cryshtian Amador Lizardi said.

The Guadalajara airport recently expanded its operational capacity with the opening of a second runway as part of a 22 billion-peso (US $1.3 billion) Master Development Plan.

GDL served 18.7 million passengers last year and handled 12.9 million passengers through August this year, 4.8% more than during the same period in 2025.

With reports from Informador and El Economista

World.title: Education Ministry signs deal with UNESCO to guide responsible AI use in schools
World.content:
Mexico has a new ally as it decides how classrooms across the country will use artificial intelligence. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has agreed to support the Public Education Ministry (SEP) with technical assistance, teacher training and research into how to responsibly use AI and other new technologies.

Education Minister Mario Delgado Carrillo and UNESCO Assistant Director-General for Natural Sciences Lidia Arthur Brito signed the letter of intent on Monday at Mexico City’s Muralism Museum (the historic headquarters of the SEP). The agreement aims to drive the digital transformation of education in Mexico and guide the safe and inclusive use of AI in classrooms.

El cambio tecnológico avanza a pasos gigantescos, pero su impacto en el bienestar de nuestras niñas, niños y jóvenes requiere atención inmediata. Hoy, más del 70% de las y los docentes detecta problemas de ansiedad e insomnio en sus alumnos, el 66% nota dificultades en la… pic.twitter.com/nnFCxb7uWR — Mario Delgado (@mario_delgado) September 8, 2026

The agreement aims to strengthen the capabilities of the National Education System in the face of the rapid expansion of digital platforms.

“We need to understand what happens behind the screens and how digital platforms are designed; platforms whose algorithms can use artificial intelligence to learn our habits, offer us content that captures our attention, and extend the time we spend on them,” Delgado said.

“This situation is particularly sensitive for younger generations, so we must act responsibly to protect their well-being and ensure a healthy educational environment,” he noted.

The collaboration entails technical assistance from UNESCO, the exchange of international experiences, specialized studies, and training for teachers, students and education officials. The goal is to incorporate new technologies as a support for learning, rather than as a substitute for the teaching role, critical thinking or school community interaction.

The agreement also opens the door to establishing rules for the use of cell phones and other digital devices within schools.

Meanwhile, Arthur said that for UNESCO, technology must serve people and education, not the other way around.

In the educational sphere, she said, this entails preserving what no technology can replace: The human relationship between students, critical thinking, creativity, dialogue and the social dimension of learning.

“For this reason, we are making our technical expertise and the knowledge UNESCO has developed regarding technology, education and the ethics of artificial intelligence available to the Secretariat of Public Education and the entire education sector,” she said.

The scope of the agreement will depend on the extent to which the Education Ministry implements it. The challenge will reside in incorporating AI without using it as a substitute for teaching — ensuring that it strengthens public education and preserves the central role of the school community.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Vance reacts to a protester by calling the Mexican flag ‘symbol of the far left’
World.content:
A man waving a Mexican flag interrupted JD Vance during his speech at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday, prompting the U.S. vice president to label the protester an “idiot” and describe the tricolor as “a symbol of the far left.”

The disruption occurred while the vice president was talking about the constitutional right of birthright citizenship, which President Donald Trump has sought to restrict, and caused Vance to pause momentarily.

Embed from Getty Images

As the protester — who had also been waving a Palestinian flag — was being escorted out of the American Airlines Center, he tossed the Mexican banner onto the stage.

The incident wasn’t broadcast on the live television feed, but Vance described the events from the podium.

“What the people at home missed is that we just had a protester interrupting us and waving the Mexican flag,” Vance said. “Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”

The crowd cheered and chuckled, chanting “USA! USA!” while Vance sought to return to the second half of his keynote address.

“I had a whole speech written,” he said, “ but I think I have to change it, because we just discovered a symbol of the far left — an idiot waving … a Mexican flag.”

On several occasions, Vance returned to the incident as a broader political point, later telling the crowd that while the demonstrator waved a foreign flag, Republicans would continue “to wave the American flag and fight for the American dream.”

He praised Trump’s immigration policy, outlining the administration’s efforts to reduce illegal immigration, while calling it “the first government in the last 80 years to reverse the border invasion.” He also highlighted immigration while arguing that Republicans were prioritizing jobs for U.S. citizens.

After the incident, NBC correspondent Garrett Haake posted a comment on social media, wondering if the episode had been staged.

“Vance’s quippy response to a protestor who interrupted and threw a Mexican flag on stage was SO quick it kind of makes you wonder if that wasn’t entirely a surprise,” Haake wrote.

Prior to the convention, Vance has primarily spoken about Mexico in the context of U.S. border security, illegal immigration and drug cartels.

In a visit to the Mexico-U.S. border in March 2025, he described U.S. actions and tariffs as a good-faith effort to help prevent Mexico from turning into a “narco state,” while also consistently supporting the designation of Mexican drug cartels as foreign terrorist organizations.

With reports from Newsweek, Fox News, N+ and La Jornada

World.title: El Jalapeño: Trump suggests renaming New Mexico as ‘New America,’ Mexico as ‘South America’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

WASHINGTON, District of Columbia — Following a series of social media posts proposing the rebranding of the Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario and the state of New Mexico, which he now calls “New America,” U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Tuesday that the country of Mexico itself change its name to “South America.”

“We’ve looked at the maps, folks, and frankly, having a Mexico and a New Mexico — which, by the way, will soon be New America, very prestigious, very beautiful — it’s extremely redundant and confusing for everyday people,” Trump posted on Truth Social. “Nobody knew maps were this complicated, but under South America, it works very nicely, keeps everything clean, and frankly, everyone is saying it’s a tremendous idea.”

The proposal, unveiled directly across social media alongside a digitally altered map rendered in thick red marker and an AI-generated video, aims to streamline continental nomenclature while bestowing what White House aides subsequently described as “unprecedented brand clarity” upon the Western Hemisphere.

In Mexico City, federal officials received the social media posts with the practiced composure typical of bilateral relations. “We have taken note of the online activity,” said a spokesperson for the Foreign Affairs Ministry, pausing to review a map that has remained unchanged since 1821. “While we appreciate the administrative enthusiasm from our northern neighbor, Mexico will continue to be called Mexico, as updating all of our official letterhead would introduce an unnecessary diplomatic expense.”

International trade analysts pointed out that a full renaming would require altering thousands of bilateral treaties, cross-border shipping manifests and billions of dollars in consumer packaging. Cartographers also noted that despite the digital sticker graphics shared on social media, global geographic standards will remain governed by international consensus rather than individual online posts.

When asked by reporters how the administration planned to resolve the obvious naming conflict with the twelve sovereign nations already occupying the continent of South America, White House aides briefly paused, consulted a wall map, and clarified that those countries could simply be referred to as “Farther South America” going forward.

World.title: Officials report 63% drop in Chiapas homicides: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Chiapas homicides down 63% : Speaking from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Sheinbaum touted security gains under Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, saying “people feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago.” Officials reported the daily homicide rate fell 63% in the first eight months of 2026 compared to 2024, with 9,949 arrests and 18.6 tonnes of drugs seized in the southern state since Sheinbaum took office.

: Speaking from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Sheinbaum touted security gains under Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, saying “people feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago.” Officials reported the daily homicide rate fell 63% in the first eight months of 2026 compared to 2024, with 9,949 arrests and 18.6 tonnes of drugs seized in the southern state since Sheinbaum took office. 📚 Pencils over screens after poor PISA scores : Responding to this week’s PISA results showing 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below basic level in math, science and reading, Sheinbaum announced new math and reading textbooks for teachers and students, and highlighted plans to regulate device use in schools while pushing a “return to pencil and paper.”

: Responding to this week’s PISA results showing 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below basic level in math, science and reading, Sheinbaum announced new math and reading textbooks for teachers and students, and highlighted plans to regulate device use in schools while pushing a “return to pencil and paper.” 🏥 CJNG ‘clandestine hospital’ found in Jalisco: García Harfuch confirmed that a property in Tecalitlán used by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel to treat injured members was uncovered during the search for a missing 20-year-old man, who was among eight people freed from the site.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, capital of the southern state of Chiapas.

At the start of the mañanera, Sheinbaum said that since Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office in December 2024, and “with the coordination with the federal [Security] Cabinet,” the security results in Chiapas have been “very good, not just in the reduction of homicides and other high-impact crimes, but also in the perception [of insecurity].”

“People feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago,” she said.

Later in the press conference, security officials presented the latest data on homicides, high-impact crimes and arrests in Chiapas, a state where violence increased significantly in 2024, especially near the border with Guatemala.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks on how the government plans to improve both the teaching and learning of mathematics and reading in Mexican schools. Her comments came three days after the publication of PISA testing results that showed that around four in 10 Mexicans 15-year-olds scored below the basic level in science, mathematics and reading.

Homicides down 63% in Chiapas compared to 2024

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa noted that the homicide rate in Chiapas remained “quite stable” between 2015 and 2023 before increasing significantly in 2024, a year in which an average of 2.4 murders per day were committed in the state.

She noted that the daily homicide rate in the first eight months of this year was 0.9, representing a reduction of 63% compared to 2024. The year-over-year decline was 10%, according to the data presented.

Figueroa also reported that the daily homicide rate in Chiapas in August — 0.9 — was 64% lower than the rate in December 2024, the month Ramírez was sworn in as governor.

With regard to high-impact crimes, among which are homicides, kidnappings, violent robberies and acts of extortion, the daily incidence in Chiapas in August was 2.7, a reduction of 44% compared to November 2024. The data presented by Figueroa showed that the daily incidence of high-impact crimes rose 8% between August 2025 and August 2026.

Later in the press conference, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that 9,949 people were arrested in Chiapas between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum took office — and Aug. 31, 2026, for allegedly committing high-impact crimes. Authorities seized 1,545 firearms and 18.6 tonnes of drugs in the state in the same period.

Sheinbaum outlines strategies to improve educational outcomes

A reporter asked the president whether Mexico’s education system needs to be strengthened in light of the PISA results published this week. In testing for the OECD’s Program for International Student Assessment, 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below the basic level in the science/math/reading triad, more than double the 19.7% average across OECD countries. Education Minister Mario Delgado on Wednesday addressed the low scores earned by Mexican students by blaming “the excessive use of cell phones and computer screens.”

Sheinbaum asserted that “education in Mexico is getting stronger,” before acknowledging that Mexican students have ground to make up.

“We have to make progress in mathematics. We’re going to have a special textbook next year for the learning of mathematics, to help the teachers and the students,” she said.

Sheinbaum subsequently highlighted that Mexico wasn’t the only country to score poorly in the reading domain of the PISA testing.

She said that “all the countries of the world” scored poorly on reading, “with the exception of four or five, due to the use of digital platforms.”

“[That was] acknowledged by the education area of the OECD. Young people, girls and boys, stopped reading and understanding what they read due to the excessive use of digital platforms, which is something that we’re now addressing,” Sheinbaum said, referring to a plan to implement national regulations on the use of devices in schools.

“[We’re going to] return to pencil and paper, pen and paper, and reading,” she said.

Sheinbaum said the teaching of reading and writing in Mexican schools will also be supported by a new textbook.

She said that the new textbook (or likely textbooks for different grades) will include poems and short stories that girls and boys “should know.”

Clandestine CJNG hospital discovered in Jalisco

A reporter asked García Harfuch about the discovery of a clandestine Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) hospital in the state of Jalisco.

🚔 En rueda de prensa se informó que la Vicefiscalía en Personas Desaparecidas, en coordinación con la Guardia Nacional y la Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional, realizó un operativo en Tecalitlán que permitió rescatar a ocho hombres y detener a seis personas. (1-3) pic.twitter.com/Vbe47OAf8T — Fiscalía del Estado de Jalisco (@FiscaliaJal) September 10, 2026

The Informador newspaper reported on Thursday that the search for a 20-year-old man who went missing in Tlaquepaque in July led authorities to a property in the municipality of Tecalitlán that was used as a clandestine hospital by the CJNG. Informador noted that six people were detained at the property. Eight alleged victims of forced recruitment, including the missing 20-year-old, were freed.

García Harfuch confirmed that injured “organized crime people” were treated at the property. He added that investigations related to the discovery of the property are still being carried out.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: The ultimate guide to contemporary Mexican restaurants in Guadalajara
World.content:
Mexican Independence Day celebrations this month offer a great opportunity to celebrate and rediscover Mexican food, and what better way to do it than through five restaurants that are putting a contemporary spin on traditional Mexican cuisine?

From chilaquiles with poblano chile sauce to eggplant tamales and corn pancakes, here are some of the best contemporary Mexican restaurants in Guadalajara to try right now.

Ixtle

Located in Zapopan, Ixtle defines itself as a kitchen true to its roots: A relaxed concept that takes corn and Mexican ingredients as its starting point, reinterpreting them through international techniques and references.

In the mornings, guests can enjoy innovative dishes such as the Jarocho Breakfast, featuring eggs in hoja santa with longaniza, banana and confit mushrooms, or waffles made from maize accompanied by a blend of caramelized miso, maple syrup, honey, mascarpone and macadamia butter.

Lovers of traditional hot café de olla will appreciate Ixtle’s reinterpretation of a staple of Mexican cuisine — the café de olla latte, served cold with orange peel and a touch of foamy milk.

At night, the menu becomes more elaborate, drawing on a wider range of international influences and featuring dishes that are designed to be shared. The Mediterranean tuna tiradito, served with red peppers in pil-pil sauce and nixtamalized tomato paste, is a must-try.

Best for: Breakfasts with friends or a date night

Breakfasts with friends or a date night Location: C. Miguel León Portilla 478, Santa Fe, 45168 Zapopan, Jalisco

C. Miguel León Portilla 478, Santa Fe, 45168 Zapopan, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/ixtle_rest

Teté Cocina de Barrio

Spearheaded by siblings Mario and Karla Papa, Teté has been delighting tapatíos for over a decade through a cuisine that blends Mexico’s culinary heritage with flavors introduced by the different cultures that have settled in the country.

With an approach that prioritizes seasonal ingredients, the menu at Teté not only changes every month, but it is a complete surprise for diners, who do not know what they will have for dinner until dishes start arriving.

Guests are also in for another surprise: Teté does not have waiters. Instead, everyone does a bit of everything, with the chefs themselves guiding diners throughout the meal.

With no waiters and no menu, Teté defines itself as a restaurant that “doesn’t repeat menus, but experiences.” It’s no wonder this unpretentious restaurant in the Moderna neighborhood has made it to coveted culinary rankings around the world.

Best for: Date night

Date night Location: C. Rayón 830, Moderna, 44170 Guadalajara, Jalisco

C. Rayón 830, Moderna, 44170 Guadalajara, Jalisco Website: tete-cocina-de-barrio.mailchimpsites.com

Amorcito Mío

Located in the heart of Zapopan Centro and just steps away from the Zapopan Basílica, Amorcito Mío offers a warm atmosphere and home-cooked-style recipes.

Although the breakfast menu offers international dishes such as sandwiches and paninis, it is simultaneously a celebration of Mexican food, albeit with a twist.

Guests will be surprised by the variety of sauces featured on the chilaquiles menu beyond the traditional red and green. Expect chilaquiles with poblano chile sauce, spicy peanut sauce and a super spicy sauce made from güero chiles and habanero.

To balance the heat, Amorcito Mío offers a varied selection of Mexican breads, including pan dulce staples like conchas, as well as traditional bolillo and birote.

While breakfasts highlight authentic Mexican flavors, the menu shifts in the afternoon and evening to feature wood-fired pizzas and a blend of Italian and Mediterranean dishes.

Best for: Casual gatherings with friends

Casual gatherings with friends Location: Calle 5 de Mayo 275, Zapopan, 45100 Zapopan, Jalisco

Calle 5 de Mayo 275, Zapopan, 45100 Zapopan, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/amorcito_mi

Bruna

View this post on Instagram A post shared by BRUNA (@bruna_mx)

With a terrace surrounded by lush gardens and sculptures, Bruna generates excitement from the very first moment, offering diners an almost theatrical experience.

Since opening in 2015, chef Óscar Garza has drawn inspiration from Mexican abuelitas’ recipes and street-food flavors, reinterpreting them with contemporary techniques and an artistic presentation.

Among the dishes that stand out for their meticulous presentation is the chile en nogada, which returns to the menu each year during the patriotic month. Las probaditas de mole, literally meaning “little tastes of mole,” features a rainbow of colors and flavors that pushes the boundaries of classic mole poblano.

If you are looking for something sweet and original, be sure to try the bruleated corn cream, a dessert that blends the traditional flavor of corn with the classic French twist of crème brûlée.

Best for: Special occasions

Special occasions Location: Lerdo de Tejada No. 2418, Col. Lafayette, Guadalajara, Jalisco

Lerdo de Tejada No. 2418, Col. Lafayette, Guadalajara, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/bruna_mx

Tikuun Comedor Local

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tikuun comedor (@tikuun.comedor)

Spearheaded by chef Carlos Espinosa, Tikuun has been open for over a decade, but only recently began receiving the recognition it deserves.

Situated in the trendy Colonia Americana, it features a constantly rotating menu that showcases new preparations and seasonal variations throughout the year. Although the menu draws inspiration from different cultures and cuisines, the restaurant’s manifesto promises a distinctly Mexican essence in each dish.

Standout recent offerings include roasted eggplant with cured nopal, aged cotija, salsa macha made with chia and Kalamata olives, requesón cheese and garlic confit, as well as octopus with recado negro, chinchayote, sweet potato and beet.

The intimate, almost home-like atmosphere allows guests to savor the experience at a leisurely pace, whether ordering a la carte or opting for the tasting menu.

Best for: An intimate dinner with friends

An intimate dinner with friends Location: Emeterio Robles Gil 50, Col. Americana, 44600 Guadalajara, Jalisco

Emeterio Robles Gil 50, Col. Americana, 44600 Guadalajara, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/tikuun.comedor

Gabriela Solís is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: Dominican Republic Murder Rate Falls to 7.39 per 100,000
World.content:
DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · SECURITY

Key Facts — The number The Dominican Republic’s accumulated murder rate stands at 7.39 per 100,000 inhabitants through 4 September 2026, according to the joint task force’s 164th weekly crime report.

— The trend The rate has fallen every year since 2022, when it was 13.20. Last year closed at a validated 8.7, the presidency says.

— The map Authorities say 28 territories covering 80 percent of the country now record single-digit murder rates.

— The week Five murders and 34 people wounded were logged in the latest weekly period, alongside 563 robberies and 171 traffic accidents.

— The region Independent crime trackers put Jamaica near 49, Haiti and Trinidad and Tobago around 40, and Puerto Rico near 15 murders per 100,000 — all far above the Dominican figure.

The Dominican Republic is on track to close 2026 with its lowest murder rate in decades — a number the government of Luis Abinader has made the centerpiece of its security record, and one its critics say deserves a closer look at the fine print.

The Dominican Republic’s accumulated homicide rate reached 7.39 per 100,000 inhabitants as of 4 September 2026, the Fuerza de Tarea Conjunta — the joint police-military task force that produces the country’s weekly crime statistics — reported in its 164th weekly analysis, published on 11 September.

If the trend holds, 2026 will be the safest year in the country’s modern crime statistics. The comparison set released with the report shows the accumulated rate at 8.74 for the same period of 2025, 9.65 in 2024, 11.49 in 2023 and 13.20 in 2022 — an almost unbroken decline of roughly 44 percent in four years.

A Quiet Week Behind the Headline Number

The weekly report that produced the 7.39 figure counted five murders and 34 people wounded by violence in the period under review, in a country of about 11 million. It also logged 563 robberies and 171 traffic accidents — a reminder that everyday insecurity in the Dominican Republic is less about homicide than about street robbery and some of the deadliest roads in the hemisphere.

Geographically, the improvement is broad. The task force says 28 territories, together covering 80 percent of the national territory, now post single-digit murder rates — meaning the remaining hotspots, concentrated in parts of Santo Domingo and a handful of provincial cities, account for a growing share of the killings that remain.

Two Sets of Books

There is a caveat built into the number, and the government itself acknowledges it. The weekly task-force figures are operational police statistics — preliminary counts that can be revised. The presidency announced in March that 2025 closed at a validated rate of 8.7 per 100,000, based on 951 intentional homicides, after the Interior and Police Ministry’s crime-data analysis center CADSECI and its operational technical unit consolidated and validated the year’s records. Notably, that validated figure came in 0.6 points above the task force’s own preliminary estimate for the year — validation cut the number up, not down.

The 8.74 in this week’s comparison set is a different beast: the accumulated operational rate to the same September cut-off last year, not a full-year close. That distinction is exactly where the political argument lives. Opposition voices have long questioned which deaths enter the official count, how “intentional homicide” is defined against broader violent-death categories, how foreign-national victims are treated, and how often cases are reclassified after the weekly snapshot. None of that overturns the trend: available independent analyses of Dominican homicide data all point the same way. But it does mean the 7.39 should be read as a strong operational signal, not a final audited statistic.

An Outlier in a Violent Neighborhood

Set against the region, the Dominican number is striking. Independent crime-data trackers put Jamaica’s murder rate near 49 per 100,000, Haiti’s and Trinidad and Tobago’s around 40, and Puerto Rico’s near 15. Those comparisons come with their own methodology warnings — different countries count differently, and Haiti’s statistics are fragmentary in the best of times — but the orders of magnitude are not in dispute.

Within Latin America as a whole, where regional averages still sit well into double digits, a rate in the sevens would place the Dominican Republic among the safer countries on the continent. Security analysts such as InSight Crime have noted the country’s trajectory, while cautioning that low homicide rates coexist with persistent organized crime, drug transshipment and contract killing markets that rarely show up in the headline number.

Abinader’s Security Card

For President Luis Abinader, the statistics are political capital. Citizen security was one of his administration’s flagship promises, and the government now opens nearly every security presentation with the homicide curve. The validated 8.7 close for 2025 was announced from the National Palace itself — a sign of how central the number has become to the official narrative.

Critics counter that the homicide rate is the wrong single lens: robbery, extortion and femicide weigh heavily in public perception surveys, and trust in the police remains fragile. The weekly report’s own 563 robberies in seven days illustrate why many Dominicans say they do not feel as safe as the murder statistics suggest they should.

Still, the direction of travel is now long enough to be undeniable. A country that recorded 13.20 murders per 100,000 just four years ago is measuring itself in the sevens — and in a Caribbean basin where several neighbors are moving the other way, that divergence may be the Abinader government’s most durable claim on the record.

World.title: Mexico’s INE ‘Has Given In’ on Policing Elections, Council Member Warns
World.content:
MEXICO · POLITICS

Key Facts — The accusation INE council member Arturo Castillo said at the opening of the 2026–2027 electoral process that the institute “appears to have given in” on its duty to watch over and arbitrate elections.

— The context Mexico’s biggest-ever electoral process started September 10: some 102 million citizens will be eligible to vote on June 6, 2027.

— The reply Council member Arturo Chávez answered that one council member does not speak for the INE and accused critics of joining a campaign to discredit it.

— The alliance Sergio Aguayo, Denise Dresser, Mauricio Merino, José Woldenberg and hundreds more signed a call for a Democratic Alliance for Election Observation.

— The flashpoints Early Morena campaigning, “pre-folded ballots” left over from 2024, and whether government social-program workers may register as election observers.

— The president’s answer INE president Guadalupe Taddei closed the session saying the institute “will not be intimidated by absolutely anyone.”

Mexico’s electoral referee opened the 2027 campaign season by arguing with itself — a sitting council member says the INE has surrendered its job of policing the parties, while a civic alliance of academics and journalists organizes to watch every step of the vote.

The formal starting gun for Mexico’s 2027 elections fired on Thursday, September 10, in an extraordinary session of the INE’s General Council — and the first voice to define the day was that of a man inside the institution accusing it of surrender. “The INE appears to have given in on its function of watching over and arbitrating the elections,” said council member Arturo Castillo Loza, opening what became a public reckoning over the credibility of Mexico’s electoral authority.

The process now underway is, by the institute’s own description, the largest in Mexican history: about 102 million citizens will be eligible to vote on June 6, 2027, in federal midterms and state contests. Castillo called the moment “the perfect scenario for a questioned election.”

What Castillo Said

Castillo’s charge, reported by Reforma, was specific. “In recent months the referee has renounced watching that the political parties keep to the electoral calendar, and renounced preventing parties and governments from meddling in the organization and observation of the elections,” he said. “These decisions will directly affect the equity of the contest.”

Without naming him, Castillo pointed to Armando Ayala, a Morena aspirant in Baja California who — as Castillo noted — openly boasts of having already campaigned for 75 days. Under Mexican law, campaigning outside the official windows is prohibited; enforcing those windows is precisely the function Castillo says the council has abandoned.

The Council Fights Back

The reply came from Arturo Chávez, a newer council member, who drew a constitutional line around Castillo’s remarks: “When a council member speaks individually, the INE does not speak. The INE speaks only in its institutional decisions.” He went further: “We know that the loss of some privileges leads some to renounce this noble institution and join a campaign to discredit it. They will not succeed.”

Nine council members used the session to flag the challenges of the cycle — organized-crime interference, political violence, and annual budget cuts to the institute. Council member Carla Humphrey demanded tight coordination between the INE and security agencies so citizens can “vote in peace” on June 6, 2027. Martín Faz noted this will be the first process run by technical directorates appointed by president Guadalupe Taddei rather than by the General Council, and warned staff that their “first obligation is not to a person or an administrative hierarchy — it is to the Constitution.” Uuc-Kib Espadas, visibly angry, turned on the parties themselves: all seven, he said, had “given in” by failing to challenge the “pre-folded ballot” fraud of 2024, and now had no right to silence. “Do not give in again,” he told them, pledging INE presence at all 170,000 polling stations.

Taddei closed the session by rejecting “bad omens from inside or outside this institute” and promising the INE “will not be intimidated by absolutely anyone.”

What the Parties Demanded

Opposition parties used the opening to press the same demand from different angles: impartiality. For the PAN, Senator Verónica Rodríguez told the council: “We do not want an INE favorable to Acción Nacional. We want an INE without a blue shirt, but also without a guinda one,” — a reference to Morena’s maroon — “capable of telling the federal Executive, a governor, a party or any power: this far and no further.”

PRI president Alejandro Moreno asked the council members how they wanted to be remembered — “as those who defended democracy, or those who bent before power” — and accused the institute of a double standard: investigations and precautionary measures for the opposition, “tolerance and shielding” for Morena. Juan Ignacio Zavala of Movimiento Ciudadano said early and illegal campaigning had become a habit “created by Morena and adopted by the PRIAN,” though Morena, he added, “takes the medal as the most cheating party.”

Morena’s president, Ariadna Montiel, attended an INE session for the first time and answered none of the specific accusations directly, saying her party would comply with the law and accusing conservatives of preparing a “dirty war” of fabricated charges.

The Citizens Step In

The same day, a group of academics, journalists and civil-society figures published a signed call for a Democratic Alliance for Election Observation, reported by El Universal. Among the signatories are four of the best-known names in Mexican civic life: political scientist Sergio Aguayo, journalist Denise Dresser, former electoral councilor Mauricio Merino and José Woldenberg, the founding president of the INE’s predecessor institute. The document, circulated by the Institute for the Rule of Law and Democracy, also carries signatures including former electoral magistrates María del Carmen Alanís and María Marván Laborde and jurist Diego Valadés.

The alliance proposes mass citizen observation of every stage of the 2026–2027 process — not only election day — with special attention on the states that will elect governors. It warns of risks to freedom of expression and electoral legitimacy, and describes both the INE and the electoral court, the TEPJF, as facing “a process of political capture” — the signatories’ position, not any official finding.

Why This Matters for Foreigners in Mexico

The INE is not an abstraction for the expatriate community: it issues the voter infrastructure that underpins the country’s political stability, and the 2027 midterms will define the second half of the term of President Claudia Sheinbaum, whose government is simultaneously resisting U.S. pressure over the cartel fight and defending its electoral flank at home. The specific disputes to watch are procedural but telling — whether early campaigning by ruling-party aspirants is sanctioned, whether “pre-folded ballots” trigger automatic cancellation, and whether the government’s Servidores de la Nación social workers may register as election observers, a point opposition parties say blurs the line between state and party.

None of this threatens daily life, investments or residency. But Mexico’s elections have since the 1990s been the anchor of its democratic credibility with foreign partners and markets. A referee publicly accused by one of its own members of giving in — and defended by another as the target of a smear campaign — is a signal that the 2027 vote will be fought over the rules as much as over the candidates.

World.title: Venezuela Power Crisis Casts Shadow Over Washington’s Oil Deal Timetable
World.content:
Venezuela · Energy

Key Facts —The question. El Estímulo asks whether Venezuela’s power crisis endangers Washington’s oil plans: blackouts hit several states again this week while the government negotiates what the outlet calls the biggest oil deal in the country’s history. —The deficit. Sector analysts put the grid’s structural shortfall at about 2,000 megawatts against national demand of more than 14,000, according to El Estímulo, which reports that more than half the population lives under power rationing. —The plan. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced agreements with GE Vernova in Caracas on September 3: restart existing assets within six to twelve months, then 1 gigawatt of new capacity in two years and 5 more gigawatts in the following four. —The outages. A severe fluctuation on Tuesday night cut power across greater Caracas and at least ten states; another cut hit on Thursday night. Corpoelec offered no technical explanation. —The workaround. Since June, a regulatory reform of the Hydrocarbons Law has required oil companies — Chevron included — to install their own generation and run off the national grid where possible, according to El Estímulo. —The stakes. Economist Asdrúbal Oliveros estimates Venezuelan oil output will grow by more than 280,000 barrels a day this year — growth that needs electricity the current system cannot reliably supply.

Venezuela’s power crisis is colliding with Washington’s oil timetable: as blackouts swept Caracas and at least ten states this week, El Estímulo asked whether a grid running some 2,000 megawatts short can carry what it calls the biggest oil deal in the country’s history.

A Week of Outages, No Official Explanation

On Tuesday, September 8, at around 7:18 p.m., a severe fluctuation in the National Electric System interrupted service and triggered voltage drops across greater Caracas — including the Distrito Capital — and at least ten states, among them Miranda, La Guaira, Aragua, Carabobo, Anzoátegui, Sucre, Nueva Esparta, Zulia, Táchira, Mérida, Trujillo and Barinas, El Nacional reported. Parts of Guarenas and Guatire, satellite cities east of the capital, went dark; residents reported smaller fluctuations earlier the same day.

On Thursday night, several states lost power again, El Estímulo reported on Friday. How long each cut lasted is impossible to establish: the state utility Corpoelec offered no technical explanation, and information was pieced together, as usual, on social media under the hashtag #SinLuz — “without light.”

The pattern is chronic. Rotating blackouts and simultaneous failures have become routine across much of the country, on a system that sector analysts estimate is running with a structural deficit of about 2,000 megawatts against national demand of more than 14,000, El Estímulo reported. According to the outlet, more than half of Venezuelans live under some form of power rationing, and daily outages — scheduled or not — hit the provinces harder than Caracas.

Wright’s Plan: Six to Twelve Months Just to Stabilize

The latest plan to reverse the deficit arrived on September 3, when US Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced in Caracas a set of agreements with GE Vernova to intervene in electric infrastructure tied to the oil industry and to recover components of the national grid together with state oil company Pdvsa and Corpoelec. Acting president Delcy Rodríguez called the deal a “historic step” — the first time a government of the Chavista movement has contracted a US company to maintain or renew the country’s electric service.

Wright’s own timetable is sobering. The first phase aims to restart assets that already exist — among them the Guri hydroelectric dam, which Wright said produces only half of the energy it was designed for because turbines and transmission lines have gone without maintenance — within six to twelve months. Only then would come 1 gigawatt of new capacity in two years, and another 5 gigawatts in the four years after that. Full stabilization, on that schedule, is a six-year project with first improvements visible within a year.

That is the tension at the heart of the story: the ceremony was immediate, the megawatts are not. The same week that Washington’s energy chief toured Venezuela to unveil the package, the grid failed twice in three days.

Why Oil Needs the Grid

Electricity is not a side issue to the oil deal — it is a precondition. Economist Asdrúbal Oliveros told Unión Radio this week that rising oil and mining output puts pressure on a system already operating without margin. “It is what economists call a supply constraint,” he said — an obstacle that slows growth because it is not in step with the pace of the country. Carabobo state, the heart of Venezuela’s industrial base, is suffering one of its most critical electricity situations, with deterioration that has worsened over the past three months.

Part of the official answer is to take the oil industry out of that bottleneck. Since June, a regulatory reform of the Organic Hydrocarbons Law has required oil companies operating in Venezuela — Chevron included — to install their own power generation and function, as far as possible, off the national grid, according to El Estímulo. But as the outlet notes, that does not solve the underlying problem: even if new fields generate their own electricity, the expansion promised under the agreement with Nabep — more wells, more rigs, more treatment plants — still depends on contractors, transport and the cities where the workforce lives, all of which run on the public grid.

Oliveros estimates Venezuelan oil production grew by some 100,000 barrels a day in 2025 and will close this year with an increase of more than 280,000 barrels a day — nearly triple — with another 300,000 projected for 2027, according to El Estímulo. The visible economic effects, he cautions, will only be felt toward the second half of 2027 and in 2028 — roughly the same horizon on which Washington’s promised new generation capacity is supposed to arrive.

The Questions Left Hanging

For foreign residents and investors, the opacity surrounding both the oil contract and the power plan leaves the same questions El Estímulo poses: how much will fixing the grid cost, who will pay for it — and will the lights stop going out? Until the answers arrive, every megawatt of promised oil growth travels through a network that failed twice this week alone.

As The Rio Times reported this morning, Venezuelan crude production is already holding at a seven-year high. Sustaining and expanding it is exactly what the power system, in its current state, is least prepared to do.

Frequently Asked Questions

How bad is Venezuela’s power crisis right now?

Sector analysts estimate a structural deficit of about 2,000 megawatts against demand above 14,000. More than half the population faces rationing, and this week alone outages hit greater Caracas and at least ten states on Tuesday night, with further cuts on Thursday night. Corpoelec has given no technical explanation.

What did the US announce for Venezuela’s electric grid?

On September 3 in Caracas, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced agreements with GE Vernova, Pdvsa and Corpoelec: restart existing assets — including the Guri dam, running at half capacity — within six to twelve months, then add 1 gigawatt in two years and 5 more gigawatts over the following four.

Does the power crisis threaten the US-Venezuela oil deal?

Yes, according to El Estímulo’s analysis: oil expansion needs electricity the grid cannot reliably supply. A June reform forces oil firms to generate their own power, but contractors, transport and workers’ cities still depend on the public network.

World.title: Cuba Blackout Alert: Grid Expects 2,000 MW Shortfall at Friday Peak
World.content:
CUBA · ENERGY

Key Facts — The forecast Cuba’s state utility UNE expects 2,000 MW of peak-hour impact on Friday 11 September, with 1,330 MW available against 3,300 MW of demand.

— Thursday’s reality The grid fell short by 2,267 MW at 8:40 p.m., worse than planned, after units in Cienfuegos and Felton tripped, and service was disrupted around the clock.

— The dead plants Six big thermoelectric units are down for breakdowns or maintenance at Mariel, Felton, Renté, Santa Cruz and Nuevitas.

— No fuel 106 distributed generators are offline for lack of fuel, and both of Havana’s floating power barges are out of service.

— The year so far Cuba has suffered seven total national grid collapses in 2026, three of them in July alone and two within 24 hours in early August.

Cuba’s electricity utility has told 11 million people to expect a 2,000-megawatt hole in Friday night’s power supply — a shortfall so large it would leave three-fifths of peak demand unmet in a country where entire towns have already spent more than a hundred days without light.

Cuba’s Unión Eléctrica (UNE) forecast in its morning bulletin on Friday 11 September 2026 that the national grid would be unable to meet 2,000 MW of demand at the evening peak, the worst daily figure announced this week after 2,130 MW on Thursday.

The official note, republished by the state daily Granma, puts available generation at 1,330 MW against a forecast peak demand of 3,300 MW. In plain terms: when Cubans cook dinner tonight, the state expects to be missing about 60 percent of the electricity the country wants.

Thursday was already worse than planned. The deficit peaked at 2,267 MW at 8:40 p.m. — above the forecast — after unit 3 of the Cienfuegos plant and unit 1 of the Felton plant dropped offline, and the service was disrupted for the full 24 hours, UNE said.

What 2,000 MW Looks Like on the Ground

The abstract megawatt arithmetic translates into a geography of darkness. Havana’s electric company reported 51 circuits cut for generation deficit on Friday morning. In Sancti Spíritus province, 75 MW were offline across circuits in Banao, Mayajigua and Yaguajay. In Holguín, several circuits had passed 22 hours without power, according to the provincial utility’s own logs.

Independent tracker CiberCuba, which compiles the official provincial reports, recorded no active total collapse on Friday — the grid is technically “interconnected” — but that says nothing about how many homes actually have electricity. Energy Minister Vicente de la O Levy has acknowledged that some Cuban settlements have gone more than a hundred days without power.

Frustration is spilling into the streets. In late July, women and children from the Havana neighbourhood known as El Fanguito blocked Avenida 23 until authorities restored power, and on Friday Cubans were protesting government plans to restrict the installation of private solar panels — the one workaround many households and small businesses have found, according to 14ymedio.

A Grid Running on Fumes

The official bulletin reads like a casualty list. Down for breakdowns: unit 5 at Máximo Gómez in Mariel, unit 2 at Lidio Ramón Pérez in Felton, and unit 6 at Antonio Maceo in Renté. In maintenance: another unit at Renté, plus units at Santa Cruz del Norte and the Diez de Octubre plant in Nuevitas. These are the workhorse thermoelectrics of the system — most of them decades old and cannibalised for parts.

The fuel picture is worse. UNE reports 106 distributed-generation plants — the diesel engines that are supposed to cover peak demand — out of service for lack of fuel. Both floating power barges moored in Havana Bay, the Regla and Melones units, are offline, as are the fuel-oil plants at Mariel and Moa. The only growth sector is solar: photovoltaic parks delivered 5,120 MWh on Thursday with a midday peak of 795 MW — useful at noon, irrelevant at 8:40 p.m.

Seven Collapses and Counting

The 2026 tally now stands at seven complete collapses of the national grid, according to CiberCuba’s running count: three in July within eight days, then two inside 24 hours on 2 and 3 August, when a frequency oscillation knocked the system back down just as engineers were restoring it. “We keep moving forward on the restoration of our system, overcoming all kinds of difficulties, with a total energy siege,” the energy minister wrote then — language that did little for households measuring outages in days.

Each collapse resets a slow, fragile reboot: microsystems island-by-island, hospitals and water pumps first, ordinary neighbourhoods last. Between collapses, the system simply runs a permanent deficit of 1,700 to 2,300 MW most evenings this month — Friday’s 2,000 MW forecast is, grimly, routine.

What It Means for Residents and Visitors

For foreigners in Cuba — a smaller group by the month, as The Rio Times reported with the collapse of tourism arrivals — the practical advice is unchanged: expect outages of 12 to 20 hours outside hotel cores, carry power banks and cash, and do not count on mobile data, since cell towers fail with the grid. Hotels that remain open run on diesel generators, which is why the fuel shortage hits them too.

There is no official horizon for improvement. The government blames the US sanctions “siege” for starving it of fuel and spare parts; independent analysts point to decades of underinvestment in plants that are now failing faster than they can be repaired. Both can be true at once — and neither will keep the lights on tonight.

World.title: US Approves Four Refurbished Black Hawk Helicopters for Argentina
World.content:
ARGENTINA · DEFENSE

Key Facts — The deal The U.S. State Department approved a possible Foreign Military Sale of four refurbished UH-60L Black Hawk helicopters plus equipment to Argentina, notified to Congress on Thursday, September 10.

— The price The notification to Congress estimates US$140 million; Infobae reports an estimated value of US$40 million against that ceiling. The final contract price has not been set.

— The recipient The Army Aviation Command, whose Bell UH-1H and Huey II helicopters are decades old. Argentina currently flies a single Black Hawk, used for presidential transport.

— The package Two General Electric T700-GE-701D engines, radios, navigation and identification systems, rescue hoists, a Bambi Bucket firefighting rig, spares and training; contractor Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company.

— The timing The approval lands in the sharpest Argentina-Britain confrontation over the Falklands in years — sanctions on 45 companies, criminal complaints, and Milei’s suspended London trip.

— The fine print Washington says the sale “will not alter the basic military balance in the region” and requires no extra U.S. personnel in Argentina.

Four second-hand American helicopters would not normally make headlines. This week they do — because they arrive as Argentina and Britain square off over the Falklands, and because Washington is unmistakably choosing a side in public.

The United States has approved the possible sale of four refurbished Black Hawk helicopters to Argentina, a modest defense purchase that would barely register in a normal week. Notified to Congress on Thursday, September 10, at the height of the Falklands confrontation between Buenos Aires and London, it is anything but normal — a small, pointed signal of where Washington stands.

The U.S. ambassador in Buenos Aires, Peter Lamelas, announced the move on X: “Argentina will receive refurbished Black Hawk helicopters in staggered deliveries, starting with four units, to strengthen defense and respond to emergencies. It’s not just equipment: it’s arriving on time and saving lives.”

What Argentina Is Buying

The aircraft are UH-60L Black Hawks — an older variant of a Sikorsky design that has been in service for close to 50 years and now flies in more than thirty countries, including Colombia and Brazil. The Argentine request, described in regional reporting as covering reconditioned airframes, is being processed as a U.S. Foreign Military Sale, meaning the seller is the U.S. government rather than a private dealer.

Beyond the four helicopters, the notification lists two General Electric T700-GE-701D engines — the family that also powers the Apache attack helicopter — plus heading and attitude reference systems, Identification Friend or Foe transponders, high- and very-high-frequency radios, a Garmin GTN-750 navigation unit and an emergency locator transmitter. Rescue and emergency equipment includes a fast-rope extraction system, hoist gear and a Bambi Bucket for aerial firefighting, alongside helmets, spares, tools, documentation, crew training and logistics support. The prime contractor is Sikorsky, the Lockheed Martin subsidiary based in Stratford, Connecticut. The State Department said it had no offset agreement on record for the deal.

The Price Question

What Argentina will actually pay is not yet fixed — the approval covers a possible sale, and final contracts in such cases routinely come in below the notified ceiling. That ceiling, in the notification sent to Congress on September 10 (Transmittal 26-79), is US$140 million for the complete package. Argentine media headlined that figure; Infobae, citing the official statement, reports an estimated value of US$40 million against the US$140 million cap. Specialist outlet Zona Militar reports the Army expects to take the first four aircraft in December — initially in the United States, for crew transition training.

For scale: even at the full ceiling, the package is a fraction of the cost of the Danish F-16 fighter program — but the Black Hawks fill a gap money alone has not fixed. The Army Aviation Command still relies on Bell UH-1H and Huey II helicopters that have been flying for decades. Argentina’s only Black Hawk until now has been a single VIP aircraft assigned to presidential transport. Defense Minister Luis Petri identified Black Hawks as an Army priority back in 2024, and analyst Andrei Serbin Pont anticipated in Infobae that a first pair could arrive before the end of this year, with two more in 2027.

One Piece of a Bigger Rearmament

The helicopters slot into the broadest Argentine military modernization drive in decades. The Air Force is integrating F-16s bought from Denmark — a second batch of six is due this month — and has been testing Link 16 data connections, the NATO-standard system, between the F-16s and the P-3C Orion patrol aircraft acquired from Norway. The Army has taken delivery of Stryker vehicles, is upgrading TAM 2C tanks and has received Unimog U 4000 trucks.

The buildup has domestic critics. Deputy Agustina Propato, vice-chair of the lower house Defense Committee, has warned that military salaries have lost 80 percentage points of purchasing power since 2023 and that 19,000 personnel have left the armed forces in the same period — an argument that hardware without people is a hollow modernization.

Why This Lands in the Falklands Row

The State Department’s language was formulaic — the sale “will support the foreign policy goals and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a major non-NATO ally,” will help Argentina with border security, counter-transnational crime and disaster response, and “will not alter the basic military balance in the region.” But the calendar does the talking. Argentina has in three weeks sanctioned 45 companies over Falklands oil activity, added criminal complaints against executives, and seen President Javier Milei suspend a planned trip to London. Britain has vowed to be “relentless” in defending the islanders.

And Washington has its own history in this fight. President Donald Trump recently suggested he might not side with Britain in a renewed sovereignty dispute — complaining to GB News that Britain had not joined the U.S.-Israeli campaign against Iran. The Trump administration has meanwhile propped up Milei financially, including a US$20 billion central-bank swap line agreed in October 2025 that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says was repaid in January. Four utility helicopters will not change any military equation in the South Atlantic. As a diplomatic marker, they are considerably louder.

What It Means for Foreigners in Argentina

For expatriates and foreign businesses, the direct impact is nil: this is equipment for border security, emergency response and Army aviation, not a policy that touches residency, taxes or daily life. The relevance is directional. Every U.S. approval of Argentine military hardware deepens the interoperability between the two armed forces and tightens the Washington-Buenos Aires axis that defines Milei’s foreign policy — just as the Falklands dispute pushes Argentina and Britain further apart. Watch the delivery schedule: if the first two Black Hawks arrive before year-end as anticipated, the next milestone in this relationship is already on the calendar.

World.title: Air Transat Counts US$84 Million Cost of Cuba’s Tourism Collapse
World.content:
CUBA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The Cuba bill Suspending its Cuba flights has cost Transat 116 million Canadian dollars (about US$84 million) in lost revenue over the nine months to 31 July 2026.

— The quarter Revenue rose 3 percent to C$792.7 million (about US$573 million), but Transat posted a net loss of C$106.6 million (about US$77 million) for May to July.

— The fuel shock A 56 percent jump in fuel prices added a gross C$105 million (about US$76 million) in the quarter, with a cumulative hit of roughly C$175 million (about US$126 million) since the crisis began.

— The lifeline Transat has fully drawn a C$150 million (about US$108 million) federal resilience facility and secured a further C$250 million (about US$181 million) emergency government loan.

— The market Canadian arrivals in Cuba fell to 127,645 between January and July, down more than 70 percent, and no direct Canada-Cuba flights remain.

Cuba’s tourism collapse has crossed the Florida Straits and landed on a Montreal balance sheet: Air Transat, the Canadian leisure airline that built a franchise on flying Canadians to Cuban beaches, is now surviving on government credit while its former winter stronghold stays dark.
