Air Transat’s parent company, Transat A.T. Inc., reported its third-quarter results on Thursday 10 September 2026, and the numbers show what seven months without Cuba have done to Canada’s largest leisure airline.

The suspension of flights to the island, in force since 9 February 2026, cut revenue by C$35 million (about US$25 million, at roughly 1.38 Canadian dollars to the US dollar) in the May-to-July quarter alone. Over the first nine months of the fiscal year, the Cuba hole reached C$116 million (about US$84 million), the company said.

The figures, first framed in the Cuban context by the independent outlet 14ymedio on Friday, confirm that the Cuban market — historically about 9 percent of Air Transat’s offering, according to the newspaper — has turned from cash machine into millstone. The airline has avoided giving any date for a return.

From Winter Cash Machine to Write-Off

For decades, Canada was Cuba’s tourist lifeline, and Air Transat was its busiest shuttle. From Montreal and Toronto, the airline flew package holidaymakers to Varadero, Cayo Coco, Holguín and Santa Clara — often several times a day in high season. Canadians made up the island’s largest source of visitors by a wide margin.

That ended abruptly in February, when Cuban airports warned they could no longer guarantee jet fuel. Air Transat was among the first carriers to halt flights and send empty aircraft to bring thousands of holidaymakers home. What was first billed as a pause until 30 April became a rolling postponement — and on 5 June the airline announced an indefinite suspension, citing “the current geopolitical situation in Cuba.”

Air Canada and WestJet, together with its Sunwing vacation arm, followed with indefinite suspensions of their own. Since then, Canadian arrivals — 127,645 from January to July, down more than 70 percent from 2025 levels — have dwindled to a trickle after February, according to Cuban statistics cited by 14ymedio. The newspaper notes that not a single direct flight now links Canada and Cuba.

Fuel, Not Just Cuba

Cuba is only part of Transat’s pain. Fuel prices rose 56 percent year on year between May and July, adding a gross C$105 million (about US$76 million) to costs in the quarter and roughly C$175 million (about US$126 million) cumulatively since the fuel crisis began, chief financial officer Jean-François Pruneau said. Higher pilot salaries under a new collective agreement and persistent Pratt & Whitney engine problems added to the strain.

The airline chose not to pass the costs on to passengers, chief executive Annick Guérard told analysts, because competitors flooded the market with discounts. “We had never seen such a highly competitive network,” she said — one promotion after another all summer. Revenue still grew 3 percent to C$792.7 million (about US$573 million) on 6 percent more traffic, but the load factor slipped to 84.7 percent from 85.0 percent a year earlier, and adjusted operating income swung from a positive C$81.2 million (about US$59 million) to a negative C$0.9 million (about US$650,000).

“Our third-quarter results were significantly impacted by sustained higher fuel prices, which remained elevated well beyond expectations and were the primary driver of lower profitability,” Guérard said in the company’s statement.

Kept Afloat by Ottawa

Cash and equivalents shrank to C$243 million (about US$176 million) at the end of July. Transat has now fully drawn its C$150 million (about US$108 million) credit under the federal Liquidity for Airline Sector Resilience facility, and on 9 September — the day before results — it secured a further C$250 million (about US$181 million) emergency loan from the Canada Enterprise Emergency Funding Corporation under the existing Large Employer Emergency Financing Facility agreement.

The new loan matures in 2035 and carries interest of 1.22 percent for the first three years. It comes with conditions: Transat committed to further cost-cutting beyond its existing “Elevation” programme. The federal lender already holds preferred shares and warrants that could give it close to a fifth of the airline’s voting stock — a measure of how deep the state now sits in Transat’s cockpit.

What It Means for Travellers

For Canadians and other foreigners with Cuba plans, the message is blunt: there is no direct air bridge, and none is scheduled. Travellers who still go route themselves through Mexico, Panama or the United States on carriers such as Aeroméxico, Copa and American, which continue to serve the island. Ottawa’s travel advisory warns of shortages of food, medicine, fuel and electricity, even inside resorts.

The collapse is visible on the Cuban side too. Authorities have closed or “compacted” dozens of hotels this year to save power, Spain’s Meliá completed its exit on 24 July with a 79.4-million-euro (about US$92 million) provision, and visitor arrivals overall have collapsed this year, as The Rio Times reported earlier this week. Guérard’s stated priorities are now a loyalty programme by year-end and a premium-cabin refit in 2027 — not Havana.

Whether Air Transat ever returns to Cuba depends less on the airline than on the island’s fuel supply and Washington’s sanctions calendar. For now, the route map of Canadian leisure aviation has a hole exactly where its oldest winter sun used to be.

World.title: Don Rufo: Ecuador Navy Finds 10 Missing Crew of Boat Sunk in US Strike
World.content:
Ecuador · Security

Key Facts —The rescue. Ecuador’s navy located ten missing crew members of the fishing vessel Don Rufo on September 10, two days after US forces destroyed the boat in the Eastern Pacific. Sixteen people were aboard; the ten found had moved away from the strike site and are now on the naval unit BAE Atahualpa. —The count. Don Rufo is the sixth Ecuadorian vessel destroyed by US Southern Command since August 28 and the ninth Ecuadorian boat attacked this year, according to Ecuadorian reporting. —The US claim. Washington says the vessel served as a floating refueling station for drug-running speedboats and was linked to Los Choneros, which Ecuadorian media describe as the country’s oldest criminal gang. —The photos. US Marines released photographs of the boardings that preceded the sinkings — crews on deck with their hands up, held at rifle point — covering the vessels María Candelaria, Conquista 2 and Los Tres Hermanos. —The diplomacy. The strikes unfolded as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Quito on September 9 and told Ecuadorians the operations are not meant to kill fishermen. —The open wound. Eight crew members of the Fiorella, a boat that vanished on January 20, remain missing; their families met government human-rights officials for the first time this week.

Ecuador’s navy found ten missing crew members of the Don Rufo, a fishing vessel destroyed in a US strike on September 8, as Washington released boarding photos that give the US boat campaign its first concrete Ecuadorian face — and hand Quito a consular and sovereignty dossier.

Ten Missing Fishermen Found Alive After Two Days

The Ecuadorian Navy announced on September 10 that it had located the ten missing crew members of the Don Rufo, the fishing vessel destroyed by US forces two days earlier. In a statement on X, the institution said the men “are aboard the naval unit BAE Atahualpa and will be transferred to port, so that the competent authorities can continue with the corresponding procedures.”

Sixteen people were aboard the Don Rufo when US forces intervened on September 8. According to the Ecuadorian Navy, the ten now located had “moved away from the place of the intervention,” while Southern Command said the crew members it removed from the boat were transferred to the Ecuadorian authorities. “After clearing the boat, US forces sank it,” the command said.

The navy did not disclose where the ten men were found. It said the discovery resulted from continuous aerial and maritime search and exploration operations since September 8, with coordinated deployment of naval and air assets, according to reporting by the Quito-based outlet Primicias.

Washington said on the day of the operation that the Don Rufo was serving as a suspected floating resupply station supporting alleged drug-trafficking operations at sea, and that it was linked to Los Choneros, the gang whose top leader, José Adolfo Macías Villamar, known as Fito, is imprisoned in the United States after being extradited, according to Primicias.

The Photos Washington Released

Until this week, the public face of the US campaign was a series of black-and-white videos, filmed from helicopters, showing already-emptied boats being blown up. That changed when US Marines published color photographs of the boardings that preceded the destruction.

Marine Forces South released images of the boarding of the María Candelaria carried out on Saturday, September 5, and days later of the same procedure carried out on the Conquista 2 on Wednesday, September 2, Primicias reported. In the second case, the photographs show the crew gathered on deck with their hands raised while a boat full of heavily armed Marines points rifles at them and begins the boarding. The images also show crew members being detained and taken off their vessel onto the US military boat before the bombing.

The 24th Marine Expeditionary Unit separately published photographs of an August 28 operation against Los Tres Hermanos, the first of the attacks disclosed in the past two weeks, according to Primicias. Southern Command’s own press log lists six “interdictions of narco-terrorist refueling vessels” between August 28 and September 8 — matching the six Ecuadorian boats — plus a separate “lethal kinetic strike” announced for September 9 whose target nationality was not identified. Together, the releases confirm a pattern: US personnel board the Ecuadorian boats with weapons drawn, remove the crews, and only then destroy the vessels.

Six Ecuadorian Boats in Two Weeks, Nine This Year

The Don Rufo is the sixth Ecuadorian fishing vessel destroyed by Southern Command since August 28, all in the Eastern Pacific, and the ninth attacked this year, according to Ecuadorian reporting. The United States did not claim the first three cases between January and March — among them the Fiorella — but Southern Command has acknowledged the six operations carried out since late August.

Washington frames the offensive as support for the “war” that President Daniel Noboa has waged against criminal gangs since 2024. The US government says intelligence identifies the vessels as providing logistical support and fuel resupply to speedboats that leave the Ecuadorian coast carrying large quantities of cocaine toward North America.

Ecuadorian courts, however, have so far found little to hold the crews on. Fishermen removed from the bombed boats and handed to Ecuadorian authorities were freed in at least two of the six reported cases for lack of evidence, Primicias reported; the crew of a third vessel was also released under conditions after being processed for alleged illicit association. In a related case, 32 fishermen from the coastal province of Manabí are being prosecuted while 28 remain free, according to the outlet.

Rubio in Quito: “Not Meant to Kill Fishermen”

The escalation at sea coincided with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Quito on Wednesday, September 9. Pressed by journalists on whether fishermen unconnected to drug trafficking could lose their lives, Rubio answered: “Here no one intends to kill fishermen.” The biggest risk, he said, is that criminal organizations “continue operating,” because “they are indeed killing.” He confirmed the operations will continue.

For the Noboa government, which has made security cooperation with Washington the centerpiece of its foreign policy, the sinking of Ecuadorian-flagged boats with Ecuadorian crews creates a delicate file: Quito must now answer to fishing communities and to congress about what happens to its citizens once US forces hand them over, and under what authority foreign warships are destroying Ecuadorian vessels in international waters.

The Fiorella Families Still Wait

Not every crew has been found. Eight fishermen from the Fiorella, which disappeared on January 20 after setting out from the Manabí port of Jaramijó, according to Amnesty International, remain missing almost eight months later. On Thursday, September 10, their relatives held their first meeting with representatives of the Human Rights Undersecretariat of the Ministry of Government to hear what has been done and what investigations exist, local media reported.

“We have to keep the hope that they will help us,” one relative told the television channel Ecuavisa. Amnesty International has called for an urgent investigation into the possible US role in the attack on that vessel. For foreigners living in Ecuador, the week marks a turning point: a US military campaign that had unfolded mostly in grainy aerial footage now has names, faces and survivors on Ecuadorian soil — and a government in Quito that must decide how loudly to ask Washington for answers.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to the crew of the Don Rufo?

Ecuador’s navy located the ten missing crew members on September 10, two days after US forces destroyed the vessel on September 8. Sixteen people were aboard; the ten found had moved away from the intervention site, while those removed by US forces were handed to Ecuadorian authorities. The ten are aboard the naval unit BAE Atahualpa awaiting transfer to port.

How many Ecuadorian boats has the US destroyed?

Six since August 28, all acknowledged by US Southern Command, and nine attacked this year in total, according to Ecuadorian reporting. Washington did not claim the first three incidents between January and March, including the Fiorella, whose eight crew members are still missing.

Why does the US say it bombs these boats?

Washington says the vessels act as floating refueling stations for speedboats carrying cocaine from Ecuador’s coast toward North America and links them to the Los Choneros gang. Ecuadorian courts have freed many of the detained fishermen for lack of evidence.

World.title: Colombia Extraditions Reach 73 in De la Espriella’s First Five Weeks
World.content:
COLOMBIA · POLITICS & SECURITY

Key Facts — The number President Abelardo de la Espriella says he has signed 73 extradition orders in his first 36 days in office, most of them requested by the United States.

— The pace That is roughly two signatures a day — triple the monthly average recorded under the previous government of Gustavo Petro.

— The names Signed cases include alleged border-bloc commander Geovany Andrés Rojas, alias “Araña”, and retired navy lieutenant Julián David Mosquera Dussán, wanted in the US on drug charges.

— The catch A signature is not a transfer: several of those named, including alias “HH” and alias “Pinocho”, are fugitives and would only be extradited once captured.

— The context The tally landed days after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s 8 September visit to Barranquilla, as Colombia joined Washington’s “Shield of the Americas” security initiative.

Five weeks into his term, Colombia’s new president has turned the extradition decree into the signature tool of his security offensive — and he says the count will keep rising “without truce or hesitation”.

The Palace of Justice on Bogotá’s Plaza de Bolívar. Colombia’s Supreme Court reviews every extradition request before the president signs the final order. (Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Colombia extraditions have become the daily drumbeat of the new government. President Abelardo de la Espriella announced on his social-media accounts on Thursday that he had completed 73 signed extradition orders since taking office on 7 August — a pace no recent Colombian administration has matched.

“One of my favorite sections as president: the relentless signing of extraditions. With the decisions I have just subscribed, we have completed 73 signed extraditions,” he wrote. “Let the bandits be very clear about it, because this number will keep rising without truce and without hesitation.” He vowed there would be no leniency for organized crime and “narcoterrorism”, La FM reported. In an earlier message on 26 August he had put the same policy in blunter terms: “no refuge, no privileges and no leniency” for criminals.

Five Weeks, Five Milestones

The count has climbed in public view. In his first week in office the government formalized its first five extraditions — executive resolutions 308 through 312 of 2026, processed by the Justice Ministry on 13 and 14 August — two bound for the United States, the others for Peru, Panama and the Dominican Republic. Among them were Armando Luis Suárez Calvo, accused of moving cocaine through the ports of Barranquilla and Santa Marta for structures including the Clan del Golfo, and Didier Ignacio García Rodríguez, wanted in the US over cocaine hidden in fruit exports.

By 26 August — day 16 — the president said he had signed more than 30, with the presidency’s legal secretary Andrés Barreto putting the figure at “around 30”, as Infobae reported. Three days later Caracol counted 41 signatures in 19 days. By 9 September the tally stood at 70, before Thursday’s announcement took it to 73.

The Rio Times documented the opening phase of this drive when De la Espriella closed negotiation tables and signed the first high-profile orders in late August, dismantling what remained of his predecessor’s “Total Peace” policy.

Who Is on the List

The most prominent names were announced on 26 August: Willington Henao Gutiérrez, alias “Mocho Olmedo”; Carmen Evelio Castillo Carrillo, alias “Muñeca”; Geovany Andrés Rojas, alias “Araña”, identified as a leader of the Comandos de la Frontera, a trafficking structure active along Colombia’s southern border; Gabriel Yepes Mejía, alias “HH”; and Fredy Castillo Carrillo, alias “Pinocho”. All five were requested by US authorities on narcotics and other criminal charges. Yepes Mejía and Castillo Carrillo are fugitives — their extraditions would be executed only after capture.

A further batch authorized in early September included Javier Fernández Morales, alias “Choki”, and Fernando Vergara Palacios, alias “Pechibola”, alongside decisions involving Gustavo Durán Bautista, alias “Durán”, and José Leonel Ramírez Herrera.

One case carries particular political weight. With executive resolution 336 of 2026, signed by De la Espriella and Justice Minister Iván Cancino, the government confirmed the extradition of Julián David Mosquera Dussán, a retired navy lieutenant wanted in the United States on drug-trafficking charges — Caracol reports he is accused of selling information to trafficking groups moving cocaine north. The Petro government had granted his surrender in resolution 159 of 5 May 2026, but the defense appealed, arguing a prior Colombian case covered the same facts. The new government rejected the challenge and kept the extradition on track.

How the Process Works — and What It Does Not Mean

In Colombia, an extradition request travels through the Justice Ministry, is reviewed by the Supreme Court and only then returns to the presidency for the final signature. The 73 figure therefore counts signed orders, not completed transfers. Some of those named are still at large; others face remaining legal steps before boarding a plane.

The baseline makes the pace striking nonetheless. Official figures presented by Defense Minister Pedro Sánchez in July put the Petro government’s total at 896 extraditions between August 2022 and 31 May 2026 — about 19 a month on average, with 791 tied to drug trafficking, as El Tiempo reported. Even in its busiest year, 2025, the previous administration averaged roughly 36 a month. De la Espriella is signing at close to two a day — and his first-month tally alone equals the 73 drug-related extraditions the Petro government recorded in the first five months of 2026.

The Washington Track

The announcement coincides with a rapid warming of US-Colombia security ties. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met De la Espriella in Barranquilla on 8 September, praising the new government’s willingness to deepen cooperation on narcotics, intelligence and transnational crime. Colombia has also joined the “Shield of the Americas” (Escudo de las Américas), the Washington-promoted regional coordination initiative against trafficking organizations.

For the extradition pipeline, that relationship is decisive: most of the signed orders answer US requests, and American courts — from Georgia to Puerto Rico — are the destination for the coastal trafficking networks named in the first decrees.

What It Means for Foreigners in Colombia

For expats and investors, the extradition count is the most visible metric of a broader security reset. The same 26 August balance that reported 30-plus signatures also claimed 8,424 arrests, 21 ringleaders “impacted” and more than 31 tonnes of drugs seized since 7 August — figures the government uses to argue that territory ceded under Total Peace is being retaken.

The practical effects — safer highways, port controls, the fate of armed structures such as the Clan del Golfo and the ELN — will take longer to judge than a signature count. But the signal to Washington, and to the criminal groups reading the same headlines, is unambiguous: the extradition tap that slowed under Petro is fully open again, and the president says he is just getting started.

World.title: Costa Rica Independence Day 2026 Brings a Tuesday Holiday and Rain
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Independence Day is Tuesday, September 15 so some holidays here get moved to the nearest Monday to make a long weekend, but this one does not. The Labor Ministry has confirmed it stays on the 15th. That means Monday the 14th is a regular workday, and the celebrations run across both evenings.

This year marks 205 years of independence so expect a torch relay over the weekend, lantern parades Monday night, school parades Tuesday and rain on and off the whole time. The Independence Torch crosses from Nicaragua at Peñas Blancas around 11 a.m. Sunday, according to the Ministry of Public Works and Transport. About 22,000 students will carry it roughly 378 kilometers (235 miles) to Cartago, the Ministry of Public Education says.

The relay passes through Liberia, Cañas, Esparza, Palmares, Naranjo, Alajuela and Heredia before reaching San José on Monday evening. The national anthem will be sung at 6 p.m. at Plaza de la Democracia. The flame is due at the ruins in Cartago around 8 p.m. You can track it live at antorcha.mep.go.cr.

If you drive in San José or Cartago on Monday evening, plan around the relay. From about 5 p.m., traffic police will stop cars on Paseo Colón and Avenida Segunda so the runners can cross. Police will do the same at the Fuente de la Hispanidad, the Montes de Oca church, Curridabat and La Galera, and they will control traffic around Cartago’s central park.

The runners are on foot, so each stop lasts only as long as it takes them to pass. At rush hour, though, even short stops back up quickly. Leave early or stay off those roads between 5 p.m. and 8 p.m. On Tuesday morning, expect closures near Parque Nacional and the Legislative Assembly. President Laura Fernández will attend the main civic ceremony there. Traffic police will also be working civic events across the country.

Monday night is the desfile de faroles or the lantern parade. Children carry handmade lanterns through town centers, and Cartago holds its traditional parade that evening. Most towns hold school parades with marching bands on Tuesday. Check with your municipality for start times.

Bring an umbrella to all of it sinceThe National Meteorological Institute (IMN) says tropical wave No. 42 reaches Costa Rica this afternoon, and wave No. 43 follows on Saturday. Both are moving through a humid, unstable atmosphere, and IMN expects that pattern to last through at least Wednesday, September 16.

On the Pacific side, most of the rain falls in the afternoon, with scattered downpours and thunderstorms in the South and Central Pacific. The Caribbean and the Northern Zone are more likely to get rain overnight and in the morning. In the Central Valley, IMN expects occasional showers that become more frequent early next week. That is right when the lantern parades and school parades take place.

Wind is part of the picture too and IMN recorded gusts of 30 to 50 km/h (19 to 31 mph) in mountain areas on Friday, and up to 75 km/h (47 mph) in the North Pacific. IMN also warned earlier this week about saturated soils. Ground soaked by weeks of rain gives way more easily, so landslides and falling branches become more likely after a heavy afternoon storm.

If you are driving to Guanacaste or Puntarenas, Route 1 at Cambronero, near San Ramón, is still closed. A truck damaged the temporary bridge there earlier this week, and MOPT says repairs could take up to two months. Take Route 27 instead. Cars and other smaller vehicles can also use Monte del Aguacate or the local road between Río Jesús and Piedra Blanca.

If someone works for you, the 15th is a paid day off. That includes a housekeeper, a nanny or a gardener. The Ministry of Labor and Social Security (MTSS) says no worker can be required to work that day, and no one can be penalized for refusing. What you owe depends on how you pay. If you pay monthly or every two weeks, the holiday is already built into the wage. You pay the usual amount even if the person takes the day off. If you pay weekly for work outside a commercial business, add one day’s wage for the holiday on top of the days worked.

If the worker agrees to work on the 15th, the day is paid double. In practice, that means one extra day’s wage on top of what you would normally pay. Any overtime that day is paid at triple the regular hourly rate. The rule has a simple purpose. The law treats Independence Day as a day everyone is entitled to take off without losing income and is why working it costs double.

Hotels, restaurants, bakeries, theaters and gas stations are among the businesses the law allows to open on the holiday. Many other shops and most government offices will be closed, so call ahead before you plan errands for Tuesday. The celebrations run from the torch’s arrival on Sunday through Tuesday’s parades. Leave extra time on the road, carry rain gear, and check the latest IMN and MOPT updates before you set out.

World.title: Costa Rica Nears 49,000 Short-Term Rentals as Tourist Numbers Lag
World.content:
Costa Rica now has nearly 49,000 active short-term rental listings, more than double the number in 2019, while international arrivals have yet to return to pre-pandemic levels, according to a new study by the Center for Tourism Studies (CET). The report, prepared by CET director Víctor Umaña and released Wednesday, counts 48,985 active listings across 243 markets on platforms including Airbnb, Vrbo and Booking.com.

The CET estimates those listings generated about $813.5 million in revenue in the 12 months ending in June 2026. The average nightly rate stood at $204, with average occupancy of 43.7% and annual revenue of $16,606 per listing, according to the study. Entire homes account for 83.3% of listings in the sample analyzed, and 66.4% are tied to hosts who manage more than one listing.

The CET describes the market as professionalized, noting that short-term rentals are no longer mainly occasional exchanges between private individuals. The typical property has 2.3 bedrooms and supply has grown far faster than demand. The CET estimates that short-term rental inventory rose from roughly 22,500 listings in 2019 to 48,985 by June 2026, while traditional lodging tracked by the Costa Rica Tourism Board (ICT) grew 13.3%, from 50,264 to 56,950 rooms between 2019 and 2025.

Over a similar period, international arrivals fell 6.2%, from 3.14 million in 2019 to 2.94 million in 2025. The study calculates that the number of international visitors per available lodging unit dropped from about 43 in 2019 to 28 in 2025-2026. The CET says demand is becoming the main constraint on the market. In the 213 markets with year-on-year data, inventory was essentially flat at minus 0.2%, while revenue per listing rose 8.7%, growth the study attributes more to pricing and occupancy than to new supply.

The destination data show wide gaps in earnings. Cabo Velas, which covers Flamingo and Conchal, leads with average annual revenue of $28,800 per listing, followed by Tamarindo at $28,640 and Nosara at $26,100. Nosara also posts the highest average nightly rate, at $384, and the highest occupancy, at 53%. Jacó, with 3,786 listings, has the lowest occupancy among the main destinations, at 40%.

The Greater Metropolitan Area (GMA) has the largest single inventory, with 4,025 listings and 50% occupancy. It also has the lowest earnings, with an average nightly rate of $61 and $7,200 in annual revenue per listing, reflecting smaller units and shorter stays.

Destination Active listings Avg. nightly rate Avg. occupancy Annual revenue per listing Greater Metropolitan Area 4,025 $61 50% $7,200 Jacó 3,786 $306 40% $23,371 Cahuita / Southern Caribbean 3,779 $126 46% $13,400 Tamarindo 3,598 $336 47% $28,640 Cóbano / Santa Teresa-Montezuma 2,860 $274 50% $21,300 Sardinal / Playas del Coco 2,537 $214 48% $16,500 Bahía Ballena / Uvita 2,184 $217 46% $17,500 Quepos / Manuel Antonio 1,902 $259 47% $25,806 Cabo Velas / Flamingo-Conchal 1,678 $346 48% $28,800 Nosara 1,537 $384 53% $26,100 La Fortuna 1,397 $151 44% $14,900

Source: Center for Tourism Studies (CET), based on AirDNA data for the 12 months ending June 2026.

Nationally, the CET calculates a density of 9.4 short-term rentals per 1,000 residents. That places Costa Rica slightly above Barcelona, at 9.0, and above every large city in the comparison, including Rio de Janeiro, New York and Mexico City, though well below Mallorca, Hawaii and Crete.

The study places Costa Rica in the most permissive of four regulatory categories, alongside Belize, Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town. Hosts must register under Law 9742, but there are no national limits on nights rented, no zoning restrictions and no tax specific to short-term rental lodging, according to the CET comparison.

On housing, the report says short-term rentals can push up land values and residential rents in tourist destinations with limited housing supply, adding pressure on workers employed in tourism. It also notes that many coastal villas and condominiums were built specifically for visitors, so restricting them would not necessarily return units to the long-term housing market.

The CET ends by saying that effective policy would need to distinguish between homes converted into short-term rentals and properties developed for tourism from the outset. The study describes its analysis as descriptive and cautions that its market figures are third-party estimates built from public platform data, with methodologies that differ.

World.title: Benyahti Brandon committed to stand trial for La Democracia murder of Paul Smith Jr.
World.content:
Benyahti Brandon committed to stand trial for La Democracia murder of Paul Smith Jr.

By Breaking Belize News Staff: La Democracia resident Benyahti Jareai Brandon, 27, has been committed to stand trial in the High Court for the murder of Paul Nigel Smith Jr. and the attempted murder of Tyrece Lewis Allen.

Brandon appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, where his Preliminary Inquiry began and concluded with his committal to the October session of the High Court, scheduled to commence on October 7, 2026.

During the proceeding, the police prosecutor tendered more than 15 witness statements and 13 documentary exhibits forming part of the prosecution’s case. Those include a Scenes of Crime report, post-mortem documents relating to Smith, Brandon’s caution statement and notes of interview, chain-of-custody documents, an arrest warrant and a medico-legal form relating to Allen.

Brandon was also given an alibi warning and provided the court with the names of two men he intends to call as witnesses at his trial.

The charges stem from a February 3 shooting on First Street in La Democracia Village. Police say Smith was walking with his girlfriend and Allen at around 9:00 a.m. when a gunman emerged from behind a house and fired several shots in their direction.

Smith attempted to flee but collapsed and was later pronounced dead at the Western Regional Hospital. Allen suffered a gunshot wound to the knee, was treated and later released. Police subsequently reported that surveillance footage from the area assisted investigators in identifying Brandon as a suspect.

Brandon was arrested and first arraigned on February 5 on charges of murder and attempted murder and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison. In August, he was provided with 83 pages of disclosure, five DVDs and three photographs ahead of Friday’s Preliminary Inquiry.

Brandon has not been convicted of either offence. The charges will now proceed to trial before the High Court.

World.title: Ellis ‘Juice’ Meighan committed to stand trial for 2024 Placencia murder of Roy Lee Burgess
World.content:
Ellis ‘Juice’ Meighan committed to stand trial for 2024 Placencia murder of Roy Lee Burgess

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Ellis Gilbert Meighan, also known as “Juice,” has been committed to stand trial in the High Court for the 2024 murder of Roy Lee Burgess and the attempted murder of American national Maia James in Placencia.

Meighan, who turned 34 on September 5 while on remand, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday for his Preliminary Inquiry. At the conclusion of the proceedings, the Chief Magistrate ruled that there was sufficient evidence for the case to proceed to trial.

He was committed to the October session of the High Court, which begins October 7, 2026.

During the Preliminary Inquiry, the prosecution tendered more than 35 witness statements along with numerous documentary and physical exhibits forming part of the case against Meighan.

Among those statements were three given to police by James following the April 14, 2024 shooting. The prosecution’s evidence also includes medical records, a post-mortem report on Burgess, photographs of the crime scene and autopsy, ballistic evidence, recovered projectiles and a firearms report.

Meighan did not provide the court with the names of any alibi witnesses he intends to call at trial. He was informed that he has seven days to submit those names in writing.

The charges stem from a shooting on April 14, 2024, along the Placencia Road, which left 32-year-old Burgess dead and James seriously injured. Contemporary reports said Burgess, James and Burgess’ 13-year-old son were inside a vehicle when gunfire erupted. James, then 26, suffered a gunshot injury to her face or head and was later taken abroad for medical treatment, while the child escaped unharmed.

Meighan subsequently left Belize and was apprehended by U.S. authorities in San Diego in May 2024. After spending more than a year in U.S. custody, he was deported to Belize on September 9, 2025 and arraigned three days later on charges including murder, attempted murder, use of deadly means of harm and dangerous harm. He was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Earlier this year, Meighan was provided with 181 pages of disclosure and 22 original photographs forming part of the prosecution’s case.

Meighan has not been convicted of the offences. The prosecution will now be required to prove the charges against him when the matter proceeds to trial in the High Court.

World.title: Man fined $460 for piece of crack the size of a rice grain and pipe
World.content:
Man fined $460 for piece of crack the size of a rice grain and pipe

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man must pay $460 in fines after pleading guilty to possession of a crack pipe and possession of a small quantity of crack cocaine reportedly found inside the pipe.

Dario Fabian Flowers, 44, a labourer of Magazine Road, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court this week, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a pipe used in connection with smoking a controlled drug and possession of 0.5 grams of crack cocaine.

Flowers told the court that the quantity of crack cocaine was only about the size of a grain of rice.

The Magistrate fined Flowers $155 for possession of the pipe and $305 for possession of the crack cocaine, for a total of $460. He has until November 30, 2026, to pay the fines.

In default, Flowers faces one month in prison on the pipe charge and two months on the drug possession charge. The sentences were ordered to run concurrently, meaning he would serve a maximum of two months if the fines are not paid.

Police say Flowers was stopped at around 1:45 a.m. on September 8 while officers were conducting a mobile patrol on King Street near the terminal area.

During a search, police reportedly found a metal pipe with rubber attached concealed near the front zipper area of Flowers’ three-quarter pants. Officers said a white substance resembling crack cocaine was observed inside the pipe.

Flowers was escorted to the police station and subsequently charged with the two drug-related offences.

World.title: Convicted police officer Dexter Diego apologizes to 14-year-old victim for unlawful sex with her; faces separate trial for allegedly raping 10-year-old girl
World.content:
Convicted police officer Dexter Diego apologizes to 14-year-old victim for unlawful sex with her; faces separate trial for allegedly raping 10-year-old girl

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Convicted police officer Dexter Diego expressed remorse in the High Court this week as Justice Nigel Pilgrim heard mitigation ahead of his sentencing for four counts of unlawful sexual intercourse involving a minor.

Diego, 29, pleaded guilty on July 27 to the four counts involving a girl who was 13 years old when the sexual relationship began. His trial had been scheduled to begin that day, but he entered guilty pleas before Justice Pilgrim. Public reports say the court subsequently ordered a prison report, social inquiry report and victim impact statement ahead of sentencing.

Addressing the court during Wednesday’s mitigation hearing, an emotional Diego apologized to the victim, her family, the court, the Belize Police Department and his own family.

“I am fully aware of my decisions that I have made. I know that they were wrong,” Diego told the court, adding that he regretted the pain his actions had caused.

His sister also testified as a character witness, describing her brother as a helpful and respectable person who provided for his stepmother. She told the court that the case has taken a heavy toll on their family and asked Justice Pilgrim to show leniency when imposing sentence.

The court also heard an emotional victim impact statement from the girl, who said Diego had gained her trust by acting as a confidant before pressuring her into a sexual relationship. She told the court that the experience left her ashamed and embarrassed, forced her to relocate and affected her life.

Diego is also before the courts in a separate case involving another minor. On May 4, 2026, the interdicted police officer was arraigned in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on four counts of rape of a child. Prosecutors allege that three of the offences occurred in December 2024, when the girl was 10 years old, while a fourth allegedly occurred in 2025, when she was 11. Diego was remanded to the Belize Central Prison because the Magistrate’s Court could not grant bail on the charges.

The new charges were brought while Diego was already before the courts in connection with the case for which he has now pleaded guilty. The four rape charges remain pending allegations, and Diego has not been convicted in that separate matter.

World.title: Belize and Guyana strengthen cooperation through public sector knowledge exchange
World.content:
Belize and Guyana strengthen cooperation through public sector knowledge exchange

By Zoila Palma: A delegation from the Government of Belize conducted a three-day Knowledge Exchange visit to the Cooperative Republic of Guyana from September 8 to 10, 2026, aimed at strengthening capacity in public-sector management, digital transformation, procurement and project cycle management.

The exchange, coordinated by the High Commission of Belize in Guyana, provided Belizean officials with an opportunity to engage their Guyanese counterparts, examine institutional practices and learn about digital tools and systems being used to improve government service delivery, project implementation and oversight.

The Belize delegation included officials from the Ministry of Finance, Investment, Economic Transformation, Civil Aviation and E-Governance. Discussions focused on project monitoring and oversight, public-sector investment programme planning, procurement reforms, e-Procurement, digital identification and digital government services.

Officials also examined Guyana’s National Digital Management Authority and its experience with E-ID and digital transformation. Presentations highlighted digital systems and innovations supporting service delivery in areas including health, public safety and law enforcement, and agriculture.

Chief Executive Officer for Economic Transformation Carlos Pol said the exchange provides Belize with an opportunity to identify practical approaches that could support the country’s development priorities. “Knowledge sharing among countries in the region allows us to learn from practical experiences, including both successes and challenges. This exchange will help Belize identify approaches that can strengthen project management, procurement, digital transformation, and overall public-sector effectiveness.”

CEO for E-Governance Jose Urbina highlighted the importance of digital innovation in modernizing government services. “Digital transformation is no longer simply about introducing technology; it is about rethinking how Government operates and how citizens access public services,” he said.

The visit is expected to lead to continued technical cooperation, including support for Belize’s digitalization efforts, healthcare workforce capacity-building, PSIP management and oversight, and e-Procurement. The Government of Belize thanked the Government of Guyana, the High Commission of Belize in Guyana and the Inter-American Development Bank for facilitating the exchange.

World.title: International News: Guatemalan Riot police responds to road blockages as fuel price protests continue
World.content:
International News: Guatemalan Riot police responds to road blockages as fuel price protests continue

By Zoila Palma: Today, road blockades continued across Guatemala as protesters demonstrated against rising fuel prices, disrupting traffic on major highways and sections of Guatemala City.

The demonstrations have affected thousands of commuters and disrupted the movement of essential goods, including food, medicine and fuel., Prensa Libre reports.

Blockades have been reported along several of the country’s main highways, as well as on the Periférico Ring Road near the entrance to the Bethania neighborhood and the Atlantic Highway at key entrances and exits to the capital.

Some blockades, including those in Cuyotenango, Suchitepéquez, and Río Hondo, Zacapa, have lasted more than 24 hours.

Minister of the Interior Marco Antonio Villeda has ordered protesters to clear the roads within 30 minutes, warning that those who refuse could be arrested and brought before the courts.

In addition, Guatemalan officials announced a joint operation involving the National Civil Police and the Army to clear blocked routes, following a Constitutional Court ruling ordering the removal of the blockades.

The business sector has called for immediate action, citing significant economic losses caused by the disruptions.

World.title: International News: Latin America faces growing drone threat as criminal groups take to the skies
World.content:
International News: Latin America faces growing drone threat as criminal groups take to the skies

By Zoila Palma: Drones are rapidly becoming a powerful tool for organized crime across Latin America, with criminal groups increasingly using the technology for surveillance, smuggling, coordination and attacks, while governments struggle to keep pace.

A report by the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) recorded around 670 armed-drone events since 2018, with more than 72% occurring between January 2025 and August 21, 2026.

The threat has become particularly visible in Mexico, Colombia and Brazil, CNN reports.

In Brazil, a 2025 police operation in Rio de Janeiro saw a bomb dropped from a drone during a massive raid against the Comando Vermelho criminal organization.

Mexican cartels have also used drones to monitor security forces, territorial rivals and border areas, while attaching explosives to some devices.

In Colombia, armed groups have increasingly incorporated drones into attacks and surveillance, with ACLED identifying the country as the epicenter of armed-drone activity in the region.

Experts say criminal groups are moving beyond experimental drone use toward organized and repeatable operations.

Governments across the region are responding with counter-drone technology, intelligence operations and increased surveillance, but experts warn that criminal innovation is advancing faster than many governments can adapt.

World.title: Keon Mossiah brings Gold to Belize, makes history as First IMMAF Champion
World.content:
Keon Mossiah brings Gold to Belize, makes history as First IMMAF Champion

By Zoila Palma: Belizean mixed martial artist Keon Mossiah, who proudly hails from Santa Elena, Cayo, has made history becoming the first Belizean to win a gold medal at the International Mixed Martial Arts Federation (IMMAF) Pan American Championships.

Mossiah secured the historic victory at the 2026 IMMAF Pan American Championships in Monterrey, Mexico, where he represented Belize against talented fighters from across the Americas.

His gold medal marks a major milestone for Belizean amateur mixed martial arts and adds to the country’s growing success at international IMMAF competitions.

Mossiah’s achievement also highlights the continued development of mixed martial arts in Belize and the work of the Belize Mixed Martial Arts Federation, which has been creating opportunities for local athletes to compete at the international level.

Mossiah now returns home with a historic distinction as Belize’s first IMMAF champion, bringing gold and national pride back to Belize.

World.title: Market Bag: Peppers hit $700, lettuce now $1,500 as food prices continue to soar
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Food prices continue to rise at the Coronation Market in downtown Kingston as farmers struggle with the effects of a worsening drought, pushing up the cost of several essential produce items.

Among the more expensive items this week are lettuce, which is selling for $1,500 per pound, and Scotch bonnet peppers and sweet peppers, both priced at $700. Other items seeing steep increases include carrots at $500 per pound; Irish potatoes and pumpkin at $400 each; onions at $350; and sweet potatoes at $350.

With the rising costs, ISSA-certified nutritionist Orandy Smith is encouraging Jamaicans to “work with what is working with you” when preparing meals and making food choices.

Speaking on the latest episode of Market Bag with host Carlysia Ramdeen, Smith said some ingredients remain essential in his household, regardless of price.

“Because my food must be flavourful, regardless of what the cost for seasoning, I’m going to buy them…I must do my onion, I must do my tomato, I must do my escallion, I must do my thyme, I must do my garlic, I must do all of my seasonings. So all of them are non-negotiable,” he said.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Jamaica finish second in mixed 4x100m at Ultimate Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Ackeem Blake take the start in mixed's relay 4x100m final during the World Athletics Ultimate Championship at the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre, in Budapest on September 11, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica finished second in the mixed 4x100m relay final on Friday’s opening day of the inaugural Ultimate Championships at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary,

The team of Ackeem Blake, Tina Clayton, Kadrian Goldson and Jonielle Smith clocked 39.72 seconds to finish a step behind the USA team that set a national record 39.64 seconds to win the event. Great Britain was third in 40.26 seconds.

In the only individual track final contested by a Jamaican, Megan Simmonds was fifth in the 100m hurdles with a season’s best 12.42 seconds (0.1m/s). American world record holder Masai Russell completed an unbeaten season, winning with 12.22 seconds, just overtaking the field at the end with Nigeria’s Tobi Amusan placing second with 12.34 seconds and Nadine Visser of the Bahamas third with 12.39 seconds.

Lamara Distin only cleared one height in the women’s high jump, finishing joint sixth with 1.86m as Yaroslava Mahuchikh won with 1.99m, ahead of two Australians – Nicola Olyslagers-1.96m and Eleanor Patterson-1.91m.

Meanwhile, Nickisha Pryce qualified for Saturday’s final of the women’s 400m after she was third in her semi-final, running 49.72 seconds, after leading through the first 200m.

World leader and Diamond League winner Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic won with 49.58 seconds ahead of Salwa Eid Nasa of Bahrain who clocked 49.67 seconds.

Cuba’s Roxana Gomez was fourth in 50.34 seconds to get the other qualifying spot.

Stacey-Ann Williams was sixth in her semi-final, clocking 50.43 seconds from lane nine.

Also on Friday, Ackera Nugent failed to complete her 100m hurdle semi-finals after she fell at the ninth hurdle, while two-time world champion winner Danielle Williams just missed qualifying after she placed fifth in 12.72 seconds (-0.2m/s). National champion Demisha Roswell was eighth in 13.04 seconds.

Orlando Bennett was also fifth in his 110m hurdles semi-final, running 13.29 seconds (0.7m/s), while Demario Prince was seventh in 13.58 seconds after hitting a hurdle near the end of the race. Tyler Mason was seventh in his semi-final in 13.46 seconds (0.6m/s).

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Stalled by squatters
World.content:
FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Squatters have taken over hundreds of acres of privately owned land across this parish, with approximately 58 acres of a 147.48-acre property at Flamingo Beach already illegally occupied, threatening to derail a major development for which a plan has been submitted to the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC).

Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager, who on Thursday raised the alarm during the corporation’s regular monthly meeting, said the growing problem has resulted in the TMC being inundated with complaints from frustrated landowners.

“We have had a number of landowners coming to the corporation to report instances where individuals have occupied and begun developing their properties without the owners’ permission,” Gager said.

He warned that the scale of the illegal occupation is undermining the development of the parish he described as having significant potential for growth.

Gager said the situation at Flamingo Beach was particularly concerning.

“There is a submitted plan here for that property that will help to build Trelawny, but we cannot proceed because there is this problem of squatting,” he bemoaned.

“Approximately 58 acres of [well-known attorney] Gordon Brown’s property has been illegally occupied,” Gager added.

Efforts to get a comment from Brown were unsuccessful as, up to press time he did not return the phone call as promised.

Meanwhile, according to the mayor, at another property in Flamingo Beach, 11 acres of a 57.6-acre parcel have also been informally settled.

Explaining the extent of the problem, he pointed to Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny — which recently made news headlines following the early-morning demolition of about 20 structures — where approximately 12 acres of the property have been informally occupied.

Gager also referenced significant squatting on sections of 344.5 acres of land in an area called Tilston; Hague, where one acre has been informally settled; and Hague Cave Island, where four acres of the property have similarly been occupied.

Gager, who is also chairman of the TMC, said squatters are relying on claims of adverse possession which, for privately owned land, is based on undisturbed occupation of at least 12 years.

“Once they get a little cut on it they try to say that they have been there for over 12 years, when in fact they weren’t there,” he said.

“We find that the law-abiding citizen who pays their taxes, buy their land for maybe later on in their years when things get bad and they want to protect their future, they are now met with a problem that they might have to… find extra money to take it to the Supreme Court level,” the mayor added.

Gager pushed back against criticism of the TMC and the Government over the squatting crisis, insisting that the authorities have been taking steps within their remit.

“We must do all that we can and, as the municipality, I must note that we have been serving our notices on those that occupy the lands,” he said, adding that notices have also been served on landowners to facilitate court action.

He said the TMC is frequently contacted by property owners seeking help, but its ability to resolve disputes is ultimately limited when matters enter the judicial system.

“All we can do sometimes is have a discussion and try to guide them into the right process where they are going,” said Gager.

Pointing to the substantial structures being erected in some of the settlements, he questioned whether everyone occupying the properties could legitimately be regarded as people without the means to legitimately acquire property.

The mayor said he has seen two- and three-storey houses, split-level structures and buildings apparently configured to accommodate renters and commercial activity.

“I can see houses that are really arranged for business, so that renters can accommodate. How can we be so lawless?” he asked.

Gager urged politicians, members of the police force, social workers, and ordinary citizens not to facilitate or encourage illegal occupation, warning that continued squatting could tarnish Trelawny’s development prospects.

“This cannot continue in a growing parish. The future of this parish is great; let us not mar the beauty of this parish by encouraging squatting,” he urged.

World.title: $6.8-m payout for unjust redundancy
World.content:
The Industrial Disputes Tribunal.

THE Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) has ordered Spectrum Insurance Brokers to pay a former employee $6.8 million after it found that his dismissal by way of redundancy in 2019 was “unjustifiable”.

In a ruling handed down on Tuesday the IDT rejected the company’s arguments that it was facing financial challenges at the time it decided to make the position of Claims Manager Laurel Smith redundant.

Initially, lawyers representing the company had argued that the IDT lacked the jurisdiction to hear matters regarding redundancies after the Ministry of Labour sent the dispute for its hearing in 2021.

Lawyers representing Spectrum took the matter to the Supreme Court seeking to challenge the authority of the IDT, but in a 2023 ruling the court said there was no legal basis for it to grant a stay of the judicial review proceedings.

When the matter finally started before the IDT in January 2025 the company argued that Smith’s post was made redundant as it was experiencing financial difficulties in 2019 and it was agreed that his position of claims manager would be absorbed into the operations manager position for the purpose of greater efficiency.

The company, however, admitted that Smith’s post was the only one made redundant and argued that he was offered a new post of recovery officer but he did not express an interest in that job.

It was also confirmed that there was no issue with Smith’s performance and no disciplinary matter pending against him.

Witnesses who testified on Smith’s behalf pointed out that he was a good manager and claimed that “he would be ranked among the best in the industry”.

In his testimony Smith claimed to have had a problem with how a senior manager — who was employed by the company five years after him — spoke to the staff and, after he tackled her about this, his department was faced with significant attacks, until it was indicated that his post would be made redundant.

According to Smith, he was embarrassed and traumatised by the redundancy, which affected him financially with his house being put on the market for sale.

In its ruling the IDT said despite the company’s claims of facing increasing financial challenges, the records show that its operating profit moved from approximately $17.3 million in 2018 to approximately $20.2 million in 2019, with its total revenue climbing to $19.3 million compared to a budgeted 16.5 million.

“Based on the evidence before us, we are able to make specific findings of fact that the company’s case suffered from a number of infirmities and fallacies. When weighted against the provisions… governing redundancy, their contentions, (which are more asserted that demonstrated) that this was a genuine redundancy, could not pass muster,” said the IDT panel chaired by Donald Roberts.

“The redundancy exercise fell afoul of the requirements… as the process did not satisfy the standards of fairness and the company did not show that it engaged in meaningful consultation, that it made reasonable attempts to avoid redundancy, and that it assisted Mr Smith in finding alternative employment,” the IDT added as it made the award to Smith.

World.title: Skatta upbeat as Coolie Dance rhythm takes flight, again
World.content:
BURRELL... I’m always happy whenever a new interest comes to fruition and a great song is released with the sample.

THE success of the Coolie dance rhythm sampled hit Bby WOW by Karol G, featuring Judeline and rusowsky, has once again propelled the enigmatic Cordell “Skatta” Burrell-produced beat into the spotlight.

Bby WOW is the biggest song globally at present, topping both Billboard’s Global 200 and Global 200 Excluding US charts. It is also #1 on Billboard’s Hot Latin Songs, and Hot Latin Rhythm Songs charts.

Outside of the United States, the song has so far hit #1 in Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Peru and in Spain.

Created in early 2004, the initial Coolie Dance rhythm featured more than 70 songs. Among the hits at the time were songs by dancehall acts Guinness by Jagwa, Yuh Gaawn by Bounty Killer, Geenie Dance by Elephant Man, Head Gaawn by Elephant Man, Do it To Me Baby by Ce’Cile, Gal Dem Way by TOK,

Tell Me Why by Frisco Kid, Please Mr Please by Vybz Kartel and Feel Alright by Sean Paul.

Mr Vegas’ Pull Up and Jook Gal (Wine Wine) by Elephant Man, Kiprich, Twista and YoungBloodz were Billboard chart-hitters, so too Culo by Pitbull and Nina Sky’s Move Your Body, both of which hit the Billboard Hot 100 charts in late 2004, and most recently After Hours by R&B singer Kehlani.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer on Thursday, Burrell who is also a former judge on the television reality series Magnum Kings and Queens of Dancehall, spoke about the renewed interest in the beat which he created 22 years ago.

“I’m always happy whenever a new interest comes to fruition and a great song is released with the sample,” said Burrell. “It reminds me that the riddim is timeless and has the ability to connect with generations of music lovers. I think the continued interest from international acts in sampling the rhythm has a lot to do with the original approach I made when I sat down to create it. I took a more artistic approach than musical, meaning mostly drums and percussions slightly aggressive but still groovy enough to make you feel the movement between each sound. Less sometimes means more so not crowded. My dancehall influences along with the Indian samples all together made it not only appealing to my culture but straight across the globe.”

According to Burrell, the latest sampling of the beat was brought to his attention by his publishing company.

“My publishing company was contacted after the song’s release, and we did what we could and ensured that we covered all the necessary areas that suited all parties. I think they did a great job on the production because the first thing that stood out was the beautiful synth melodies and vocal samples that played alongside the lead vocals and even though its in Spanish, the sound is captivating enough and is still enjoyed and appreciated,” said Burrell.

Unlike most of his projects, the beat for the Coolie Dance rhythm was not created in a recording studio. Burrell shared that he envisioned the production would have been a hit.

“The rhythm itself was not created in a studio. I was in New York at the time and was by a friend’s house. I purchased a sample CD at a place called Samash music somewhere in Queens I think and was eager to sit with it and get creative. The first opportunity I got was in my friend’s living room. I plugged in my drum machine and put my headphones on and got to work. The process was about an hour because from listening to the samples in the car, I knew exactly how I wanted to interpret and build around it. I knew it was different and had extreme potential so when I had an offer of purchase from another producer, I made the decision not to sell it and instead use it for my own label and the minute I played it for Bounty Killer, he also gave me the nod that it was a hit,” Burrell recalled.

Though not 100 per cent sure, Burrell recalled that budding artiste at the time Jagwa may have recorded the first song on the Coolie Dance rhythm.

Prior to venturing into music production, Burrell tried his hand at becoming a recording artiste, but that didn’t work out.

“I got into music while attending The United Pentecostal Church on Grant’s Pen Road where at a very young age, I used to sit at the front bench and mimic Clevie the drummer as he played. I eventually got the opportunity to play the drums after some time and that’s where my passion grew. From beating the desk at Calabar High school classrooms to building beats and recording demos in my friend Benzly Hype’s home studio on Hillary Avenue. I was rejected as an artiste at Celestial Sound because my voice wasn’t good enough, so I decided to learn the 56 Channel Amek Hendricks Mixing Console at the first digital studio owned by Steven Ventura,” he shared.

“He gave me the opportunity to be a fly on the wall to watch and learn until I started recording and mixing. Iley Dread, however, gave me the biggest support by giving me his label, Kings Of Kings, to run for almost two years and that’s where I homed in on my passion and worked with many artistes, musicians and producers. Norris Man gave me my very first hit song and Ce’Cile and I did our very first dancehall juggling that propelled me to the mainstream lanes from which I was able to navigate my success,” the producer reminisced.

World.title: INVESTORS SNAP UP JAMAICA BOND
World.content:
NEARLY 10 months after Hurricane Melissa inflicted an estimated US$8.8 billion in damage across Jamaica, international investors have turned out strongly for the Government’s latest US$1-billion bond, allowing the country to borrow at a lower rate than initially indicated.

The bond was heavily oversubscribed after Jamaica returned to the international capital markets last week to raise funds for both debt management and general budgetary needs.

Before the offer was formally launched, investors were initially being guided to an interest rate of about 6.50 per cent. Strong demand subsequently allowed the Government to offer the bond at 6.25 per cent, according to market sources.

In simple terms, investors wanted more of the bond than Jamaica was seeking to sell, giving the Government room to offer a lower return and still attract sufficient buyers.

The strong reception is particularly notable given Jamaica’s return to the market less than a year after Hurricane Melissa caused widespread damage and disrupted economic activity.

Of the US$1 billion being raised, approximately US$600 million was earmarked to help repurchase portions of three older Government of Jamaica global bonds, while the remaining US$400 million, or about $63 billion, was intended for general budgetary purposes.

The transaction forms part of the Government’s wider liability management strategy, under which it is seeking to replace portions of older, more expensive debt with new borrowing while pushing some repayments further into the future.

At the same time that the new bond was being marketed, the Government invited holders of its 6.75 per cent notes due in 2028, 8.50 per cent notes due in 2036, and 8.00 per cent notes due in 2039 to sell some of those securities back to Jamaica.

By the time that tender offer closed on September 9, investors had submitted approximately US$476.62 million in bonds for repurchase.

After adjusting for the amortisation of the 2028 notes, the amount represented approximately US$392.23 million.

The Government is expected to determine how much of those tendered notes it will accept, with settlement scheduled for September 17. The official tender documents confirm that completion of the buyback is tied to the closing of the new international bond transaction.

“Jamaica intends to apply a portion of the net proceeds of its new notes offering announced on Wednesday, September 2, 2026 to purchase the Old Notes accepted pursuant to the Invitation at the applicable Total Purchase Price,” the Government said in its release.

The repurchase is expected to lower the Government’s annual interest bill by approximately US$3.5 million while moving part of its external debt obligations further into the future.

Beyond the savings, however, the reception to the new bond provides another test of how international investors now view Jamaica’s creditworthiness.

That assessment has changed significantly over the past decade.

When Jamaica raised US$2.05 billion on the international market in July 2015, its April 2028 bond carried an interest rate of 6.75 per cent while its July 2045 bond carried a rate of 7.875 per cent.

At the time, Jamaica was rated B by S&P Global, B– by Fitch Ratings, and Caa2 by Moody’s.

Today, the country carries a BB rating from S&P Global with a stable outlook, BB– from Fitch with a stable outlook, and Ba3 from Moody’s with a stable outlook.

The improvement has accompanied a steep reduction in public debt, with Jamaica’s debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio falling from approximately 116 per cent in 2015 to about 68 per cent today.

The ratings have also been maintained despite the economic damage caused by Hurricane Melissa.

Investor demand for the latest bond therefore provides another indication that international markets continue to place weight on Jamaica’s fiscal management and debt reduction record, even as the country faces significant reconstruction costs.

The comparison is even more striking against the backdrop of rising US interest rates.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year United States Treasury has recently moved close to five per cent amid a global bond sell-off. On Wednesday it was trading at approximately 4.8 per cent.

At a 6.25 per cent rate, Jamaica would, therefore, be borrowing at roughly 1.4 percentage points above the yield available on US Government debt.

That margin, known in the market as the spread, represents the additional return investors demand for taking the greater risk associated with lending to Jamaica instead of the United States.

The narrower that gap, generally, the more favourably investors are assessing Jamaica’s risk.

A comparison with Trinidad and Tobago provides some regional context.

Trinidad and Tobago, which carries stronger credit ratings than Jamaica, issued a 10-year US$1-billion bond earlier this year at 6.50 per cent and later raised another US$800 million through a 12-year bond at 6.20 per cent.

When Trinidad issued the January bond, its borrowing rate was roughly 2.27 percentage points above the US 10-year Treasury yield prevailing at the time.

Jamaica’s latest transaction, despite its lower sovereign credit rating, appears to have been priced at a smaller premium above US Treasuries.

That does not mean Jamaica is viewed as less risky than Trinidad across the board, since bond pricing is also affected by market conditions, maturity, and investor demand at the time of issuance.

It nevertheless points to strong appetite for Jamaican debt during the latest transaction.

The new unsecured bond is expected to mature in 2037, giving it an 11-year tenure.

Citigroup Global Markets Inc and Scotia Capital (USA) Inc acted as deal managers and joint lead underwriters. Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP and Patterson Mair Hamilton advised the managers, while the Government was advised by Paul Hastings LLP and the Attorney General’s Chambers.

World.title: IT WILL BE GREAT!
World.content:
Oblique Seville celebrates winning the men’s 100m final during the World Athletics Diamond League athletics meeting in Belgium on September 4, 2026. He is set to compete in the Ultimate Championships in Hungary. (Photo: AFP)

Despite several of Jamaica’s top athletes set to compete, retired Jamaican-born Olympic and world champion Donovan Bailey admits the World Athletics Ultimate Championships could lose some of its appeal with several of the sport’s biggest stars, including American Noah Lyles, set to miss the event.

The inaugural three-day invitational meet, which gets underway on Friday in Budapest, will feature the world’s top 16 athletes in individual track events and the top eight competitors in field events. Gold medallists from the 2024 Paris Olympics, 2025 Tokyo World Championships and this year’s Diamond League final winners earned automatic qualification while the remaining entrants were determined by the World Athletics Ranking for the period from last September to the start of this September.

However, reigning Olympic Games 100m champion and 200m world champion Lyles will be absent due to injury.

American star 400m and 400m hurdles star Sydney McLaughlin Levrone, America’s Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall, Kenyan middle-distance star Faith Kipyegon, Kenya’s 800m world champion Lilian Odira, and reigning Olympic and World Champion in the 5000m Faith Kipyegon will also be missing from the championships for different reasons.

Former world record holder Bailey, who won 100m gold for Canada at the 1996 Olympics and the 1995 World Championships, says World Athletics will miss the star power but believes it will still be a great event.

“I think that anytime that you’re having major championships and this is the ultimate championship [in] it’s first year, the big stars that are missing, it does dampen it a little bit,” he said on CBC Sports. “I think that in any sport, you want to have the greatest people of that time, appealing to the fans, catering to the crowd and breaking world records and winning stuff.”

“But I also think that there are some incredible stars that are established now and there are some really, really talented young athletes that’s going to establish themselves. I’m looking forward to it, I’m sorry for the athletes that are injured or season’s done or whatever but there’s going to be some great competition.”

With the Ultimate Championships being the first of its kind, it’s not yet viewed as a major championship on the level of the Olympics and World Championships.

However, Bailey believes it gives athletes another opportunity to compete for additional prize money as well as securing bragging rights.

“I think that championships matter, consistency matters, delivering messages matter, being confident, being injury-free matters,” he said. “We look at the Commonwealth Games or PanAm Games, some sort of regional championships — to me, the Ultimate Championships now is like a regional championships. If you win, you win and you’re going to get paid. Does it matter? Yes, it matters for the person that wins.”

“Also, it matters for everyone that competes there because they’re going to have money. If you win, it’s incredible because it’s a title and what this does next year going into, uh, 2027 [with the] World Championships and when you’re on a Diamond League starting line, the Ultimate Championship champion is another title that gets added and maybe you can demand a little bit more cash.”

Each competitor at the Ultimate Championships is guaranteed at least US$2,000 with the winner set to earn US$150,000.

Reigning 100m world and Diamond League champion Seville heads the list of 27 Jamaicans set to compete at the event.

Jamaica’s long-serving technical leader Maurice Wilson and former Olympic and world champion Michael Frater will be Jamaica’s two-man delegation in charge of the relay teams.

Men: Oblique Seville, Ackeem Blake, Christopher Taylor, Navasky Anderson, Orlando Bennett, Romaine Beckford, Bryan Levell, Tyler Mason, Demario Prince.

Women: Tina Clayton, Ackera Nugent, Danielle Williams, Lamara Distin, Nickisha Pryce, Brianna Lyston, Rushell Clayton, Shiann Salmon, Jonielle Smith, Ashanti Moore, Ackelia Smith, Demisha Roswell, Megan Simmonds, Sanique Walker, Jodean Williams, Lavanya Williams.

World.title: Ottey cleaves through dexterity competition
World.content:
Cleve Ottey bested all others by a two-second margin in what was an exciting run to the finish.

Cleve Ottey was the winner at the third round of the Point 2 Point Time Attack dexterity series, held on Saturday, August 22, at Overton Plaza, Montego Bay.

“It feels good to win. It’s been a while since I’ve had to put down such a spectacular drive, but it was great,” Ottey told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

And spectacular it was as Ottey held off rivals during the two-lap championship runs, after trading close times all event from said opposition. His Toyota Starlet took blows from familiar names like Maurice Whittingham, Christopher Addison, and Zachary Isaacs. He even had to fend off front-wheel drive charges from Kai Chuck-Dixon and Daren Givans, but in the end Ottey managed to pull out a two-second lead to seal the deal at the end of the night.

“I just settled down, kept my composure, and tried to point and shoot the car. That’s how I got the time,” said Ottey.

Running in reverse order for the championship runs, it was Givans who first did the unthinkable, posting both the fastest front-wheel drive run of the section and the fastest time until then. Once done, the massive crowd was on the edge of their seats to see if the 1:15.307 time could be beaten. It took the might of Whittingham to best the simple Corolla, with an anti-lag snorting 1:13.894. Isaacs, who had been the fastest in the main event by a 10th of a second over Ottey, lowered it even further after a 1:11.919 run. Both men would finish third and second, respectively, as Ottey continued the two-second margin trend, winning overall after completing a 1:09.916.

Givans would head back to Kingston with a class win for front-wheel drive and the respect of the Montegonian fans. Chuck-Dixon claimed the front-wheel drive with limited slip differential class in his Honda Civic. The rear-wheel drive with limited slip differential class went to Isaacs, a small consolation prize for almost winning the event.

“It was a magnificent event for all involved. The runs were superb. The drivers were excellent,” Stephen Mahoney, event organiser, said.

The series heads for conclusion in October.

World.title: EU delays key tobacco tax vote until after Swedish election
World.content:
The European Commission proposed increasing levies on cigarettes and setting minimum rates on newer products like vapes, heat-not-burn tobacco and nicotine pouches in July last year.

The plan has become a flashpoint for Sweden, which has a long tradition of using snus — a pouch of tobacco that sits between the gums. As such, Stockholm has strongly opposed raising taxes on similar nicotine pouches.

Delaying the vote gives extra time for Sweden to appoint a new finance minister and for the capitals to negotiate a way out of the current stalemate.

The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, confirmed the vote has been pushed from October to November's ministerial meeting.

Four diplomats granted anonymity to speak candidly about the sensitive negotiations said the postponement is meant to give Sweden's next government extra time to change its mind.

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said they will "continue[s] to engage bilaterally with the aim of securing unanimous political agreement at the November ECOFIN" meeting of finance ministers.

World.title: Escaping the AI safety nightmare: What can governments do?
World.content:
A case in point is that OpenAI agents hacked a German website back in May to use it as a messaging board, Reuters reported last week. OpenAI had not publicly announced the incident and responded to the Reuters reporting on X saying: “We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment.”

“[Reporting] timelines are going to need to be dramatically shortened [for incidents], and so we need much better continuous monitoring capabilities,” said Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at London-based think tank the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, adding that the data will be needed in real time “and that will be true for governments and for labs.”

Speaking at a London event for U.K. lawmakers arranged by campaign group ControlAI on Monday, computer scientist Stuart Russell said that the most concerning aspect of the Hugging Face incident for him was that “by running a thousand agents communicating with each other, they were able to generate behaviors that no one agent could do by itself,” referring to investigations showing the incident was far more severe than OpenAI first acknowledged.

“But [in] the evaluations, standard testing is done with a single AI system, not with a thousand,” he told lawmakers, so now the industry must anticipate the possibility of many agents all collaborating at once.

Out of alignment

Beyond avoiding any obvious mistakes in testing, there are issues in the culture of AI testing that are more deeply embedded.
