Michael Passaro says the matter needs to be probed. (Supplied)

"An urgent referral is not just paperwork, it represents a patient waiting for potentially life-saving care," he said.

" No patient should suffer avoidable harm because their referral was left untriaged in a box. "

The state government spokesperson said their thoughts were with the loved ones of the patients affected.

"When something goes wrong, health services must review what happened, be transparent about the findings and take action to reduce the risk of it happening again," they said.

The ABC understands MBPH has reached out to affected patients.

World.title: 84yo nan drives 2,000km to donate clothes to communities
World.content:
Barbara Carroll loads her van with boxes of donated clothes each month and heads north to the red dirt of Western Australia's remote Pilbara.

The 84-year-old op-shop owner is affectionately known as "Nan Barb" around her home town of Donnybrook, 200 kilometres south of Perth.

Ms Carroll distributes the clothes to charities and women's refuges in places such as Carnarvon, Newman, Nullagine and Roebourne, road trips routinely covering more than 2,000km.

"I don't go out to get any rewards or anything; it just comes naturally," she says.

"Somebody needs help, you help them, and that's what I do.

"They can't just go into a shop and buy clothes. They're too far out."

Her love of country music helps her pass the time on the long drives.

"I'd rather drive by myself. Take me time. I just like it on my own," she says.

Nan Barb regularly travels out to WA's remote communities to distribute clothes. (Supplied: Nan Barb)

Heart in the red dirt

Ms Carroll's community op shop is packed to the hilt with every item imaginable, from old toasters to ornate wedding dresses.

An overabundance of donated clothes from across WA's South West region led her to start the charitable campaign she calls "Nan Goes North".

Nan Barb is on a personal mission to lend a helping hand to remote towns disadvantaged by isolation. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

It is a mission that is close to her granddaughter Tara Carroll's heart.

Tara, who is a proud Wiradjuri woman, joins her grandmother's trips when she can.

"Living remotely, that's a disadvantage already because they don't have access to a lot of medical or clothing or whatever it be," she says.

"So to be able to go with Nan on these adventures with all the clothes and anything that they need, it's pretty cool."

Tara Carroll says her grandmother is an inspiration to her family. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

Nan Barb's personal connection to northern communities runs deep, having been brought up in the remote community of Nullagine, in WA's Pilbara region.

"They are her tribal family; she has a very close connection with people up there, with mob," Tara says.

" Her heart is in the red dirt. "

'We love her'

Shahenaz Kouzi is a community advocate with the Newman-based Puntukurnu Aboriginal Medical Service and former staff member at the local women's refuge.

She said both organisations had regularly received clothes donations from Nan Barb.

The Donnybrook Op Shop donates all sorts of essential clothes for babies, women and men. (Supplied: Nan Barb)

"Blankets, winter and summer clothing, baby clothes, women's and men's clothing, it's tremendous," she said.

"We love her. I wish she was my Nan."

Ms Kouzi said Nan Barb was well-known and loved by residents in the remote communities of the East Pilbara.

"They call her the angel. There are too many good words for Barb from all the Aboriginal people; they all know her," she says.

Nan Goes North

Donnybrook op shop volunteer Andrew Clifford says Nan Barb is a beloved, straight-talking local.

Andrew Clifford says Nan Barb is a local legend around Donnybrook. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

"Oh, she's a lovely lady, does a lot for the community; she's quite funny, very funny," he says.

"The way she speaks and language-wise, it's fairly rough, but it's good."

Despite the occasional mishap on her adventures, Tara Carroll says her nan always manages to find a way home.

"She's been broken down on the sides of the road, and someone always rescues her," Tara says.

" She's got good karma, I believe. "

Ms Kouzi recalls giving Nan Barb eskies full of ice to keep her cool when her van's air conditioning had broken down.

"We worry about her, but she's fit as a fiddle," she said.

Her family and community are raising money for a truck, so Nan Barb can expand her outreach and make it easier to take along a passenger, aside from her dog, Bob.

Nan Barb was raised in the remote WA community of Nullagine. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

"[The van is] too uncomfortable to take two people because there's no room for your legs," Nan Barb says.

"I don't need it, but everybody else reckons I need somebody to go with me."

World.title: 'Obnoxious' weed woven into massive mullet sculpture
World.content:
In a suburban garage on the southern Gold Coast, two longtime friends created a supersized fish that is now pride of place at one of Australia's largest outdoor sculpture exhibitions.

It started life relatively small, with the idea of sculpting a piece made entirely of red-nosed, fish-shaped soy sauce packets.

But like so many projects, its scale soon got much bigger.

Ged McCormick hopes the massive mullet inspires others to express themselves through art. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"We didn't quite think it would be here," said Ged McCormick, who sacrificed half a parking space at his Palm Beach home to bring the sculpture to life.

"We were tossing up doing it at my work or at Rusty's place, but this is just where everything started … and it keeps the neighbourhood entertained."

The concept began as an Indigenous fish trap woven from invasive plants, which the pair planned to fill with fishing line and plastic litter collected from nearby beaches.

Rusty Linnane works on ecological restoration projects, helping transform weed-infested natural areas back to their original condition. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"Then Ged said, 'How about we do a whole mullet in the style of an Indigenous fish trap,'" co-sculptor, Rusty Linnane, said.

" That's how the process went from me wanting to make a flat piece out of little sushi fish, to 'Let's make a 5-metre mullet!' "

Creating a cat's claw fish

Sold on the idea of a mega-mullet, the next conundrum for the pair was finding a weed strong enough to weave.

Drawing on his experience with ecological restoration projects, Mr Linnane identified cat's claw creeper, a South American species once imported as an exotic ornamental plant, as his target species.

Sushi shop soy sauce packets still feature prominently in the sculpture. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"It's obnoxious," Mr Linnane said, with a wry smile and a tinge of malice toward the invasive species.

He explained that the yellow-flowered vine's method was to climb a tree and smother it in foliage until it died and crashed to the ground.

"Then it will go to the next tree, and up, and so on and so on," he said.

The mullet is installed on the Currumbin foreshore as part of the 2026 SWELL Sculpture Festival. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby )

With special permission from the state government, Mr Linnane and Mr McCormick were allowed to harvest vines from an infestation in Nerang National Park.

"We started on the edge where we could walk up and see one or two vines going up big trees and we could cut them and treat the bases," Mr Linnane said.

" We were getting lengths of up to 25 to 30 metres, just by selectively picking those vines. "

Rusty Linnane and Ged McCormick wove several kilometres of vine into their mullet sculpture. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Neither artist could definitively say how many hours they spent harvesting the vines but admitted there were several unplanned trips to collect more material as the mullet began taking shape.

"It would take us about an hour to collect about 125 metres [of usable vine] … and 125 metres does about a 30-centimetre section of the fish," Mr Linnane said.

A SWELL message

After weaving kilometres of vine and stuffing the fish's guts with an almost equal length of discarded fishing line and other plastic litter, Mr Linnane and Mr McCormick moved their creation into place at the annual SWELL Sculpture Festival on the Currumbin foreshore this week.

Discarded fishing line and plastic litter was stitched into a net to create the mullet's stomach. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

SWELL founder and artistic director Natasha Edwards said tens of thousands of people were expected to flood the festival over the next 10 days.

"This year, up to 100 local and international sculptors are transforming the coastline into a spectacular sculpture walk," Ms Edwards said.

"You can walk along barefoot, with the sand between your toes … you're really connecting art and nature together so that the environment and the artworks really speak to each other."

The woven sculpture catches the early morning sun from its vantage point on the Currumbin foreshore. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Of the many people who catch sight of his co-creation, Mr Linnane hopes at least some of them take the bait on the environmental message it is casting out.

"Don't buy one-use plastics," Mr Linnane said.

" And for every exotic species of plant out there, there's a local native that will do the exact same job, and possibly better. "

Mr McCormick too hopes the mullet gets caught in the mind of those who see it, especially younger generations.

"We're just amateurs, me and Rusty, we're just having fun," he said.

"I guess this shows any kids out there that if you want to express yourself through art, there's always an opportunity to do it."

World.title: Bikie charged over tobacco shop blaze that set man alight
World.content:
An outlaw motorcycle gang member has been charged as part of an investigation into several suspicious fires, including a blaze in Melbourne's west that left a man with life-threatening injuries this month.

The 32-year-old Delacombe man, a member of the Bandidos Outlaw Motorcycle Gang, was arrested yesterday, along with a 42-year-old Melton man, after a suspicious fire at a shop in Taylors Lakes early yesterday morning.

Emergency services responded to reports the business, on Melton Highway, had been set alight about 4:25am. No-one was inside.

Police chased the men through suburbs in Melbourne's west, with the pair eventually dumping their vehicle in Brookfield. They fled on foot and were arrested soon after.

The 42-year-old was interviewed and released pending summons.

Police allege the 32-year-old was also involved in a bungled firebombing at a tobacco shop in Melton on September 3.

Loading...

CCTV from the scene shows a ute reversing into the building, before two men get out with what appear to be jerry cans of fuel.

A few moments later, a ball of flame engulfs both men.

A 23-year-old man with significant burns was found nearby and flown to hospital, where he remains in a critical condition with significant injuries.



Detective Inspector Chris Murray, of the Arson and Explosives Squad, said the arrests and charges were a result of additional patrols in Melbourne's west.

"Since this (Melton) fire occurred, police have worked tirelessly to identify those involved at every level so we can ultimately put them before the court," he said.

"This fire didn't just damage the property — it has also had an enormous impact on one of the people involved, who remains in hospital and will never be the same again.

"Should the individual who suffered significant burns succumb to his injuries, we intend to hold those who planned and assisted with the arson personally responsible."

Police have charged the 32-year-old man with offences relating to the Melton fire, including recklessly causing serious injury, aggravated burglary, criminal damage by fire and reckless conduct endangering life.

Detectives will investigate whether the Melton and Taylors Lakes fires were connected to other similar incidents.

Anyone with information should contact Crime Stoppers via 1800 333 000 or www.crimestoppersvic.com.au.

World.title: ‘These waters aren’t safe’: New oil supply fears as Houthis seize key island, Saudi pipeline attacked
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war ‘These waters aren’t safe’: New oil supply fears as Houthis seize key island, Saudi pipeline attacked Mohammed Ghobari , Eman Abouhassira and Yasmine Ghania Updated September 12, 2026 — 11:20am ,first published 10:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aden/Dubai: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis reached the strategic island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, four Yemeni government sources said, moving to tighten their grip on a vital global shipping route in the widening Middle East war. Meanwhile, the vital East-West oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, which has helped relieve the logjam in the Strait of Hormuz, was shut down by a drone attack coming from Iraq, Saudi officials said. This put further pressure on Gulf oil flows at a time when diplomatic efforts to ease war have stalled. Satellite imagery shows smoke from fires burning on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline. EUMETSAT If the Houthis can gain control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, their backer Iran could gain a critical advantage in its war with the US, reducing supplies through a second major corridor and further raising oil prices. The New York Times reported that since the war began at the end of February, at least 22 sailors had been killed in the Middle East. “These waters aren’t safe,” said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, an analyst at Windward, a maritime intelligence company.



The Houthi attacks could represent a dangerous escalation. Sources said Saudi Arabia has asked Washington for military help at a time when higher fuel prices during the war have tarnished US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party politically ahead of November’s midterm elections. Two sources from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised Yemeni government said its forces had pulled out of Perim and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, which faces the island. A satellite image of Perim Island taken on Friday. Pléiades © CNES 2026, Distribution Airbus DS via AP The war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran six months ago. Hormuz, conduit for about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade, was effectively closed. Since then, Saudi Arabia – the world’s largest oil exporter and a close US ally – has relied on the Red Sea route. Gulf states, industry sources and Trump have discussed pipeline expansion as one possible workaround. Existing pipeline capacity was shut down temporarily as a precaution after several attacks on the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh and Medina regions, state media reported, citing a source at the Saudi energy ministry.



Both Baghdad and Riyadh said the attack had originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate. Iraq dismissed a military commander on Saturday in response to the attack. Saudi Arabia has opted against retaliation so far following a request from the Iraqi prime minister, the Saudi foreign ministry said in a statement. The kingdom reserves the right to “take all measures necessary” to protect its interests, the statement said. Iraq’s government condemned attacks. A supporter raises a rifle during a Friday rally in Houthi-controlled Sanaa, Yemen, to celebrate the rebel group’s capture of Perim Island. AP Photo/Osamah Abdulrahman The 1200-kilometre pipeline is the key alternative route for Saudi oil to reach global markets, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. It has been shipping 4 million to 5 million barrels per day in recent months, amounting to 4 per cent to 5 per cent of global supply, according to ship tracking companies and analysts. The attack resulted in some injuries and damage that was being assessed, the Saudi foreign ministry said without detailing the impact on exports.



Saudi crude supply fell to the lowest levels in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, partly due to attacks on ships transiting Bab el-Mandeb by Houthi-linked groups. Oil prices dipped on Friday after surging a day earlier, but Bloomberg reported that Brent futures were trading at about $US105 a barrel on speculation about the impact of the latest violence on energy supplies in the region. The Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said maritime navigation remained safe for all shipping except Saudi vessels subject to a previously announced ban. Yemeni government forces indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthis – mountain fighters who withstood years of devastating Saudi airstrikes during Yemen’s civil war – in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline. They announced they would deploy weapons and aircraft to eliminate any movement of the “terrorist” Houthi militias in strategic areas, including the road leading to the coastal city of Mokha, which the militant group captured on Thursday along with the Red Sea islands of Hanish.



Reuters has reported that the dramatic Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast came with direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said. Iran describes the Houthis as an ally but publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are “not a proxy”. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump at least twice on Thursday to request US military help in fighting the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday, confirming an earlier report by Axios. Washington told Riyadh it was not willing to take direct military action for now, but would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, the two sources said.



The White House did not address a Reuters question on any phone calls between the two leaders, but a senior administration official speaking on the condition of anonymity said Washington was in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaSeptember 11 attacks ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on Maria Tsvetkova , Idrees Ali and Joseph Ax Updated September 12, 2026 — 10:10am ,first published September 11, 2026 — 11:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day. In New York, family members of the victims joined Vice President JD Vance, former president George W. Bush, who was in office on 9/11, and ex-presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8.46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Centre’s North Tower. A woman and child pause at the memorial on Friday morning. Spencer Platt/Pool Getty Images North America via AP The site of the World Trade Centre attacks, pictured on Friday, now the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, a sombre recitation that lasts for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001.



Elsie Caldwell carried a photograph of her son Kenny Caldwell to hear his name and all the others read aloud. She last spoke to him that morning a quarter-century ago. “Mom, I just want to let you know that I love you,” Caldwell said he told her in a final phone call. She is one of many relatives of victims whose remains never were recovered. Other moments of silence, marking when the other three planes hijacked by al-Qaeda terrorists crashed and the two towers collapsed, followed. For the first time, a seventh silence was observed to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward. Sombre ceremonies were held across the country to mark the 25th anniversary. Bloomberg New York City Fire Department (FDNY) members visit the memorial ahead of the ceremony. Bloomberg



An attendee with a tattoo of the Twin Towers at the memorial in New York on Friday. Bloomberg US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wiped away a tear as he revisited the place where the attacks killed 658 of his then-colleagues – including his brother, Gary Lutnick – at the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald. Gregory Carafello came to the ceremony to honour the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald. Carafello himself was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate. “Everyone should realise that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families,” he said. “These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work.” Former president Joe Biden, Vice President JD Vance and former president George W. Bush. AP Photo/Pamela Smith



Former president Bill Clinton, former first lady Michelle Obama and former president Barack Obama listen to speakers at the memorial in New York. Olga Fedorova/POOL EPA via AP At the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, where American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building’s west flank, killing 184, senior military leaders gathered amid heavy rain to watch the unfurling of an American flag before US President Donald Trump chronicled some of the stories of those aboard who perished in the crash: a woman pregnant with her first child, a family of four headed to Australia, three sixth-graders on a field trip. “In those harrowing days after the attacks, we saw the authentic spirit of our nation,” Trump said at the ceremony. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump at a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein An American flag is unfurled at the Pentagon early on Friday morning. Bloomberg



US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth watched the flag unfurling ceremony as rain fell at the Pentagon. Bloomberg The president and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who also delivered remarks, both used their speeches to make the case for the Iran war, which they have defended as necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Related Article September 11 attacks The day that changed America and shaped the world we know today “We salute our first responders and law enforcement, and we love them,” Trump said. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.” Trump added: “September 11th reminded us of the terrible power of hate. The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail, and to win.”



The Washington Post reported that Trump, ahead of his remarks, at times appeared to be struggling to keep his eyes open. The president got back to the White House about 2.30am from his trip to Dallas. White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected claims suggesting the president was asleep. Loading “[He] was solemnly listening and remembering the victims and heroic first responders who tragically lost their lives on that fateful day. Anyone ridiculously claiming the president was asleep is lying,” he said. A ceremony was also being held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington.



The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security. But for many whom the attacks directly affected – the victims’ families, first responders and rescue workers – the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter-century ago and the heartbreak that followed. Loading Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower. Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him to her father’s grave last week and was attending a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday.



“This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing that they won’t ever get to know each other,” Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. “My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather. Related Article September 11 attacks Australians remember lost loved ones 25 years on from September 11 attacks “We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added. The attacks initiated the “war on terror”, which led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements – a promise being tested by the current Iran war. At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks.



At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colours Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected. Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Rudy Giuliani, former mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony. Bloomberg Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died. Patrick Whalen’s father, also named Patrick, was a New York City firefighter who responded to the attacks and continued working at Ground Zero for months amid the dust and rubble. In 2020, he was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer linked to exposure to toxic carcinogens, and died in 2021.



Related Article September 11 attacks John Howard witnessed the 9/11 attacks as PM. It changed his leadership forever “The government told him it was safe to breathe, and, obviously, it was not true,” the younger Whalen said after a New York City Fire Department memorial service this week. Information that the air at Ground Zero was safe to breathe came from the US Environmental Protection Agency. Its former administrator, Christine Todd Whitman, apologised in a 2016 interview with The Guardian, saying the agency did its best with the knowledge it had. The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show. Twenty-six have died this year alone. A woman mourns at the September 11 memorial plaza in Lower Manhattan. Dave Sanders/Pool The New York Times via AP

World.title: Bombshell call: Zak Butters nominates the Western Bulldogs
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Bombshell call: Zak Butters nominates the Western Bulldogs Jake Niall September 12, 2026 — 10:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters has nominated the Western Bulldogs as his preferred destination. The Power confirmed that the club had been informed by Butters of his choice of club, the Dogs beating Geelong for his services provided they can secure him via free agency or a trade. Zak Butters has nominated the Western Bulldogs. AFL Photos Port Adelaide will have to decide whether to match the massive, nine-year offer to Butters or force a trade. If they choose not to match, they will receive pick No.5 in the national draft – the selection after Port’s first pick. Their early draft choices will be needed to match the likely bid at pick No.1 for their academy gun Dougie Cochrane.



Geelong had likewise offered Butters a nine-year deal. Related Article Money Talks

AFL 2026 Buttering up the Power: The Cat-and-Dog fight to land an AFL superstar Richmond and Collingwood had been the other clubs vying for Butters during this season. Butters, who hails from Darley near Bacchus Marsh, grew up as a Bulldogs fan. The Bulldogs had recently increased their offer to Butters, which will likely be the biggest in AFL history. Assuming they can navigate a trade or land the 26-year-old champion via free agency, the arrival of Butters will be a coup for the Bulldogs and their coach Luke Beveridge.



Butters had formed a friendship with Bulldogs’ skipper Marcus Bontempelli which the club had felt was a factor in their favour in the intense competition for the Port star. Should Port match the free agency offer, the Dogs could well need to find draft capital by trading a player or players out. In May, Port coach Josh Carr had told this masthead that the Power would match a free agency bid and force a trade if he departed. But the landscape has shifted since then since Port have finished 15th, drawing an earlier compensation pick if they do not match. Of the many flow on effects from Butters’ call is that it might make it easier for Geelong to land St Kilda ruckman Rowan Marshall. The Cats are in the pole position to snare Toby Greene as an unrestricted free agent if he leaves the Giants. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Bring on the the Zak attack: The Cats’ semi-final showed they sorely need it



Butters’ decision is a bombshell move that will drastically shape this year’s trade period. The Port Adelaide star ended months of speculation about this future late last month when he confirmed he was heading back to Victoria. Butters told Port officials at his exit meeting that he would exercise his restricted free agency rights to join a Victorian team. Butters’ decision ended at least 18 months of speculation about his playing future. “I’ve made the decision to head home,” the 25-year-old said last month.



“It’s obviously been one that I’ve wrestled with for a while now, and it’s been quite tough to get to the bottom of it. It’s been a tough decision in my life, and one that I haven’t taken lightly. “I’m probably at a stage in my life where I’d like to get back around some family and friends, and enjoy some more time with them and cherish more moments with them. But in saying that, I’ve also really enjoyed my time at the footy club and here in Adelaide, and it’s felt like home for me as well.”

World.title: No need for midterm election emergency, says Trump’s ‘transparency’ aide
World.content:
Exclusive WorldNorth AmericaUS midterm elections No need for midterm election emergency, says Trump’s ‘transparency’ aide Michael Koziol September 12, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dallas: The man Donald Trump recruited to the White House to conduct a pre-election “government transparency” project says there is no need for an emergency declaration before the November 3 midterm elections, as prospects of the president attempting such a ploy diminish. John Solomon, a conservative media entrepreneur who became a special government employee in June, was behind the administration’s release of formerly classified documents in July purporting to show widespread election “meddling” by foreign countries and a cover-up by the “deep state”. John Solomon (left) was hired by the White House to run the “Government Transparency Taskforce”. Bloomberg Trump aired the claims in a primetme address to the nation, upon which MAGA operatives such as Steve Bannon openly called for the president to declare a national security emergency relating to the midterm elections, and predicted Trump would do so during the last week of August. That window has come and gone, and Solomon told this masthead there was no momentum for such a move. “I don’t get a sense that people are concerned about election security,” he said.



Solomon made the comments on the sidelines of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, and said he was speaking in his capacity as a journalist, not a government employee. He played down the prospects of Trump trying to call an emergency that could restrict mail-in voting or dispatch the National Guard to patrol polling stations, for example. Donald Trump and Solomon shake hands on July 16, the day of the president’s address about election integrity. Bloomberg “Nothing I’ve seen as a reporter indicates that that’s on the table right now. It could be,” Solomon said. “But there’s a lot of really valuable things that have happened to grow confidence in the election.” That included a request to allow states to use a Department of Homeland Security database to check voter information against federal citizenship and social security records.



The Trump administration has asked the conservative-majority Supreme Court to permit use of the tool. The courts are also weighing Trump’s attempts to restrict mail-in ballots through an executive order and a new directive by the US Postal Service, although time is running out. Solomon said: “The solutions that have been in place have seemed to grow confidence. But we’ll know on election day.” Trump’s former chief strategist Steve Bannon, who remains an influential MAGA voice. Bloomberg MAGA activists such Bannon and his fellow broadcaster on right-wing channel Real America’s Voice, Wayne Allyn Root, have been building the case for Trump to declare a national security emergency before the midterms, in an example of what Bannon refers to as shifting the Overton window of what is possible. “You will have enough evidence by mid-August to show that we have a massive problem,” Bannon told the masthead in July.

World.title: Academy alumni take to big stage together in Roosters finals tilt
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Academy alumni take to big stage together in Roosters finals tilt Chris Barrett September 12, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the block of units they called home as teenagers, Siua Wong, Robert Toia, Salesi Foketi and Benaiah Ioelu usually just ate with each other. But now and then, there was a high-powered guest list at the Sydney Roosters academy housing in Kingsford. Benaiah Ioelu, Robert Toia, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong have come through the ranks together. James Brickwood “At least once a month not only Nick [Politis] but the whole board would come over for dinner,” said back-rower Wong. “It was pretty cool having that relationship. A lot of us young boys moving from outside of Sydney coming in, hearing about the board, you feel a bit nervous. But for them to be so down to earth and express a lot of humility to get to know some of the young boys was something that I really loved.



“I think that’s one of the big values of this club, being a family club, and it definitely showed through that.” Several years after those evenings hosting club chairman Politis, and fellow directors such as Mark Bouris and Luke Ricketson, the quartet is in the big time as the Roosters’ semi-finals campaign gets going. Wong was the first graduate of the academy and made his NRL debut in 2023. Getty Images Wong, 23, Toia, 22, and Foketi, 20 are in the starting side for Sunday’s clash against minor premiers Penrith at CommBank Stadium. Ioelu, 22, is a reserve. Their appearance together at the pointy end of the season is validation of the Roosters’ decision to establish an academy in 2021 after visiting the facilities of Spanish football giants Barcelona FC.



Determined to produce more of their own, the eastern suburbs club can also count homegrown Roosters Hugo Savala, Victor Radley and Billy Smith in the line-up against the Panthers. The graduates emerged from a carefully designed program engineered by Politis and Roosters coach Trent Robinson and led by three-time premiership winners and one-club servants Mitchell Aubusson and Jake Friend. Foketi has made his mark on the edge for the Roosters in his second season in the top grade. Getty Images The grand plan is for the entire Roosters squad to eventually be comprised of players from their development system. “The dream is to one day have 17 players playing on the paddock that have come through our academy. So to have all those boys play on the weekend is great,” said Friend, a defence guru with the Roosters who was the academy’s inaugural head coach.



“We don’t have a big junior base obviously but with the guys we get, we want to breed long-term NRL players.” The former dummy-half said with potentially three teams joining the NRL over the next three seasons, it was even more important for clubs to grow their own and retain them. Toia makes a break against North Queensland in round 22. Getty Images Underpinning the Roosters’ approach is an attention to detail aimed at forging a lasting association with the tri-colours. From dinners with the board in the academy units, to nutrition advice from champion fullback Anthony Minichiello and one-on-one video sessions with Friend and Aubusson, now the Roosters rugby league director, the first batch of academy alumni learned from the best. “You look at the soccer academies, they’re a business in a sense. You develop a player and you get a transfer fee,” Friend said.



Related Article NRL 2026 ‘I love the Sharks’: From boyhood fan to Cronulla’s billionaire backer “You don’t get that in rugby league. They do have an ability to leave. But we’ve seen some guys probably have the opportunity to leave and stay. I think that’s got to do with the Roosters academy. We want to keep as many of them as we can.” Wong, who was scouted by the Roosters in Auckland at the age of 14 and has been a mainstay in Robinson’s side for the past two seasons, said on the eve of the finals his time in the academy was one of the best experiences of his life. “Nick, Aubbo and Jake Friend set up a great environment for us boys to develop and I think it’s shown through the footy players that we’ve been able to become,” he said. “It really instilled in me what it is to be a Rooster, and what that means on the field and off the field, and I feel like that’s so important for young players coming through.”



It also left a lasting mark on Toia, who has since become a Queensland State of Origin centre. “When we moved out was when we realised how great we had it,” he said. “Being there, you could tell how much the Roosters care.”

World.title: BBL sell-off plans will be on the right side of history
World.content:
SportCricketBig Bash Opinion BBL sell-off plans will be on the right side of history

Colin Smith September 12, 2026 — 9:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cricket NSW’s negative commentary on Big Bash League clubs privatisation plans suggests it will threaten the system, risks long-lasting impacts at all levels and endangers a model that is “the envy of the world.” While it is concerning rhetoric, it is also, on the evidence, not supported by facts and backs the wrong side of history. Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird defended the privitisation move for the Twenty20 franchises. George Chan Strip away the emotion, and Cricket Australia’s case for external investment in the clubs is straightforward and offers an exciting path that ensures global leadership in growing TV audiences (and hence media rights) and attendances. Critically, it also reinforces Test cricket. BBL and TV audiences have grown significantly following CA’s decision in 2023–24 to cut the BBL to 44 games.



However, fielding Australia’s centrally contracted stars in the league is a challenge. The salary pool intended to keep Australia’s best players at home has been increased from $1.9 million to more than $3 million per squad. That’s just to remain competitive with emerging leagues in South Africa and the United Arab Emirates — competitions that didn’t exist five years ago and can potentially outbid the BBL for Australian players. It helps to be clear about what “cricket” now includes because the debate is too often framed as T20 eroding the “real” game. The success of the Indian Premier League has given cricket financial security. AP It isn’t. Even the Board of Control for Cricket in India — an organisation with every incentive to focus on T20 — calls Test cricket “the bedrock of our game” and backs it with a financial incentive scheme for players who prioritise red-ball cricket. Modern cricket is a dual-format sport: Tests supply history and depth, and T20 provides the commercial engine that funds the lot. Since the Indian Premier League’s 2008 launch, T20 has grown.



Sixteen leagues operate worldwide, 87 nations entered qualification for the 2026 T20 World Cup cycle, and cricket (T20) will return to the Olympics in 2028 at Los Angeles after a 128-year absence. Not coincidentally, India is a favoured bidder for the 2036 Olympics. No comparably short, spectator-friendly format in any other sport has built anything like it. But none has become a standalone financial engine for its parent sport the way T20 funds cricket. A huge crowd celebrated 2014 IPL champions Kolkata Knight Riders in Kolkata, India. Getty That’s the opportunity NSW is arguing Australian cricket should avoid. The IPL is worth roughly $18.5 billion, built almost entirely on media rights.



Another perspective Investigation

Australian soccer How A-League’s biggest investor got a $140m get out of jail free card It sits within the world’s top 10 sports leagues by value and holds the sixth-highest sports broadcast rights value globally. IPL club owners have gone shopping abroad - Reliance, GMR, RPSG, Sun Group - because there’s only one Mumbai Indians licence at home. South Africa sold its entire domestic T20 competition to those same IPL groups in 2022 and has recorded broadcast growth of up to 47 per cent locally and 257 per cent in Indian media reach. England sold 49 per cent stakes in each of its eight franchises in The Hundred league for more than £500 million, keeping counties in majority control and ring-fencing 10 per cent for the grassroots. None of these boards let in outside capital out of desperation. They let it in because they could see where T20’s value was heading and who controlled the playbook to get there.



In all cases, these countries own their T20 leagues, with investors and shareholders in the clubs. NSW’s counter-argument is that its model works — the Sixers and Thunder are “successful and healthy,” profits are reinvested, and participation among 5-to-12-year-olds is up 80 per cent. All true, but this sidesteps the question of whether a wholly state-owned model can fund an escalating global talent-salary war for the next decade. In Australia, there are four sports leagues that are “must-haves” and “must-broadcast” - the NRL, AFL, Australian Open tennis and cricket (Test and BBL). There are genuine governance lessons here. The A-Leagues took private equity money in 2021 while individual clubs slid towards insolvency. But the lesson isn’t “don’t sell” — it’s “don’t sell vaguely”.



Editor's pick Australian cricket Sell off the BBL, or sell out to sports betting: Cricket’s huge call Money without a mechanism to enforce disciplined use just buys time, not a turnaround. The ECB’s Hundred sale is that template because it embeds discipline: tiered distribution, a grassroots share, and spending guardrails for the counties. None of this makes privatisation risk-free, or Cricket Australia’s process above reproach — NSW’s complaint is that four conditions agreed by all state chairs in June went unmet before the CA Board pressed ahead. But a complaint about process isn’t a case against the substance, and on the substance the global evidence is clear: leagues combining private capital for the BBL clubs only with disciplined guardrails are growing broadcast value and building the star power that keeps players and crowds in the BBL, not lost overseas. Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird and CEO Todd Greenberg address the media pack in Sydney this week. Getty Images



Importantly, investing in the BBL clubs ensures that the exciting growth and professionalisation of women’s BBL continue – as is happening with WPL in India. Cricket NSW built the two most successful clubs in the competition’s history. It should be shaping this conversation from a position of strength, rather than resisting it. With the likely sale of the Melbourne Renegades to external investors, NSW will be the sole owner of two clubs in the BBL. Furthermore, there is no example globally across leading sports leagues of a single owner of two clubs in the same league. Colin Smith of Global Media and Sports has spent two decades advising the world’s biggest sports and media rights holders and broadcasters on sports media rights, including cricket media rights and design models for the BBL.

World.title: ‘It’s the Wild West’: How a shaken Sydney is grappling with the gang war
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney's ganglands ‘It’s the Wild West’: How a shaken Sydney is grappling with the gang war Mostafa Rachwani September 12, 2026 — 9:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ahmad Hraichie has buried many gangsters in his time as a Muslim undertaker. He’s buried small time runners, heads of crime families and everyone in between. He knows death and its sudden movements well. But even he is shaken by the escalating gangland violence in western Sydney. Muslim undertaker Ahmad Hraichie says the community is “frustrated” at inaction on gang violence. Sitthixay Ditthavong “There were rules before: you don’t shoot innocent people, you don’t shoot kids or women, you don’t shoot at funerals,” he says. “It’s wild now, there are no rules.” “Yeah, it’s gangsters, but gangsters once had ethics and morals and integrity. They’d help an old lady on the street.



“Now it’s brazen, it’s lawless, like the Wild West.” Hraichie is speaking at the Muslim morgue under Lakemba Mosque where Louis Meehan was washed and prepared for burial on Saturday, as per the strict Islamic protocols on death. A body must be washed, wrapped in a white shroud, prayed over and buried as soon as possible, part of a broader Islamic belief in death being a transition from life to the afterlife. Delays are seen as holding the soul back from moving to the next phase of existence. Meehan was shot dead behind his boxing gym in the Punchbowl Community Centre car park on Wednesday night, as community members and school students watched on.



He died under a hail of gunfire from an assailant who fled in a silver Lexus. Police believe the attack is linked to organised crime in western Sydney. Meehan had posted photos online wearing merchandise linked to the Alameddine crime gang, which is locked in a murderous war with rival gang the Coconut Cartel. Meehan’s killing was the third in a little over a week. University student Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed in Glen Alpine on Tuesday last week. The next day, Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot in the doorway of a Merrylands West home. Two men were arrested on Friday in connection with that shooting, including an alleged drone operator. In the two years to June, 19 people died amid escalating violence, a Herald analysis found, including 100 shootings and 52 firebombings. The violence has coalesced into a haze that hangs over western Sydney, a dread looming over a region that has known violence before but not like this. “It’s getting worse, and it is driven by many factors, including the intoxicating draw of social media and the internet,” Hraichie says. “It’s brazen now. People are doing it in the middle of the day, and part of that is the internet.



“The world has become so fast and people are struggling. And to these kids, it’s all about the lifestyle, the haircuts, the cars, the money. It’s all about living in this moment, right now, no future. “It’s an alien world,” he says, shaking his head. Like many in western Sydney, Hraichie has seen different eras of gang violence break out. There were the gangland wars of the 1980s, the postcode wars of the late 2010s, the feud between the Hamzy and Alameddine families. Muslim undertaker Ahmad Hraichie says gang violence is a “cancer”. Sitthixay Ditthavong With a regional robustness charged by generations of migrants from wartorn backgrounds who won’t be shaken by much, the violence remained for a while as cultural background noise, shrugged at and ignored.



But it has since spilled out into community spaces, into daylight, and into the cultural consciousness with brazen acts. As more innocent people die than ever before, Hraichie says frustration is growing at a lack of action from authorities. “There isn’t fear, there’s frustration,” he says. “I don’t think fear is part of the equation or vocabulary for these parts. But people are frustrated: why haven’t these guys been stopped?” That sense of frustration hardly abated when acting Assistant Police Commissioner Grant Taylor said on Thursday that gangland shootings were “part and parcel of life in a big metropolis”. “It always looks like crime is out of control but, when you look at it, we’re on track,” Taylor said.



“We always have about eight organised crime murders a year. We’ve had six, and then last night made seven. It’s always going to be part and parcel of life in a big metropolis; this is no different.” The comments were swiftly shot down by Premier Chris Minns, who said the violence was shocking and the community “shouldn’t have to put up with” it. Related Article Exclusive

NSW State Parliament Gangland violence threatens Labor’s grip on outer Sydney “I’d hate it for anyone to believe that we’re accepting of the status quo, or we believe that it’s normal, or that it’s acceptable, or that we just have to turn a blind eye,” Minns said. “I don’t think any premier or any political leader can ever make the claim or promise that murder will stop in a big state like NSW, but we can promise arrests, and we can promise longer jail time for the people who are involved.”



Criminologist Dr Vincent Hurley, who spent 23 years as a NSW Police detective, said that if the violence was not curbed soon, it could start to have lasting cultural consequences. “The names that they adopt almost set in train this narrative that tarnishes the rest of the community,” he said. Related Article Editorial

Crime Authorities must get their acts together on organised-crime killings The Herald's View Editorial “I think the frustration is that it seems to be every day, all day, and that’s probably not the case. And I think they find it frustrating because people stereotype them. It wears them down over time, and people can’t break away from their surname, from their culture.” Hurley warned that without urgent intervention, communities could become insular and pull away from the rest of Sydney, culturally and economically.



“They’re going to bunker down and become very protective of themselves, and it’ll be us versus them, even if they’re not involved in any type of crime,” he said. “Just by the mere fact of stereotyping, it’s going to have a massive effect on kids at school, who then want to go out and get a job; they probably won’t leave that geographic area. These areas will become siloed. “Ultimately, I really feel sorry for the community members of these cultural groups because they have no control over the narrative.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Tom Lynagh is Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Can he be a saviour, too?
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion Tom Lynagh is Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Can he be a saviour, too? Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter September 12, 2026 — 7:52am

September 12, 2026 — 7:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There won’t be a huge audience for the opening game of Super Rugby AUS early on Saturday afternoon, when Queensland host the Western Force at Ballymore. But those rugby-hungry types who do tune into Stan Sport will be watching intently – and none more so than Wallabies coach Les Kiss, who has problems to resolve before naming an updated squad on Monday for Tests against the Springboks and the All Blacks. Loading He’ll be assessing whether Jock Campbell is worth recalling to replace Tom Wright, and he’ll keep tabs on Zac Lomax’s return from injury, in the fascinating position of No.13 for the Force. But mostly Kiss will be on his couch studying the men duelling in the No.10 jerseys: Tom Lynagh and Harry McLaughlin-Phillips.



Some fingers may be crossed. The Wallabies need another five-eighth to join the squad after Carter Gordon broke his leg in Mendoza. Carter Gordon (R) broke his leg Test against the Pumas in Mendoza. Getty Images Ben Donaldson and Declan Meredith are in the squad, but both have failed to claim the No.10 jersey this year, so filling Gordon’s vacancy isn’t necessarily just for a third-cab-off-the-rank player. It could be for the top job, if the right man stands up. Setting aside the experienced options of James O’Connor and Bernard Foley – who haven’t trained in a team environment for a few months – and Japan-based Noah Lolesio, who is not available in October under regulation 9, the here-and-now candidates boil down to Lynagh, McLaughlin-Phillips and Tane Edmed.



The latter played 10 Tests last year but is now down the pecking order behind Meredith, Donaldson and McLaughlin-Phillips, who was also called into the Wallabies squad last month ahead of him. But McLaughlin-Phillips, a running No.10, is a developing youngster you’d select as a third cab. Lynagh is not, and if he can prove his fitness, the Reds playmaker has the class to not only return to the Wallabies but to become the assertive game controller the side badly needs. Tom Lynagh has had a nightmare run of injuries with the Wallabies and Reds. Getty Images But all of that comes with a very big if. Hence, the crossed fingers. Lynagh has played just 17 minutes this year, after suffering a string of soft-tissue injuries dating back to this time last year, when he tore a hamstring playing for the Wallabies against Argentina.



Lynagh was not considered for the spring tour so that he could have an off-season to get stronger and more physically resilient. It didn’t have the desired effect. Lynagh suffered repeated tears of the soleus (lower calf) muscle throughout the Super Rugby season. Wallabies five-eighth Tom Lynagh pictured in Coogee last year. Dion Georgopoulos The long absence, combined with a lack of public information about Lynagh’s status, saw the odd conspiracy theory pop up, including that he didn’t even want to play rugby. They were all wrong – Lynagh re-signing with Queensland in May was proof of his desire – but as Reds coach, Kiss played the long-game and put Lynagh on a go-slow conditioning plan to build sufficient resilience in his body to get through full games, and full seasons. Lynagh put on five kilograms of muscle, but again, it didn’t fix the problems.



As the months dragged on, Lynagh suffered multiple setbacks with the injured calf, each time re-setting the comeback clock. Brilliant and brittle in equal parts, Lynagh is now Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Though he is extremely tough in games and doesn’t shirk contact – as seen in the Lions series – Lynagh has also became known as a flighty trainer, who is hyper-aware of any tweak or injury niggle he feels in his body. One theory at Ballymore is that Lynagh’s past life as a schoolboy cricketer may have contributed to a propensity for back tightness.



Whatever the reason, a wary Lynagh often sat out sessions and could not complete a full week of training. Given Joe Schmidt rigidly demands as much to be selected, the blond No.10 fell out of the Wallabies reckoning. Edmed, a no-frills but durable type, was called up, and Gordon was also poached back from league (only to also start picking up injuries). This year, the Wallabies’ long-standing problem at No.10 hasn’t gone away. If anything, it has become more acute. Harry McLaughlin-Phillips trained with the Wallabies in Perth in July. Getty Images The Wallabies’ forwards have improved hugely but the backline’s work - and game management in particular - has gone the other way. Ryan Lonergan has been outstanding at halfback but the work of several options at No.10 has been B-grade. The Wallabies’ ability to exit their half via the boot has been mostly dire this year, and the game direction has gone from mediocre to muddled as Tests have worn on.



It comes with a very obvious fitness caveat, but Lynagh at his best presents as the solution: a tough, long-kicking five-eighth, with a strong voice and the heads-up composure to run a game. Related Article NRL 2026 PNG Chiefs in war over name as NZ Rugby threatens legal action So getting Lynagh back on the field and keeping him there is the name of the game. If any coach can do it, it’d be Kiss, who managed him effectively in the first half of 2025. If Kiss can get Lynagh back into that same shape and mindset, the 23-year-old could be a key factor in the Wallabies’ campaign at the Rugby World Cup. “I’m really enjoying Tom in a playmaker role and a decision-maker within the team,” new Reds coach Vern Cotter said this week. “He’s got a great head on his shoulders. He sees the game well. He’s calm and decisive, so I’m looking forward to having him run the game for us.”



Just to be “careful”, Cotter said he’ll give Lynagh 40 minutes at Ballymore and then everyone will wait and see how he pulls up. There may be crossed fingers.

World.title: ‘These waters aren’t safe’: New oil supply fears as Houthis seize key island, Saudi pipeline attacked
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war ‘These waters aren’t safe’: New oil supply fears as Houthis seize key island, Saudi pipeline attacked Mohammed Ghobari , Eman Abouhassira and Yasmine Ghania Updated September 12, 2026 — 11:20am ,first published 10:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aden/Dubai: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis reached the strategic island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, four Yemeni government sources said, moving to tighten their grip on a vital global shipping route in the widening Middle East war. Meanwhile, the vital East-West oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, which has helped relieve the logjam in the Strait of Hormuz, was shut down by a drone attack coming from Iraq, Saudi officials said. This put further pressure on Gulf oil flows at a time when diplomatic efforts to ease war have stalled. Satellite imagery shows smoke from fires burning on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline. EUMETSAT If the Houthis can gain control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, their backer Iran could gain a critical advantage in its war with the US, reducing supplies through a second major corridor and further raising oil prices. The New York Times reported that since the war began at the end of February, at least 22 sailors had been killed in the Middle East. “These waters aren’t safe,” said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, an analyst at Windward, a maritime intelligence company.



The Houthi attacks could represent a dangerous escalation. Sources said Saudi Arabia has asked Washington for military help at a time when higher fuel prices during the war have tarnished US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party politically ahead of November’s midterm elections. Two sources from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised Yemeni government said its forces had pulled out of Perim and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, which faces the island. A satellite image of Perim Island taken on Friday. Pléiades © CNES 2026, Distribution Airbus DS via AP The war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran six months ago. Hormuz, conduit for about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade, was effectively closed. Since then, Saudi Arabia – the world’s largest oil exporter and a close US ally – has relied on the Red Sea route. Gulf states, industry sources and Trump have discussed pipeline expansion as one possible workaround. Existing pipeline capacity was shut down temporarily as a precaution after several attacks on the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh and Medina regions, state media reported, citing a source at the Saudi energy ministry.



Both Baghdad and Riyadh said the attack had originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate. Iraq dismissed a military commander on Saturday in response to the attack. Saudi Arabia has opted against retaliation so far following a request from the Iraqi prime minister, the Saudi foreign ministry said in a statement. The kingdom reserves the right to “take all measures necessary” to protect its interests, the statement said. Iraq’s government condemned attacks. A supporter raises a rifle during a Friday rally in Houthi-controlled Sanaa, Yemen, to celebrate the rebel group’s capture of Perim Island. AP Photo/Osamah Abdulrahman The 1200-kilometre pipeline is the key alternative route for Saudi oil to reach global markets, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. It has been shipping 4 million to 5 million barrels per day in recent months, amounting to 4 per cent to 5 per cent of global supply, according to ship tracking companies and analysts. The attack resulted in some injuries and damage that was being assessed, the Saudi foreign ministry said without detailing the impact on exports.



Saudi crude supply fell to the lowest levels in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, partly due to attacks on ships transiting Bab el-Mandeb by Houthi-linked groups. Oil prices dipped on Friday after surging a day earlier, but Bloomberg reported that Brent futures were trading at about $US105 a barrel on speculation about the impact of the latest violence on energy supplies in the region. The Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said maritime navigation remained safe for all shipping except Saudi vessels subject to a previously announced ban. Yemeni government forces indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthis – mountain fighters who withstood years of devastating Saudi airstrikes during Yemen’s civil war – in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline. They announced they would deploy weapons and aircraft to eliminate any movement of the “terrorist” Houthi militias in strategic areas, including the road leading to the coastal city of Mokha, which the militant group captured on Thursday along with the Red Sea islands of Hanish.



Reuters has reported that the dramatic Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast came with direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said. Iran describes the Houthis as an ally but publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are “not a proxy”. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump at least twice on Thursday to request US military help in fighting the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday, confirming an earlier report by Axios. Washington told Riyadh it was not willing to take direct military action for now, but would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, the two sources said.



The White House did not address a Reuters question on any phone calls between the two leaders, but a senior administration official speaking on the condition of anonymity said Washington was in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government. Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaSeptember 11 attacks ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on Maria Tsvetkova , Idrees Ali and Joseph Ax Updated September 12, 2026 — 10:10am ,first published September 11, 2026 — 11:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day. In New York, family members of the victims joined Vice President JD Vance, former president George W. Bush, who was in office on 9/11, and ex-presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8.46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Centre’s North Tower. A woman and child pause at the memorial on Friday morning. Spencer Platt/Pool Getty Images North America via AP The site of the World Trade Centre attacks, pictured on Friday, now the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, a sombre recitation that lasts for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001.



Elsie Caldwell carried a photograph of her son Kenny Caldwell to hear his name and all the others read aloud. She last spoke to him that morning a quarter-century ago. “Mom, I just want to let you know that I love you,” Caldwell said he told her in a final phone call. She is one of many relatives of victims whose remains never were recovered. Other moments of silence, marking when the other three planes hijacked by al-Qaeda terrorists crashed and the two towers collapsed, followed. For the first time, a seventh silence was observed to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward. Sombre ceremonies were held across the country to mark the 25th anniversary. Bloomberg New York City Fire Department (FDNY) members visit the memorial ahead of the ceremony. Bloomberg



An attendee with a tattoo of the Twin Towers at the memorial in New York on Friday. Bloomberg US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wiped away a tear as he revisited the place where the attacks killed 658 of his then-colleagues – including his brother, Gary Lutnick – at the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald. Gregory Carafello came to the ceremony to honour the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald. Carafello himself was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate. “Everyone should realise that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families,” he said. “These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work.” Former president Joe Biden, Vice President JD Vance and former president George W. Bush. AP Photo/Pamela Smith



Former president Bill Clinton, former first lady Michelle Obama and former president Barack Obama listen to speakers at the memorial in New York. Olga Fedorova/POOL EPA via AP At the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, where American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building’s west flank, killing 184, senior military leaders gathered amid heavy rain to watch the unfurling of an American flag before US President Donald Trump chronicled some of the stories of those aboard who perished in the crash: a woman pregnant with her first child, a family of four headed to Australia, three sixth-graders on a field trip. “In those harrowing days after the attacks, we saw the authentic spirit of our nation,” Trump said at the ceremony. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump at a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein An American flag is unfurled at the Pentagon early on Friday morning. Bloomberg



US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth watched the flag unfurling ceremony as rain fell at the Pentagon. Bloomberg The president and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who also delivered remarks, both used their speeches to make the case for the Iran war, which they have defended as necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Related Article September 11 attacks The day that changed America and shaped the world we know today “We salute our first responders and law enforcement, and we love them,” Trump said. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.” Trump added: “September 11th reminded us of the terrible power of hate. The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail, and to win.”



The Washington Post reported that Trump, ahead of his remarks, at times appeared to be struggling to keep his eyes open. The president got back to the White House about 2.30am from his trip to Dallas. White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected claims suggesting the president was asleep. Loading “[He] was solemnly listening and remembering the victims and heroic first responders who tragically lost their lives on that fateful day. Anyone ridiculously claiming the president was asleep is lying,” he said. A ceremony was also being held in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington.



The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security. But for many whom the attacks directly affected – the victims’ families, first responders and rescue workers – the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter-century ago and the heartbreak that followed. Loading Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower. Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him to her father’s grave last week and was attending a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday.



“This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing that they won’t ever get to know each other,” Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. “My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather. Related Article September 11 attacks Australians remember lost loved ones 25 years on from September 11 attacks “We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added. The attacks initiated the “war on terror”, which led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements – a promise being tested by the current Iran war. At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks.



At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colours Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected. Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Rudy Giuliani, former mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony. Bloomberg Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died. Patrick Whalen’s father, also named Patrick, was a New York City firefighter who responded to the attacks and continued working at Ground Zero for months amid the dust and rubble. In 2020, he was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer linked to exposure to toxic carcinogens, and died in 2021.



Related Article September 11 attacks John Howard witnessed the 9/11 attacks as PM. It changed his leadership forever “The government told him it was safe to breathe, and, obviously, it was not true,” the younger Whalen said after a New York City Fire Department memorial service this week. Information that the air at Ground Zero was safe to breathe came from the US Environmental Protection Agency. Its former administrator, Christine Todd Whitman, apologised in a 2016 interview with The Guardian, saying the agency did its best with the knowledge it had. The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show. Twenty-six have died this year alone. A woman mourns at the September 11 memorial plaza in Lower Manhattan. Dave Sanders/Pool The New York Times via AP

World.title: Bombshell call: Zak Butters nominates the Western Bulldogs
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Bombshell call: Zak Butters nominates the Western Bulldogs Jake Niall September 12, 2026 — 10:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters has nominated the Western Bulldogs as his preferred destination. The Power confirmed that the club had been informed by Butters of his choice of club, the Dogs beating Geelong for his services provided they can secure him via free agency or a trade. Zak Butters has nominated the Western Bulldogs. AFL Photos Port Adelaide will have to decide whether to match the massive, nine-year offer to Butters or force a trade. If they choose not to match, they will receive pick No.5 in the national draft – the selection after Port’s first pick. Their early draft choices will be needed to match the likely bid at pick No.1 for their academy gun Dougie Cochrane.



Geelong had likewise offered Butters a nine-year deal. Related Article Money Talks

AFL 2026 Buttering up the Power: The Cat-and-Dog fight to land an AFL superstar Richmond and Collingwood had been the other clubs vying for Butters during this season. Butters, who hails from Darley near Bacchus Marsh, grew up as a Bulldogs fan. The Bulldogs had recently increased their offer to Butters, which will likely be the biggest in AFL history. Assuming they can navigate a trade or land the 26-year-old champion via free agency, the arrival of Butters will be a coup for the Bulldogs and their coach Luke Beveridge.



Butters had formed a friendship with Bulldogs’ skipper Marcus Bontempelli which the club had felt was a factor in their favour in the intense competition for the Port star. Should Port match the free agency offer, the Dogs could well need to find draft capital by trading a player or players out. In May, Port coach Josh Carr had told this masthead that the Power would match a free agency bid and force a trade if he departed. But the landscape has shifted since then since Port have finished 15th, drawing an earlier compensation pick if they do not match. Of the many flow on effects from Butters’ call is that it might make it easier for Geelong to land St Kilda ruckman Rowan Marshall. The Cats are in the pole position to snare Toby Greene as an unrestricted free agent if he leaves the Giants. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Bring on the the Zak attack: The Cats’ semi-final showed they sorely need it



Butters’ decision is a bombshell move that will drastically shape this year’s trade period. The Port Adelaide star ended months of speculation about this future late last month when he confirmed he was heading back to Victoria. Butters told Port officials at his exit meeting that he would exercise his restricted free agency rights to join a Victorian team. Butters’ decision ended at least 18 months of speculation about his playing future. “I’ve made the decision to head home,” the 25-year-old said last month.



“It’s obviously been one that I’ve wrestled with for a while now, and it’s been quite tough to get to the bottom of it. It’s been a tough decision in my life, and one that I haven’t taken lightly. “I’m probably at a stage in my life where I’d like to get back around some family and friends, and enjoy some more time with them and cherish more moments with them. But in saying that, I’ve also really enjoyed my time at the footy club and here in Adelaide, and it’s felt like home for me as well.”

World.title: No need for midterm election emergency, says Trump’s ‘transparency’ aide
World.content:
Exclusive WorldNorth AmericaUS midterm elections No need for midterm election emergency, says Trump’s ‘transparency’ aide Michael Koziol September 12, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A
