Dallas: The man Donald Trump recruited to the White House to conduct a pre-election “government transparency” project says there is no need for an emergency declaration before the November 3 midterm elections, as prospects of the president attempting such a ploy diminish. John Solomon, a conservative media entrepreneur who became a special government employee in June, was behind the administration’s release of formerly classified documents in July purporting to show widespread election “meddling” by foreign countries and a cover-up by the “deep state”. John Solomon (left) was hired by the White House to run the “Government Transparency Taskforce”. Bloomberg Trump aired the claims in a primetme address to the nation, upon which MAGA operatives such as Steve Bannon openly called for the president to declare a national security emergency relating to the midterm elections, and predicted Trump would do so during the last week of August. That window has come and gone, and Solomon told this masthead there was no momentum for such a move. “I don’t get a sense that people are concerned about election security,” he said.



Solomon made the comments on the sidelines of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, and said he was speaking in his capacity as a journalist, not a government employee. He played down the prospects of Trump trying to call an emergency that could restrict mail-in voting or dispatch the National Guard to patrol polling stations, for example. Donald Trump and Solomon shake hands on July 16, the day of the president’s address about election integrity. Bloomberg “Nothing I’ve seen as a reporter indicates that that’s on the table right now. It could be,” Solomon said. “But there’s a lot of really valuable things that have happened to grow confidence in the election.” That included a request to allow states to use a Department of Homeland Security database to check voter information against federal citizenship and social security records.



The Trump administration has asked the conservative-majority Supreme Court to permit use of the tool. The courts are also weighing Trump’s attempts to restrict mail-in ballots through an executive order and a new directive by the US Postal Service, although time is running out. Solomon said: “The solutions that have been in place have seemed to grow confidence. But we’ll know on election day.” Trump’s former chief strategist Steve Bannon, who remains an influential MAGA voice. Bloomberg MAGA activists such Bannon and his fellow broadcaster on right-wing channel Real America’s Voice, Wayne Allyn Root, have been building the case for Trump to declare a national security emergency before the midterms, in an example of what Bannon refers to as shifting the Overton window of what is possible. “You will have enough evidence by mid-August to show that we have a massive problem,” Bannon told the masthead in July.

World.title: Academy alumni take to big stage together in Roosters finals tilt
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Academy alumni take to big stage together in Roosters finals tilt Chris Barrett September 12, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the block of units they called home as teenagers, Siua Wong, Robert Toia, Salesi Foketi and Benaiah Ioelu usually just ate with each other. But now and then, there was a high-powered guest list at the Sydney Roosters academy housing in Kingsford. Benaiah Ioelu, Robert Toia, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong have come through the ranks together. James Brickwood “At least once a month not only Nick [Politis] but the whole board would come over for dinner,” said back-rower Wong. “It was pretty cool having that relationship. A lot of us young boys moving from outside of Sydney coming in, hearing about the board, you feel a bit nervous. But for them to be so down to earth and express a lot of humility to get to know some of the young boys was something that I really loved.



“I think that’s one of the big values of this club, being a family club, and it definitely showed through that.” Several years after those evenings hosting club chairman Politis, and fellow directors such as Mark Bouris and Luke Ricketson, the quartet is in the big time as the Roosters’ semi-finals campaign gets going. Wong was the first graduate of the academy and made his NRL debut in 2023. Getty Images Wong, 23, Toia, 22, and Foketi, 20 are in the starting side for Sunday’s clash against minor premiers Penrith at CommBank Stadium. Ioelu, 22, is a reserve. Their appearance together at the pointy end of the season is validation of the Roosters’ decision to establish an academy in 2021 after visiting the facilities of Spanish football giants Barcelona FC.



Determined to produce more of their own, the eastern suburbs club can also count homegrown Roosters Hugo Savala, Victor Radley and Billy Smith in the line-up against the Panthers. The graduates emerged from a carefully designed program engineered by Politis and Roosters coach Trent Robinson and led by three-time premiership winners and one-club servants Mitchell Aubusson and Jake Friend. Foketi has made his mark on the edge for the Roosters in his second season in the top grade. Getty Images The grand plan is for the entire Roosters squad to eventually be comprised of players from their development system. “The dream is to one day have 17 players playing on the paddock that have come through our academy. So to have all those boys play on the weekend is great,” said Friend, a defence guru with the Roosters who was the academy’s inaugural head coach.



“We don’t have a big junior base obviously but with the guys we get, we want to breed long-term NRL players.” The former dummy-half said with potentially three teams joining the NRL over the next three seasons, it was even more important for clubs to grow their own and retain them. Toia makes a break against North Queensland in round 22. Getty Images Underpinning the Roosters’ approach is an attention to detail aimed at forging a lasting association with the tri-colours. From dinners with the board in the academy units, to nutrition advice from champion fullback Anthony Minichiello and one-on-one video sessions with Friend and Aubusson, now the Roosters rugby league director, the first batch of academy alumni learned from the best. “You look at the soccer academies, they’re a business in a sense. You develop a player and you get a transfer fee,” Friend said.



Related Article NRL 2026 ‘I love the Sharks’: From boyhood fan to Cronulla’s billionaire backer “You don’t get that in rugby league. They do have an ability to leave. But we’ve seen some guys probably have the opportunity to leave and stay. I think that’s got to do with the Roosters academy. We want to keep as many of them as we can.” Wong, who was scouted by the Roosters in Auckland at the age of 14 and has been a mainstay in Robinson’s side for the past two seasons, said on the eve of the finals his time in the academy was one of the best experiences of his life. “Nick, Aubbo and Jake Friend set up a great environment for us boys to develop and I think it’s shown through the footy players that we’ve been able to become,” he said. “It really instilled in me what it is to be a Rooster, and what that means on the field and off the field, and I feel like that’s so important for young players coming through.”



It also left a lasting mark on Toia, who has since become a Queensland State of Origin centre. “When we moved out was when we realised how great we had it,” he said. “Being there, you could tell how much the Roosters care.”

World.title: BBL sell-off plans will be on the right side of history
World.content:
SportCricketBig Bash Opinion BBL sell-off plans will be on the right side of history

Colin Smith September 12, 2026 — 9:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cricket NSW’s negative commentary on Big Bash League clubs privatisation plans suggests it will threaten the system, risks long-lasting impacts at all levels and endangers a model that is “the envy of the world.” While it is concerning rhetoric, it is also, on the evidence, not supported by facts and backs the wrong side of history. Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird defended the privitisation move for the Twenty20 franchises. George Chan Strip away the emotion, and Cricket Australia’s case for external investment in the clubs is straightforward and offers an exciting path that ensures global leadership in growing TV audiences (and hence media rights) and attendances. Critically, it also reinforces Test cricket. BBL and TV audiences have grown significantly following CA’s decision in 2023–24 to cut the BBL to 44 games.



However, fielding Australia’s centrally contracted stars in the league is a challenge. The salary pool intended to keep Australia’s best players at home has been increased from $1.9 million to more than $3 million per squad. That’s just to remain competitive with emerging leagues in South Africa and the United Arab Emirates — competitions that didn’t exist five years ago and can potentially outbid the BBL for Australian players. It helps to be clear about what “cricket” now includes because the debate is too often framed as T20 eroding the “real” game. The success of the Indian Premier League has given cricket financial security. AP It isn’t. Even the Board of Control for Cricket in India — an organisation with every incentive to focus on T20 — calls Test cricket “the bedrock of our game” and backs it with a financial incentive scheme for players who prioritise red-ball cricket. Modern cricket is a dual-format sport: Tests supply history and depth, and T20 provides the commercial engine that funds the lot. Since the Indian Premier League’s 2008 launch, T20 has grown.



Sixteen leagues operate worldwide, 87 nations entered qualification for the 2026 T20 World Cup cycle, and cricket (T20) will return to the Olympics in 2028 at Los Angeles after a 128-year absence. Not coincidentally, India is a favoured bidder for the 2036 Olympics. No comparably short, spectator-friendly format in any other sport has built anything like it. But none has become a standalone financial engine for its parent sport the way T20 funds cricket. A huge crowd celebrated 2014 IPL champions Kolkata Knight Riders in Kolkata, India. Getty That’s the opportunity NSW is arguing Australian cricket should avoid. The IPL is worth roughly $18.5 billion, built almost entirely on media rights.



Another perspective Investigation

Australian soccer How A-League’s biggest investor got a $140m get out of jail free card It sits within the world’s top 10 sports leagues by value and holds the sixth-highest sports broadcast rights value globally. IPL club owners have gone shopping abroad - Reliance, GMR, RPSG, Sun Group - because there’s only one Mumbai Indians licence at home. South Africa sold its entire domestic T20 competition to those same IPL groups in 2022 and has recorded broadcast growth of up to 47 per cent locally and 257 per cent in Indian media reach. England sold 49 per cent stakes in each of its eight franchises in The Hundred league for more than £500 million, keeping counties in majority control and ring-fencing 10 per cent for the grassroots. None of these boards let in outside capital out of desperation. They let it in because they could see where T20’s value was heading and who controlled the playbook to get there.



In all cases, these countries own their T20 leagues, with investors and shareholders in the clubs. NSW’s counter-argument is that its model works — the Sixers and Thunder are “successful and healthy,” profits are reinvested, and participation among 5-to-12-year-olds is up 80 per cent. All true, but this sidesteps the question of whether a wholly state-owned model can fund an escalating global talent-salary war for the next decade. In Australia, there are four sports leagues that are “must-haves” and “must-broadcast” - the NRL, AFL, Australian Open tennis and cricket (Test and BBL). There are genuine governance lessons here. The A-Leagues took private equity money in 2021 while individual clubs slid towards insolvency. But the lesson isn’t “don’t sell” — it’s “don’t sell vaguely”.



Editor's pick Australian cricket Sell off the BBL, or sell out to sports betting: Cricket’s huge call Money without a mechanism to enforce disciplined use just buys time, not a turnaround. The ECB’s Hundred sale is that template because it embeds discipline: tiered distribution, a grassroots share, and spending guardrails for the counties. None of this makes privatisation risk-free, or Cricket Australia’s process above reproach — NSW’s complaint is that four conditions agreed by all state chairs in June went unmet before the CA Board pressed ahead. But a complaint about process isn’t a case against the substance, and on the substance the global evidence is clear: leagues combining private capital for the BBL clubs only with disciplined guardrails are growing broadcast value and building the star power that keeps players and crowds in the BBL, not lost overseas. Cricket Australia chair Mike Baird and CEO Todd Greenberg address the media pack in Sydney this week. Getty Images



Importantly, investing in the BBL clubs ensures that the exciting growth and professionalisation of women’s BBL continue – as is happening with WPL in India. Cricket NSW built the two most successful clubs in the competition’s history. It should be shaping this conversation from a position of strength, rather than resisting it. With the likely sale of the Melbourne Renegades to external investors, NSW will be the sole owner of two clubs in the BBL. Furthermore, there is no example globally across leading sports leagues of a single owner of two clubs in the same league. Colin Smith of Global Media and Sports has spent two decades advising the world’s biggest sports and media rights holders and broadcasters on sports media rights, including cricket media rights and design models for the BBL.

World.title: ‘It’s the Wild West’: How a shaken Sydney is grappling with the gang war
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney's ganglands ‘It’s the Wild West’: How a shaken Sydney is grappling with the gang war Mostafa Rachwani September 12, 2026 — 9:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ahmad Hraichie has buried many gangsters in his time as a Muslim undertaker. He’s buried small time runners, heads of crime families and everyone in between. He knows death and its sudden movements well. But even he is shaken by the escalating gangland violence in western Sydney. Muslim undertaker Ahmad Hraichie says the community is “frustrated” at inaction on gang violence. Sitthixay Ditthavong “There were rules before: you don’t shoot innocent people, you don’t shoot kids or women, you don’t shoot at funerals,” he says. “It’s wild now, there are no rules.” “Yeah, it’s gangsters, but gangsters once had ethics and morals and integrity. They’d help an old lady on the street.



“Now it’s brazen, it’s lawless, like the Wild West.” Hraichie is speaking at the Muslim morgue under Lakemba Mosque where Louis Meehan was washed and prepared for burial on Saturday, as per the strict Islamic protocols on death. A body must be washed, wrapped in a white shroud, prayed over and buried as soon as possible, part of a broader Islamic belief in death being a transition from life to the afterlife. Delays are seen as holding the soul back from moving to the next phase of existence. Meehan was shot dead behind his boxing gym in the Punchbowl Community Centre car park on Wednesday night, as community members and school students watched on.



He died under a hail of gunfire from an assailant who fled in a silver Lexus. Police believe the attack is linked to organised crime in western Sydney. Meehan had posted photos online wearing merchandise linked to the Alameddine crime gang, which is locked in a murderous war with rival gang the Coconut Cartel. Meehan’s killing was the third in a little over a week. University student Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed in Glen Alpine on Tuesday last week. The next day, Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot in the doorway of a Merrylands West home. Two men were arrested on Friday in connection with that shooting, including an alleged drone operator. In the two years to June, 19 people died amid escalating violence, a Herald analysis found, including 100 shootings and 52 firebombings. The violence has coalesced into a haze that hangs over western Sydney, a dread looming over a region that has known violence before but not like this. “It’s getting worse, and it is driven by many factors, including the intoxicating draw of social media and the internet,” Hraichie says. “It’s brazen now. People are doing it in the middle of the day, and part of that is the internet.



“The world has become so fast and people are struggling. And to these kids, it’s all about the lifestyle, the haircuts, the cars, the money. It’s all about living in this moment, right now, no future. “It’s an alien world,” he says, shaking his head. Like many in western Sydney, Hraichie has seen different eras of gang violence break out. There were the gangland wars of the 1980s, the postcode wars of the late 2010s, the feud between the Hamzy and Alameddine families. Muslim undertaker Ahmad Hraichie says gang violence is a “cancer”. Sitthixay Ditthavong With a regional robustness charged by generations of migrants from wartorn backgrounds who won’t be shaken by much, the violence remained for a while as cultural background noise, shrugged at and ignored.



But it has since spilled out into community spaces, into daylight, and into the cultural consciousness with brazen acts. As more innocent people die than ever before, Hraichie says frustration is growing at a lack of action from authorities. “There isn’t fear, there’s frustration,” he says. “I don’t think fear is part of the equation or vocabulary for these parts. But people are frustrated: why haven’t these guys been stopped?” That sense of frustration hardly abated when acting Assistant Police Commissioner Grant Taylor said on Thursday that gangland shootings were “part and parcel of life in a big metropolis”. “It always looks like crime is out of control but, when you look at it, we’re on track,” Taylor said.



“We always have about eight organised crime murders a year. We’ve had six, and then last night made seven. It’s always going to be part and parcel of life in a big metropolis; this is no different.” The comments were swiftly shot down by Premier Chris Minns, who said the violence was shocking and the community “shouldn’t have to put up with” it. Related Article Exclusive

NSW State Parliament Gangland violence threatens Labor’s grip on outer Sydney “I’d hate it for anyone to believe that we’re accepting of the status quo, or we believe that it’s normal, or that it’s acceptable, or that we just have to turn a blind eye,” Minns said. “I don’t think any premier or any political leader can ever make the claim or promise that murder will stop in a big state like NSW, but we can promise arrests, and we can promise longer jail time for the people who are involved.”



Criminologist Dr Vincent Hurley, who spent 23 years as a NSW Police detective, said that if the violence was not curbed soon, it could start to have lasting cultural consequences. “The names that they adopt almost set in train this narrative that tarnishes the rest of the community,” he said. Related Article Editorial

Crime Authorities must get their acts together on organised-crime killings The Herald's View Editorial “I think the frustration is that it seems to be every day, all day, and that’s probably not the case. And I think they find it frustrating because people stereotype them. It wears them down over time, and people can’t break away from their surname, from their culture.” Hurley warned that without urgent intervention, communities could become insular and pull away from the rest of Sydney, culturally and economically.



“They’re going to bunker down and become very protective of themselves, and it’ll be us versus them, even if they’re not involved in any type of crime,” he said. “Just by the mere fact of stereotyping, it’s going to have a massive effect on kids at school, who then want to go out and get a job; they probably won’t leave that geographic area. These areas will become siloed. “Ultimately, I really feel sorry for the community members of these cultural groups because they have no control over the narrative.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Tom Lynagh is Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Can he be a saviour, too?
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion Tom Lynagh is Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Can he be a saviour, too? Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter September 12, 2026 — 7:52am

September 12, 2026 — 7:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There won’t be a huge audience for the opening game of Super Rugby AUS early on Saturday afternoon, when Queensland host the Western Force at Ballymore. But those rugby-hungry types who do tune into Stan Sport will be watching intently – and none more so than Wallabies coach Les Kiss, who has problems to resolve before naming an updated squad on Monday for Tests against the Springboks and the All Blacks. Loading He’ll be assessing whether Jock Campbell is worth recalling to replace Tom Wright, and he’ll keep tabs on Zac Lomax’s return from injury, in the fascinating position of No.13 for the Force. But mostly Kiss will be on his couch studying the men duelling in the No.10 jerseys: Tom Lynagh and Harry McLaughlin-Phillips.



Some fingers may be crossed. The Wallabies need another five-eighth to join the squad after Carter Gordon broke his leg in Mendoza. Carter Gordon (R) broke his leg Test against the Pumas in Mendoza. Getty Images Ben Donaldson and Declan Meredith are in the squad, but both have failed to claim the No.10 jersey this year, so filling Gordon’s vacancy isn’t necessarily just for a third-cab-off-the-rank player. It could be for the top job, if the right man stands up. Setting aside the experienced options of James O’Connor and Bernard Foley – who haven’t trained in a team environment for a few months – and Japan-based Noah Lolesio, who is not available in October under regulation 9, the here-and-now candidates boil down to Lynagh, McLaughlin-Phillips and Tane Edmed.



The latter played 10 Tests last year but is now down the pecking order behind Meredith, Donaldson and McLaughlin-Phillips, who was also called into the Wallabies squad last month ahead of him. But McLaughlin-Phillips, a running No.10, is a developing youngster you’d select as a third cab. Lynagh is not, and if he can prove his fitness, the Reds playmaker has the class to not only return to the Wallabies but to become the assertive game controller the side badly needs. Tom Lynagh has had a nightmare run of injuries with the Wallabies and Reds. Getty Images But all of that comes with a very big if. Hence, the crossed fingers. Lynagh has played just 17 minutes this year, after suffering a string of soft-tissue injuries dating back to this time last year, when he tore a hamstring playing for the Wallabies against Argentina.



Lynagh was not considered for the spring tour so that he could have an off-season to get stronger and more physically resilient. It didn’t have the desired effect. Lynagh suffered repeated tears of the soleus (lower calf) muscle throughout the Super Rugby season. Wallabies five-eighth Tom Lynagh pictured in Coogee last year. Dion Georgopoulos The long absence, combined with a lack of public information about Lynagh’s status, saw the odd conspiracy theory pop up, including that he didn’t even want to play rugby. They were all wrong – Lynagh re-signing with Queensland in May was proof of his desire – but as Reds coach, Kiss played the long-game and put Lynagh on a go-slow conditioning plan to build sufficient resilience in his body to get through full games, and full seasons. Lynagh put on five kilograms of muscle, but again, it didn’t fix the problems.



As the months dragged on, Lynagh suffered multiple setbacks with the injured calf, each time re-setting the comeback clock. Brilliant and brittle in equal parts, Lynagh is now Australian rugby’s biggest enigma. Though he is extremely tough in games and doesn’t shirk contact – as seen in the Lions series – Lynagh has also became known as a flighty trainer, who is hyper-aware of any tweak or injury niggle he feels in his body. One theory at Ballymore is that Lynagh’s past life as a schoolboy cricketer may have contributed to a propensity for back tightness.



Whatever the reason, a wary Lynagh often sat out sessions and could not complete a full week of training. Given Joe Schmidt rigidly demands as much to be selected, the blond No.10 fell out of the Wallabies reckoning. Edmed, a no-frills but durable type, was called up, and Gordon was also poached back from league (only to also start picking up injuries). This year, the Wallabies’ long-standing problem at No.10 hasn’t gone away. If anything, it has become more acute. Harry McLaughlin-Phillips trained with the Wallabies in Perth in July. Getty Images The Wallabies’ forwards have improved hugely but the backline’s work - and game management in particular - has gone the other way. Ryan Lonergan has been outstanding at halfback but the work of several options at No.10 has been B-grade. The Wallabies’ ability to exit their half via the boot has been mostly dire this year, and the game direction has gone from mediocre to muddled as Tests have worn on.



It comes with a very obvious fitness caveat, but Lynagh at his best presents as the solution: a tough, long-kicking five-eighth, with a strong voice and the heads-up composure to run a game. Related Article NRL 2026 PNG Chiefs in war over name as NZ Rugby threatens legal action So getting Lynagh back on the field and keeping him there is the name of the game. If any coach can do it, it’d be Kiss, who managed him effectively in the first half of 2025. If Kiss can get Lynagh back into that same shape and mindset, the 23-year-old could be a key factor in the Wallabies’ campaign at the Rugby World Cup. “I’m really enjoying Tom in a playmaker role and a decision-maker within the team,” new Reds coach Vern Cotter said this week. “He’s got a great head on his shoulders. He sees the game well. He’s calm and decisive, so I’m looking forward to having him run the game for us.”



Just to be “careful”, Cotter said he’ll give Lynagh 40 minutes at Ballymore and then everyone will wait and see how he pulls up. There may be crossed fingers.

World.title: Trump welcomed to Ireland with trash-covered double
World.content:
Donald Trump's satirical double has beaten him to Dublin, as Ireland prepares to welcome the US president.

'The Trash Talker' by Wexford artist TinKicker depicts Trump emerging from a wheelie rubbish bin, covered in trash. He is posing with his post-assassination campaign fist-pump.

Images of the artwork went viral when it first appeared at CAN-AL Fest in St Mullins last month. It is now on display at the Teal House Gallery in Dublin.

The US president's visit this weekend has sparked one of the biggest security and policing operations ever undertaken by the Republic of Ireland.

He is expected to touch down on Air Force One at Dublin Airport on Saturday night (NZ time). During his two-day visit, he will visit Ireland's President Catherine Connolly at her official residence and Irish Prime Minister (Taoiseach) Michael Martin at Farmleigh House, the republic's official state guest house located inside Dublin's Phoenix Park.

World.title: One dead after house fire on Matakana Island in Bay of Plenty
World.content:
One person has died in a house fire on Matakana Island in the Bay of Plenty.

Fire and Emergency Northern Shift Manager Garreth Lewis said crews from Matakana Island, Omokoroa, Greerton, and Te Puke were called to the fire at about 4am on Saturday morning.

He said the fire was well involved upon arrival, about 10 metres by 15 metres in size.

A police spokesperson confirmed they were at the scene on Saturday morning

They said one person was being treated for burns, but wouldn't confirm if there had been any fatalities.

World.title: Explainer: Why is this flu season so bad?
World.content:
Explainer - A sharp spike in flu cases has come late in the season this year, adding to the pressure the health system is under already.

Dr Hannah Cooper, a public health physician in the health intelligence team at PHF Science, told RNZ there were a few different ways of defining a "bad" flu season.

This season was bad because a lot of people were getting flu at once - but there was no conclusive data yet to show this particular strain was making people sicker than in previous years.

What's making this flu season so bad?

Officially, flu season in New Zealand runs from May to October.

The virus causes symptoms like a fever, runny nose, cough or upset stomach, and there are many different types or strains circulating each year.

Each flu season is influenced by the one before. Last year, we saw the emergence of a strain of flu known as "Super-K".

How bad is this flu season? Afternoons Download MP3 9m

It peaked late, causing an extended flu season that means people have retained some immunity from last year's infection further into this year.

But because the season has peaked later in the year, the immunity boost those of us who got the flu vaccine gained at the start of winter has worn off a bit, leaving us more vulnerable.

Cold weather can't give you the flu, but it can make it spread faster.

Dr Hannah Cooper Supplied

According to Cooper, the cold snap felt around the country in early August would have increased transmission.

That's around the point when ambulance callouts began peaking, too, to reach an all-time high the week of 10 August.

Viruses spread more easily in cold weather, as low temperatures and dry air help viruses survive longer, while weakening your body's natural defenses at the same time.

People also spend more time inside when it's cold, sharing poorly ventilated air, which increases the chance of infection.

This, plus patchy vaccine uptake, aided transmission in the community.

As of 6 September, 1,256,766 people had received the flu vaccine - less than a quarter of the population - most of them in May.

Supplied

Even though the H3 subclade, the dominant strain this year, was around last year, New Zealanders still seemed broadly susceptible to it, Cooper said.

That said, the vaccine appeared to be a good match. Cooper stressed flu vaccines were better at reducing serious illness than preventing infection, so the high numbers of flu didn't necessarily mean this vaccine wasn't as effective.

So far, the data showed the dominant strain of flu appearing in hospitals was one that was covered by the vaccine.

How does this flu season stack up compared to those in the past?

That question, Cooper said, was very hard to answer.

Flu cases had been tallied using different methods over the years.

These days, it was done by the SARI method - that is, those presenting with Severe Acute Respiratory Infection - in the Auckland region, as a representative snapshot of the wider population.

Supplied

"I don't think that anyone would be able to say how this year compares to say 20, 30 years ago."

The country's population dynamic was also changing over time, in terms of size and co-morbidities and age structure. That meant the impact of a bad flu season in terms of pressure on hospitals in 2026 was probably quite different than it might have been in previous decades, Cooper said.

How much pressure is it putting on hospitals?

The effect of a large number of flu cases at once is hitting harder this year because the health system is already overwhelmed.

Health NZ put on more staff to ease pressure of the winter season, but clinicians in EDs in particular have said they're still overwhelmed by demand.

RNZ has previously reported hospitals were overflowing well before flu cases reached their peak, according to Health NZ data.

The occupancy rates of eight hospitals at 8am over eight days from 7 to 14 August showed most had more patients than staffed beds.

World.title: Why am I paying to withdraw my KiwiSaver? - Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

I recently found out that it can cost $300 per person in lawyer fees to withdraw KiwiSaver funds for a deposit on a house. The funds we deposit are taxed before they go in the fund, we pay fees to the fund manager, and tax on the interest, then fees to withdraw. I guess you can say we get a government contribution and employer contribution but even so it is not as good a deal for worker as the original scheme was, and it is locked in.

First, I do have sympathy for the argument that we don't have enough incentives to get people investing in KiwiSaver in New Zealand. Lots of other countries offer tax breaks that can make saving for the future a lot more appealing.

But that aside, on your point about first-home withdrawals from KiwiSaver, lawyers usually handle a lot of the process of the application, and receive the money in their trust account before it's paid out to the vendor.

They charge for their time in doing this. Sometimes, they bundle the cost of this into the overall cost of conveyancing for the purchase. The first-home withdrawal bit is usually quite small in comparison to the rest of the bill. I asked my lawyers about this and was told that they charge $325 including GST for an application.

This is specific to a first-home withdrawal, you wouldn't be paying fees for taking your money out when you are 65, for instance.

When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

I am retired since 2024 and IRD has recalculated my PIR at 10.5 percent. I was on 28 percent prior to the update. My partner is still working and on a 28 percent PIR. All our investments are held jointly. What will happen at tax time with the two different PIR?

It seems that this will depend on the type of investment you have. For things like term deposits and direct shares, you'll have an ownership split, usually 50/50, and you'll be each taxed on your proportion of the income, interest, gains and so on, at your own PIR.

But if you have a jointly held portfolio investment entity (PIE) investment, you'll be taxed on that one at the higher of your two PIR rates.

In 15 months' time I would like to retire. I am presently with an active manager KiwiSaver provider, paying high fees. However, having looked into fees and availability I'm seriously considering transferring to a passive index provider. Is it advisable, given looming retirement, to change to passive investment with overall lower fees or stay with an active manager with higher fees and moderate funds? I have a substantial amount in my KiwiSaver account and presently not making substantial gains given past down turns.

I was at an event this week where someone asked me the same question - is it better to be in a cheaper KiwiSaver fund, when you're retired and potentially not making contributions to KiwiSaver any more?

I can't give personalised financial advice, but here are some general thoughts. I would tend to say that people should not move provider simply for the fees, although they are one of the few things that are actually in our control as investors.

I can understand why, if your balance, isn't growing as much through contributions, you might be particularly keen to make sure that it's not being eroded by higher fees.

If it were me, I would compare after-fee returns over a number of years from a range of providers to get a sense of whether there are better options elsewhere.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub recently conducted some research that showed what made the difference to outcomes was really the type of fund people were in, not the provider they chose or, overall, the fees they were paying.

On that basis, I would suggest the most important thing to do is to make sure that you have a good understanding of your risk profile and time horizon, and that your invsetment fund choices align with that. A year or so before retirement is a good time to get some personalised advice, if possible, to come up with a strategy to make your money last through retirement.

World.title: Thousands of households and businesses lose internet in West Auckland
World.content:
More than 3000 households and businesses in West Auckland lost internet on Saturday morning.

A Chorus spokesperson confirmed a network outage was affecting 3100 customers in and around Swanson and Massey.

They said technicians were on site, investigating the cause and working to resolve the issue.

According to updates on Chorus's outages map, technicians had identified a fibre cut location.

World.title: Former Auckland mayor Len Brown 'singing and dancing' ahead of first CRL ride
World.content:
Len Brown on his loop finally opening Saturday Morning Download MP3 17m

After years of disruption, Auckland's City Rail Link (CRL) is finally opening on Sunday morning.

Former Auckland Mayor Len Brown was one of the infrastructure project's progenitors, with his lobbying for central government support one of the dominoes that had to fall before Auckland could cut the ribbon on its shiniest new toy.

A day ahead of the historic first ride, Brown told RNZ's Saturday Morning he would be there "singing and dancing" to celebrate the opening of the country's biggest-ever infrastructure project, 10 years in the making.

He said it could not have been done without the formation of the super city, to stop Auckland's various former councils "arguing themselves into stasis".

"The one thing that I think we did right with the CRL and in Auckland and the super city was I was adamant that when you make a decision about this stuff, stick to the plan - don't relitigate it, don't doubt yourself. 'This is what we're doing. Here's what we're going to have to pay. Here's the way we're funding it. This is the outcome we're looking for'.

"Believe your analysis and the data that you are basing your decisions on, and then go for it."

The idea for a rail tunnel through central Auckland was first raised in the 1910s. New Zealand had a well-used tram system, but in the 1950s and '60s instead opted to invest in roads and motorways.

"In the wisdom of the decision-makers at that time, they decided trams were passe, we're going to become like a city like Los Angeles. We're going to build our city around motorways," Brown explained. "And so that's literally what happened. Trams gone, motorways all over the place."

Another plan in the 1970s was derailed by the Muldoon government, which also favoured more roads.

"With the benefit of the luxury of being able to look backwards from that point to this, what became really obvious to city leaders and urban planners and transport planners was that the more roads you built in a fast-growing city, the more congested the place got. And that was what happened to Auckland."

Len Brown at the formal ground breaking for the City Rail Link Project with Auckland Transport chair Lester Levy, left, Prime Minister John Key and the Transport Minister Simon Bridges. Supplied / Auckland Council

When Brown campaigned for mayor in 2010, he said the public repeatedly told him they were sick of gridlock and wanted the CRL built - they were sick of the city being a "laughing stock".

Planning for the CRL started in the late 2000s, accelerated in 2013 when the government signalled its support, and the blueprints became a physical reality in 2016 when Auckland Council - then led by Brown - convinced the government to go halves in paying for it.

"I wanna say to your listeners, to New Zealanders generally, thank you for funding half the cost of this. this massive piece of kit."

Brown said he had "reasonable confidence that the government was going to come on board at an appropriate time and support the project", but acknowledged it was a "pretty courageous decision".

"But I felt we had to show good faith by putting skin in the game, that we recognised that it was going to be a struggle at that time for the country at large. And that we really believe this, we were totally committed to it. And as Aucklanders, you stick us together united, we can do anything. And so, that was the mantra."

The initial projected cost of $3.4 billion rose over time to $5.5b. Part of that was a design change pushed by then-Mayor Phil Goff to future-proof the network by building for nine-car trains, which the city doesn't have yet but might need in the future.

Other cost rises were blamed on inflation, Covid-19 lockdowns and staffing issues.

But Brown said cost rises like those experienced by the CRL shouldn't put communities off pursuing other large projects.

A train arrives in one of Auckland's new stations on Friday, at the official opening ceremony. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

"The one thing I will say is that my hope and expectation is really, from a small country, that we really do everything we possibly can to put in place an agreed and clear pipeline of work for what's important to build our city and the country in terms of its infrastructure and by and large stick to the plan."

Brown expected the CRL to unleash Auckland's true potential.

"I think what's most important is that the city's economy, its social life, its culture has been pretty severely constrained by its inability to get around. And, that's the reason why so many people have sort of said, 'gridlocked Auckland'.

"And I think if you have options and choices and you have less congestion on your roads, more people using public transport… if we can get public transport use in trains, buses, ferries, micro transport use up to 30 percent, 35 percent rather than the present sort of 15 percent to 20 percent that it is, that will just lighten the load on the roads. It will make the roads more available to commercial traffic.

"A fully integrated system is one that basically opens the lifeblood of the city and takes the stress off people, and makes the transport around the community a much more enjoyable option.

"I mean, I've taken the train lots over the last 10 years. And it's, look, it's relaxing. Sometimes it's a bit crowded. It's meditative. You can do your homework, you can do your work, you can read books, you know, do whatever. It's a much, much more relaxing way of getting to and from work.

"People just get so stressed out in gridlock. You know, it's a terrible thing. And they're not arriving at work or wherever they're going in a good state at all."

World.title: Tonga netball confident ahead of World Cup qualifier on home soil
World.content:
By Talaia Mika, RNZ Pacific correspondent

Five strong teams are in Tonga to compete for a spot in the World Cup Qualifiers including Tonga, who finds confidence from their home soil as they prepare to host the tournament next week.

It's a double celebration for Tonga next week, given it's their first time playing on their home soil and being able to host the Qualifiers at the same time.

Despite this, Tonga Netball Association chief executive Salote Sisifa said Tonga is confident of securing one of two remaining spots at next year's Netball World Cup in Sydney when the Pacific qualifier gets underway on home soil next week.

Sisifa, who is also president of Oceania Netball, said the experience has provided valuable lessons for the team heading into the qualifier.

"Tonga came out 9th place out of 12 top teams that were participating. And we take the learnings off that. Tonga was of course the only team from Pacific there."

The tournament in Tonga will feature five Pacific teams competing for two World Cup places, with Fiji, Samoa, Cook Islands, Papua New Guinea and Tonga all taking part.

Tonga enters the tournament after competing at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow six weeks ago, where the side made its debut and finished ninth out of 12 teams.

Tonga Netball Association chief executive Salote Sisifa Talaia Mika

Sisifa said Samoa and Fiji are likely to pose the biggest challenges based on world rankings, but she does not believe rankings tell the full story.

"If I have to be honest, in terms of ranking wise, the biggest challenge would be Samoa and then Fiji of course. And they are the next two right after Tonga in terms of ranking."

"But having said that, I don't feel at times that these world rankings really do justice in terms, and the score even, in terms of the performances of the teams. Because every team is an underdog."

She said Tonga will treat every match as a major challenge and will not take any opponent lightly.

"So going into this competition, every team is a high team for Tonga, the way we look at it and the preparations full on from Game 1 to Game 4, not leaving anything behind."

Tonga is currently ranked seventh in the world and enters the tournament as the highest-ranked team among the five Pacific nations.

Sisifa said the team is determined not only to qualify for Sydney but also to reinforce its position among the world's top 10.

"We're at number seven in the world. And, you know, we need to and we have to solidify our place as being in the top ten of world netball coming into this competition."

She said Tonga has remained in the world's top 10 for the past three years.

"It's only right that, yes, backing our team, we have sat at top ten for the last three years and coming in as the highest ranking."

Despite the confidence, preparing the squad presents its own challenges.

The players and management are spread across three countries and nine different states, with the team often having less than a week together in camp before a major competition.

Sisifa said that means the team relies heavily on the players' discipline, honesty and commitment to maintaining their fitness when they are apart.

"We highly rely on the honesty of players and their self-discipline to maintain themselves."

She also credits the coaching staff for keeping in regular contact with players and monitoring their fitness while they are based overseas.

"I have to give it to the players, their honesty, their discipline, looking after each other and themselves when they're not together and coming together."

For Sisifa, the make-up of the team also highlights a wider challenge facing netball in Tonga and across Oceania.

No members of the current Team Tonga squad live in Tonga, with the players coming from the Tongan diaspora in New Zealand and Australia.

Sisifa said Oceania Netball and Tonga need to work towards narrowing the gap between local players and the high-performance level required to compete internationally.

"What we're trying at the moment, and it's a challenge for Oceania and Tonga included, is trying to bridge the gap between local talent and high performance."

She said the tournament will also give young people in Tonga the opportunity to see elite netball played at home.

Sisifa is encouraging supporters from Tonga and the wider Pacific diaspora to attend the tournament and get behind their teams.

World.title: Country Life: Ōtaki, the small town aiming for carbon neutrality
World.content:
Drew Mackenzie cuts a small figure nestled among the roots of a giant kahikatea growing in remnant ancient forest on the outskirts of Ōtaki.

But she's part of a big vision for a circle of forests like this around the town, creating a carbon sink which it's hoped will make the community carbon-neutral.

She and husband Anthony Ryan, owners of Makahuri, which includes 20 hectares of mature forest and new plantings, were among the first landowners to sign up to the Ōtaki Carbon Forest Project which started in 2023.

So far 35 landowners have committed at least half a hectare of their property towards 32 hectares of new permanent native plantings by 2030, project lead Dianne Buchan told Country Life.

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Seventeen hectares have been planted up so far, with the project providing affordable saplings, volunteers and advice, Buchan said.

"It's a circle around Ōtaki, so we go up to the Tararuas, obviously, and then down to South Manakau Road.

"People have come to us and said, 'can we be part of the carbon forest?'.

"But they're too far away and I think if we don't have a tight boundary, we're going to end up planting trees in Auckland that we can't really count as offsetting carbon in Ōtaki."

Dianne Buchan (c) who leads the Ōtaki Carbon Forest Project with some of the projects volunteers with seedlings RNZ/Sally Round

The project is part of Energise Ōtaki, a community-driven charitable trust set up 20 years ago to make the town more energy efficient.

The charity owns a solar farm to power the town's waste water plant and returns earnings back to the community, and several energy efficiency projects including a curtain bank and repair shop.

The carbon forest project aims to absorb emissions which can't be saved through other means.

Community-led projects "touching all different parts of society" have proved successful for the town, Energise Ōtaki chair Leigh Ramsey said.

Leigh Ramsay, chair of Energise Ōtaki RNZ/Sally Round

"If you expect the government to change things fast, you're dreaming because [...] it's like turning a container ship, it takes kilometres and kilometres where a community can just swing the waka pretty quickly."

"Once [projects] get going you tend to find you sort of grow momentum and then others come on board and before you know it you've got the MPs all lining up to come and see us."

It's estimated Ōtaki and its surrounds with about 12,000 people, emit 60,000 tonnes of CO2 equivalent a year, Ramsey said.

After 50 years, 32 hectares of native forest could remove about 56,000 tonnes, according to the Tāne's Tree Trust carbon calculator.

Rhian Salmon (R) with husband Andy Whittaker with daughter Georgia RNZ/Sally Round

The sense of scale and time involved in carbon offsetting surprised Rhian Salmon, who has also committed land to the project, which she and husband Andy Whittaker own in the Ōtaki Gorge.

They have been planting "hundreds" of trees to replace old pine forest on their land.

As Associate Professor at the Centre for Science in Society at Victoria University of Wellington, Te Herenga Waka, Salmon was also involved in another tree planting project - an experiment looking into carbon sequestration from the average-sized community planting.

The results of that "really threw" her.

"The seven-year mark is an interesting one, so just imagine 800 trees growing for seven years - that amount of carbon will offset either myself flying on my own to London and back or driving from Ōtaki to Wellington for a year, and that blew me away.

"I just felt it made me realise the time component of it."

Nevertheless, it was the aspiration that was important, she said.

"I just love that it brings people together.

"I think we've got a goal, and I think there's a vision and we can just keep aiming for that, and there are some big areas of land around here that are being replanted, and they'll make a big difference."

Cam Butler looks out over new plantings, part of the Ōtaki Carbon Forest Project RNZ/Sally Round

Ōtaki Community Board chair Cam Butler has also committed land for the project.

He said it brought joy, provided a pathway for birds and set an example to other small towns.

"Also just the sheer concept of carving up a useful farm for lifestyle blocks, which don't really add to the economy or the productivity of the place, didn't sit particularly well with us.

"We always said we would never buy a lifestyle block and yep, here we are with one, and so this is our way of turning this smaller, non-useful block into something that's useful for the environment."

Buchan, the project lead, said the carbon forest project also created a sense of community.

At least 40 volunteers regularly helped nurture the seedlings, planted them and met regularly.

Students at Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Te Rito, a Māori immersion school in Otaki, have helped plant out the hill behind the school.

Teacher Patsy Matheson and daughter Amaia check out the newly planted trees at their school Te Kura Kaupapa Maori o te Rito in Ōtaki RNZ/Sally Round

Amaia reads among new plants on the hillside at her school which is part the Otaki Carbon Forest Project Supplied

"We have big planting days, and whānau come in and we have kuia planting next to their moko and usually the moko giving directions," teacher and parent Patsy Matheson said.

"We are here to re-cloak Papatūānuku and bring back the mauri of this puke, but it's also like the connections that we make with each other and the wider kura whānau is just an awesome by-product of that as well."

Butler said to get good results you had to have grand plans.

"You've got to, you know, shoot for the stars and if you miss you might still hit the moon.

"And so, with trying to do that with Ōtaki, that sets an example for the rest of the country to say, hey, this can be done, other small towns, you can do this. It's not impossible."

New plantings above Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Te Rito, the town of Ōtaki in the distance RNZ/Sally Round

World.title: Zverev powers into US Open final ahead of all-American semi
World.content:
Alexander Zverev knows what it's like to endure a long wait for a grand slam title. Now the delay's over for him, he wants to keep the drought going for American men's tennis.

Zverev will play for his second major title this year after beating Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (9-7), 7-6 (8-6) in the US Open semifinals.

Zverev will play on Monday morning (AEST) against number eight seed Ben Shelton or number 11 Frances Tiafoe, who meet this morning for the right to become the American man playing for the title. Both have been semifinalists at Flushing Meadows but neither has reached a major final.

The US is still seeking its first men's grand slam champion since Andy Roddick won in New York in 2003.

"Hopefully I can not make the American dream come true," Zverev said.

Zverev, who had long been considered the best men's player without a major, finally broke through at the French Open this year. The German followed by reaching the Wimbledon final, which he lost to Jannik Sinner, and is 24-2 in grand slam matches this season.

"Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I've had a lot of struggles at the major level. I was so close so many times and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court," Zverev said.

Now he will try to win the title that he still can't believe he let get away in 2020. Zverev won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem but then lost in a fifth-set tiebreaker, as Thiem became the first man to win the US Open title after dropping the first two sets since 1949.

Zverev was solid after going up two sets this time, and has won 13 consecutive sets after becoming the first number one-seeded man to play five-setters in each of the first two rounds of a major.

Khachanov was trying to reach his first major final after a surprising run in New York. He arrived with a losing record for the season but went on to reach his third grand slam semifinal, including second at the US Open.

He started playing better after dropping the first set and then falling behind 2-0 in the second. He finally broke Zverev's serve to tie it and it stayed even until they went to the tiebreaker. The Russian erased Zverev's first two set points in it before Zverev finished it off by winning a 34-shot rally.

Khachanov then had leads of 3-0 and 5-2 in the third-set tiebreaker before Zverev battled back.

The Shelton-Tiafoe matchup, pitting two fan favourites on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, was the clear main event on semifinal day. Ticket prices were available at surprisingly low figures for the match-up between Zverev and Khachanov, who was bidding to become the lowest-ranked US Open finalist since the ATP rankings began in 1973.

His level in the final two sets probably would have been good enough to beat Zverev early in the tournament. The number one seed at a major for the first time after Sinner pulled out with a knee injury, Zverev had to go the distance against Lorenzo Sonego and Quentin Halys in his first two rounds, spending nearly nine and a half hours on the court.

He said he and his team laughed about how poorly he was playing after the second match.

"That kind of sense of humour, it helped me," Zverev said.

"Moving forward, I was playing much better tennis. Obviously I have improved a little bit. Otherwise, I wouldn't be in the US Open final."

World.title: Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second
World.content:
Nicola Olyslagers has had the best bad night of her career after missing out on becoming a new 'Ultimate' athletics high jump champion, only to learn to her surprise that she had still leapt to the biggest payday of her life.

Australia's world champion only managed to clear 1.95m on the first night of World Athletics' inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest this morning (AEST).

She struggled with her approach on a difficult surface on a cold night as Ukraine's Olympic champ Yaroslava Mahuchikh beat her to the title with a 1.99m leap.

Olyslagers' runner-up spot earned her $US75,000 ($105,000) — $5,000 more than she pocketed for winning the world title last year — as part of the record $US10 million ($14 million) prize pot for the streamlined new event that World Athletics hopes will attract a host of new fans.

Only when speaking to reporters afterwards did Olyslagers realise just what she would be taking home.

Nicola Olyslagers clears the bar on her way to second in the high jump. (Getty Images: Christel Saneh/World Athletics)

"What? Really? I genuinely thought it was just first prize got the 150k and second was like 10,000," she said.

"You are the bearer of good news. That's fantastic."

Olyslagers, wrapped in a scarf and still shivering 40 minutes after her event, said she struggled with her approach on a firm-surface run-up but, with more than half the field exiting early, she realised that after two fails at 1.95 a clearance would be enough for second place.

She duly sailed over at the final attempt, punching the air in delight.

"That's the happiest I've ever been after a 1.95. I think I celebrated as if I'd won the whole competition and it was a really good jump," she said.

"It just showed tonight that all of us were a little bit tired but I mean, that 95 jump, I'm still living off that."

Olyslagers' domestic rival Eleanor Patterson also looked uncomfortable all evening but took joint third with a modest clearance of 1.91 a week after she'd jumped 10cm higher to win the Diamond League crown.

"It's the lowest I've jumped all year. Really, really frustrating," Commonwealth champ Patterson said.

"After the best season of my life I really wanted to enjoy it but I didn't really."

Marschall fourth as Duplantis stars again

Meanwhile, triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall managed only fourth with a best of 5.95m as Swedish superstar Armand Duplantis again revelled in being the star attraction, having seen the event open with a theme song he had both co-written and performed.

With the title secure after a faultless run to 6.20m, the spellbound full house of 20,000 willed him to clear a world record 6.32, but he narrowly failed in what would have been a remarkable 16th world best in six years.

Earlier, Australia's Ky Robinson gave it a real go in the 5,000m, leading at the bell, but got swallowed up in the run for home as Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen roared back to his best with a superbly-judged victory charge.

Sarah Billings ran well in her 800m semi-final to qualify for tomorrow's final when there will be four more Australians in action.

Abbey Caldwell and Jess Hull will go in the women's 1,500m, Mackenzie Little in the javelin and Oceania record holder Lachlan Kennedy in the men's 100m.
